item.title: [Business of Sport] Chelsea, LA Lakers & Mark Walter’s Crumbling Empire
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正崩塌的不是体育帝国，而是"资产错配"的金融炼金术

表面上这是一个体育大亨被迫抛售球队的故事，但真正的戏剧发生在保险业的资产负债表深处。Walter 玩的是一场极其古典的游戏——用"长期负债"（保险浮存金）去撬动"低流动性、高波动性"的另类资产（体育特许经营权）。这与巴菲特用 GEICO 的浮存金去买可口可乐股票是同一个模板，区别只在于：巴菲特买的是可以在纳斯达克两秒钟内变现的蓝筹股，而 Walter 买的是需要联盟批准、六个月尽调、买家池不超过 20 人的球队股权。

一个让人意外的观察：这场"帝国崩塌"其实揭示了体育资产估值体系里一个从未被公开讨论的悖论——湖人 48 小时内以 125 亿美元成交，恰恰说明了顶级体育资产已经流动性化（liquidified）到了传统金融市场都难以匹敌的程度。也就是说，Walter 之所以能被"逼卖"，反而是因为他持有的资产比想象中更值钱、更容易脱手。流动性诅咒（liquidity curse）——资产越好卖，反而越容易被监管者盯上，因为它可以随时被要求"变现证明"。

二、跨领域连接：这是 2008 年 AIG 剧本的"体育版重演"

播客里 Charlie 和 Nick 讨论的"超敞口"（overexposure）逻辑，其实和 2008 年 AIG 事件的底层结构完全同构。AIG 用保险牌照去承销 CDS，把保险浮存金间接押注到了次贷市场；Walter 用 Guggenheim 系的保险资金间接押注到了体育特许经营权。两者的共同 DNA 是：用被监管资本的"信用溢价"去获取未被监管资产的"增长溢价"，中间的差价就是所谓的"帝国"。

这就带出了一个反直觉的推论——顶级体育资本市场其实是全球最后一个"影子银行"栖息地。为什么？因为它同时满足三个条件：估值高度不透明、买家群体极小、且被主流监管框架视为"另类资产"而非金融资产。这也解释了为什么最近十年，冲入体育行业的钱越来越像"保险+PE+主权基金"的混合体，而不是过去那种"富豪个人玩票"的钱。Walter 只是第一个被点名的，不会是最后一个。

三、切尔西的"隐藏结构性利好"：多头治军的终结可能是复辟的开始

Nick 那段关于"足球俱乐部内部政治"的观察其实极其重要，但被埋在了对话末尾。他指出俱乐部内部往往会形成"Team Boehly / Team Clearlake"这样的暗线派系——这在组织行为学上叫做"股东寻租式派系化"（shareholder-induced factionalism），是所有多头股东制企业最深的病。

一个非常规的跨领域连接：切尔西现在的五体育总监架构，本质上和文艺复兴时期意大利城邦的"多头执政"（如佛罗伦萨的九人团）是同一个组织病理——分权的目的是防止篡权，但代价是每个决策都被内部政治稀释。而现在如果 Walter 和 Boehly 被迫退出，Clearlake 变成单一主导权方，切尔西反而可能进入类似美第奇家族独裁后的黄金时代——决策链条打通、球探系统统一、教练权威归位。

因此，这里有一个非常反直觉的判断：Mark Walter 的金融事故，可能成为切尔西竞技层面复兴的意外催化剂。球迷此刻最该关心的不是"我们的球队要被卖了吗"，而是"我们能不能因此终于摆脱五头马车"。历史上，重大金融危机导致的股东出清，往往比精心策划的战略并购更能治愈一家公司的组织病——因为前者是被迫的、干净的、不留妥协的。

最后一个隐藏洞察：请注意 Josh Kushner 和 Bob Iger 的组合接盘湖人这件事。Iger 本来在看维加斯扩张球队——这意味着 NBA 内部对"下一个体育娱乐超级IP"的地理迁移（洛杉矶→拉斯维加斯）已经有共识。Walter 的仓促退出，恰好让 Iger 提前锁定了"旧王座"而不是"新王座"，这在长期看未必是买家的胜利。卖家的被迫退出，未必意味着买家的战略胜利——尤其当买家自己也在追赶下一个范式转换时。

📝 转录文本

引子：Mark Walter 是谁？

Charlie, should we take a look and move into the crazy world of Mark Walter, the LA Lakers, the empire that seems to be crumbling from a sports perspective? Um, the potential impact that it has on Chelsea FC — because this is probably one of the biggest sports business stories in a very, very long time.

I tell you what, let's just start off by explaining who Mark Walter is, because he won't be a name that's necessarily all that familiar to European and Australasian sports fans.

Mark Walter is a very successful financial services tycoon from the US, and he co-founded a financial services business called Guggenheim Partners back in — I actually remember it happening, so I knew some people who were doing it with him back in the late 1990s, early 2000s, talking about 25 years ago. And he's in his mid-60s now, so he wasn't even — you know, he was 40 years old when he founded what has gone on to become an enormously successful fund, basically asset manager, huge amounts of assets under management.

He himself has effectively got his shares in Guggenheim, and that's held in an entity called TWWG, where he also has holdings in other companies that he has acquired interests in along the way, including — inter alia — insurance businesses, and including sports businesses. And he has been successful in most everything that he has done. You know, the insurance business has been a very good business to be in over the last 25 years.

体育帝国的构建：从道奇队到湖人队

And on the sports side, he — together with a guy who he had as an underling of his at Guggenheim around the turn of the century, a man known as Todd Boehly. Then Boehly left Guggenheim Partners, but with Walter's blessing, and still has very close friends, to start doing his own things. But they came together to get into sport when they bought the Dodgers.

It is broadly considered that since buying the Dodgers, they have done an outstanding job with the Dodgers. And more recently, they formed part of the new ownership group that took over Chelsea. Now, 5 years ago, Charlie, is that right?

2022, wasn't it?

Yeah, four years ago. Okay, so four years ago. And even more recently, they bought the LA Lakers, the basketball team, for an absolutely colossal $10 billion a couple of years ago.

So what you're looking at here is a massively expanding sports empire where you got the LA Dodgers, you got the LA Lakers, you've got — between those two and their friend Hans Weiss — they've got almost 40% of Chelsea and therefore of Strasbourg through BlueCo. So you've got this extraordinary successful-looking portfolio of businesses that runs from stakes in Guggenheim, a massive asset management company, to stakes in insurers, to stakes in blue-chip sports businesses across the world in some of the biggest sports in the world.

帝国崩塌：保险资金的"超敞口"问题

And suddenly it now looks like the empire might be coming crashing down. And by the empire I do mean particularly his sports empire, because what has happened here — it is alleged and said — is that effectively part of his engine for buying these massive stakes in these hugely valuable sports franchises has come through financing provided by insurance businesses that he also controls.

Now, you might say, well, so what? If he controls those businesses, then why shouldn't he use money from those businesses to buy sports stakes in sports enterprises? Well, the answer is: insurance is a highly regulated form of financial services for the obvious reason, which is that if you have an insurance premium with an insurance firm, you need to know and expect that in the event that that premium needs to be activated into a payout, that that payout can and will be made.

So insurance businesses have to be very clear about where it is that they put their money, and they have to be doubly clear when that money is being put into entities which have the same ownership as the insurance business — because no one wants to be in a situation where money which should be being used to fund payouts on insurance premiums down the track has been, let's say, siphoned off and used in ways which people weren't really aware of.

Um, now the SEC —

Well, it's overexposure. So it's overexposure, sorry, is the key bit there. So you are actually allowed to do that, as you said, but generally the regulation would cap it at about 10%. So that if an individual who owned lots of these businesses had something happened to them, and let's say their business empire collapsed, all of the businesses around it would be impacted by that. And if 40%, which is what the rumored number here that Mark Walter has exposed it to has happened, then that is a serious overexposure, and therefore breaking the rules and regulations that exist around this.

Exactly that. And the critical thing there is about the transparency, right — which is that you have to declare what it is that you're investing the money in in order that people can then say, "Okay, that's 10%." Right? If it then subsequently becomes clear that not everything has been declared in that way, and that the actual number isn't 10% but it's 40%, then you've got a problem from a regulatory perspective. And that is what the SEC — which is the US's financial regulatory authority, and enormously powerful and scary, frankly — has been investigating.

Walter 的应对：主动回购与资产变现

Now whether the SEC does or does not end up bringing a case, or if there is any proof of wrongdoing whatever it might be, at this point we can't know and we don't know. All we do know is that Mark Walter has decided, for whatever reason, that he is going to start replacing money that had been sourced from his insurance company with his own cash, right now.

Whether that's an admission of guilt on the one hand, or on the other hand, it might be him saying, "I don't even want to go down that track of getting into a fight with the SEC. I just want to make sure that we're totally, absolutely fine here, because I don't want to spend the rest of my life fighting lawsuits against the financial regulators." It could be either.

But the reality is what he started to do is liquidate his positions in sports entities in order to fund the cash that had been provided to buy those sports entities by the insurance businesses.

湖人交易：史上最大体育资产转让

Right, so — and here's where the rubber hits the road, right, Charlie? Which is: first of all, the Lakers were sold last week. Having bought them for $10 billion two years ago, he's now flipped the Lakers for $12 billion US to a consortium headed by who else than our recent friend Joshua Kushner, who had previously been readying to buy FIFA Ford Enterprises from his mate Gianni Infantino.

So that's brought in a big chunk of change for Walter to help to start the process of paying down the gap between what is allowable and what's not allowable under, as you say, the exposure rules within the insurance industry.

And it is now strongly rumored within the media that Mark Walter and his business partner Todd Boehly are entering discussions, let's say, about selling their stake in BlueCo, the owners of Chelsea, to their partners at Clearlake.

$20 billion is what he reportedly needs to earn by the end of the year.

Look, I mean the $12.5 billion that he just sold the Lakers for — it made me laugh, Charlie. I mean, look, we know what it's like doing deals. A $12.5 billion deal done in 48 hours suggests that there's something going on behind the scenes that isn't quite right. I mean that is — for the biggest, let's be clear as well — that is the biggest sports transaction involving an asset in history. And it was when the Lakers were bought last time. And a $2.5 billion profit on that transaction does look good, but make no mistake: when Walter bought the Lakers, he would have wanted a far greater return. There would have been greater ambitions for this. He was in the middle of a serious business project behind the scenes that would have improved the Lakers' value exponentially even beyond this if he could have held on to it for a bit longer. That was always the plan.

Bob Iger as well, who's joined Kushner on this, who's the former CEO of Disney — they were actually looking at an expansion franchise and were talking through a Las Vegas opportunity when this came up. Obviously, I think if you get the chance to buy into this, it's hugely appealing. Hence why probably the deal was done so quickly as well.

切尔西的估值困境

But the key thing from Walter's side is: yes, it fixes a significant part of the problem, but he's still got a lot more to raise. Now you mentioned Chelsea. He owns 12.8% of Chelsea, equal to Todd Boehly, equal to Hans Weiss. The Telegraph reported a £5 billion valuation on the club to sell those shares. Clearlake reportedly are interested in buying these shares.

As you'd expect, there's been tension at the Chelsea ownership level, very publicly reported for a very long time. So Clearlake could look at this and go, "Oh, you know, can we get these shares at a steal?" On the flip side, if they buy them too cheap, then is it valuing the club far below potentially where they have bought it for and then invested money into? And will that impact the club's valuation moving forward when clearly get to the stage, as we've discussed previously, where they will have to look at how they exit the club?

So, let's say they bought the shares off Walter for about £3 billion, which I think from discussions in the market is where the financial experts have positioned the club and said that you'd be able to justify that. They own 12%. So it means their stake is worth about 400 million, let's say.

Each.

Each, right?

Each. Yeah. But, you know, again, Boehly's is Boehly's money, I think. So, Walter needs this money to pay his problems, unless Boehly's tied up in this — which I don't think he is.

You know, it doesn't help. So, Walter can get 400 million at a £3 billion valuation, but £5 billion, right? So let's say that would be 700 million just under for Walter's stake. That's a billion dollars. So that's 1/12 of what he makes. So then let's say he's done $12.5 billion — that's taking up to $13.5 billion. If he's going to use sports assets as his premium way of generating this cash, the only way it looks like he's going to be able to do that is by selling the Dodgers, which you mentioned has been a success story.

道奇队的可能出售

I mean, I think it is one of the big success stories. They bought it, interestingly, off the McCourt family — who, you may remember, as the Marseille owners from conversations we've had previously — when McCourt got into a bit of financial distress in 2012.

And the professional show jumping league, Charlie, remember —

And the professional show jumping league. They bought it for $2.15 billion, I think, in 2012, and it's now valued at over $8 billion. 8 billion would clear the 20 billion mark if all of that money is going to Walter's pocket.

So does it mean much for Chelsea? Does it mean much for Walter if he sells Chelsea? His biggest plays here are selling his American assets, and I don't think it actually really changes much for Chelsea at all, because operationally I don't think they have been hugely involved, and Walter's always done everything behind the scenes.

深度分析：BlueCo 的债务结构与估值

Let me make some observations. So first of all, even if let's say that you did place a valuation on Chelsea of 5 billion, you would have to take into account the borrowing at BlueCo level. So in other words, that borrowing is set against all of their equity, not just Clearlake's equity. That is BlueCo borrowing, and that's believed to be about 1.5 billion.

So let's just say that you say, okay, the club's valued at five but has debt of one and a half. Then the equity valuation, the valuation of the equity in that, is 3.5. And therefore Boehly and Walter and Hans Weiss's share of that 3.5 is, let's say, 1.3, right? And as you say, therefore his share of that is a few hundred million.

I'll be interested to see if Walter and Boehly are as dissociated as you suggest. My instinct is that their links run very, very, very deep in financing terms. The fact that they're involved in all of these deals together, the fact that they work together for so long and have been involved 10, 12 years ago in slightly similar controversies around insurance funding and all this kind of stuff — I would be quite surprised to see Walter sell out of BlueCo, but Boehly stay in. I think that this will be a moment. I think it could just be Boehly's opportunity to get his money.

Yeah.

I think it could be Boehly's opportunity to just get out.

Clearlake 的战略窗口

I think this could be — not even an opportunity — I suspect that Clearlake might well say, "Right, if you guys want to get out, we'll buy you out. If you don't, then we won't." But you know what we're not going to do is pick off every time that one individual of you says, "I don't fancy anymore." We're not going to keep on sort of picking you off. Let's do it in one proper go.

As to your point about setting a valuation on the club, I'm not sure if I was Clearlake that I would worry about that too much, because I think I would hope that the market would recognize that my minority shareholders were in a weak position, and that therefore whatever valuation they were afforded does not necessarily indicate the overall value of the majority shareholding in the club.

And you've just mentioned how in the space of a couple of years, despite having done absolutely nothing with the Lakers yet, the valuation's gone from 10 to 12.5. Now, we've already discussed before that Clearlake aren't going to be looking to get out of Chelsea until 2031, that sort of time. So we're still four to five years away from exit. So I would have thought this is actually quite a good moment for Clearlake to put the squeeze on Boehly, Walter, and co. and say, "Right, guys, you know, this is the moment. You need out — you know, here you go, here's some money. Now, we're now in full control."

对切尔西运营层面的潜在影响

In terms of what that means operationally at Chelsea, I think it might have a slightly bigger impact than one might think. I think I've said before on this podcast that when you've got turmoil behind the scenes amongst investor bases and ownership bases, it tends to have effects within the club that aren't easily seen from a fan perspective. You tend to find that senior executives within the club attach themselves to one side or the other side. And there tend to be, you know, sort of team — let's say in this case Team Clearlake and Team Boehly.

We've mentioned there are five sporting directors, and what you'll probably find is that one of those sporting directors is a bit close to Todd and one of them is a bit closer to Egbali, and so on and so forth. I'm not saying I know that to be the case — this is an observation on how football clubs work in general.

So I'm a great believer that football clubs benefit from having a clearly identifiable source of authority and power within a club, who everyone then knows: if that person or that entity speaks, then it's — that's argument finished. That is then what is happening. And that then clears up a lot of the office politics and the internal sort of wranglings that go on in the meantime.

So I think it would be to Chelsea's benefit if at this point Boehly and Walter — I can't speak for Hans Weiss and his situation — but if those guys were to exit at this point, I think it would give the project a better chance of success going forward, because it's been quite clear for some time that that relationship between Boehly and Egbali have become dysfunctional.

结语：年底前的时间窗口

I expect things are going to move quite quickly on this one, because as you say, Mark Walter needs to raise all this money by December of this year to prevent it becoming a broader issue. So, you know, let's see what happens, and we can sort of, you know, keep people up to date as we go along. At the moment, it's still quite, you know, relatively early.

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Machine Learning Is a Much “Shallower” Field Than Math - Ryan Greenblatt
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"浅"不是贬义，而是ML能被AI自动化的根本原因

Greenblatt 说 ML 是"浅"领域，很多人会本能地把这理解为智力上的降级。但真正颠覆性的观察是：正是这种"浅"，使得 ML 反而比数学更容易被 AI 自我加速。

一个必须长期沉浸才能理解的抽象（如群论、同调代数），恰恰因为它需要"深度封装的直觉"才能操作，反而是 AI 短期内难以复刻的；而 scaling laws 这种"三句话讲完"的浅概念，因为其表面性，反倒可以被无数并行 agent 在实验循环里疯狂爬山。

换句话说：ML 之所以是第一个被 AI 反噬的学科，恰恰因为它不够深。 深度是护城河，浅度是加速器——这两者在同一学科中不可兼得。

二、隐藏的悖论：真正难以自动化的，不是深奥理论，而是"脏活里的品味"

这是整段对话中最反直觉的洞见。人们默认："AI 追不上人类是因为缺乏爱因斯坦式的洞察"。但 Greenblatt 反其道而行：AI 在 ML 里追不上顶尖研究者，不是因为缺少 deep insight，而是缺少那种"在超参数、日志和 CUDA 报错之间摸爬滚打养出来的肌肉记忆"——他称之为 "munging intuition"。

这里藏着一个跨领域连接——波兰尼的 tacit knowledge（隐性知识）：一个人可以骑自行车却无法把骑自行车的动作写成方程。ML 研究里 90% 的进步依赖这种隐性知识，而隐性知识的定义就是"无法被显式表达，因此难以被 next-token prediction 学到"。

于是我们得到一个漂亮的反转：深奥的数学理论（可显式化）比"脏活的品味"（不可显式化）更容易被 AI 复制。这与所有人的直觉都相反。

三、跨领域连接：ML 正在经历"炼金术→化学"的历史转折

Greenblatt 预言 2030 年低垂果实将被摘光。这让我想到一个鲜有人做的类比：当前 ML 处于化学史上 1750–1789 年之间——已经不是纯炼金术，但离门捷列夫的元素周期表还差一次范式革命。

  • 炼金术（1600 前）= 早期神经网络时代，配方靠玄学
  • 拉瓦锡时代（1780s）= scaling laws 出现，第一次有可预测的定律
  • 门捷列夫时代（尚未到来）= 尚未出现的、能解释"为什么某种架构一定 work"的深层结构理论

Greenblatt 的隐含预言其实是：2030 年之后的 ML 需要从"配方型科学"跃迁到"结构型科学"——而这一步在化学史里花了整整一百年。

更惊人的是，这个类比暗示了一件事：如果 ML 迟迟不出现自己的"门捷列夫时刻"，那么它可能永远不是一门科学，而是一种进化生物学式的"研究实践"——只能不断试出 what works，无法先验推导。这也许才是 Greenblatt 真正想说但没说出口的话：AI 研究的未来，可能更像育种师，而不是理论物理学家。

📝 转录文本

一、担忧：AI 尚未产生真正的"新理论"

One concern I have is: I think even in mathematics, as far as I'm aware, we have not seen very impressive new theory. We've seen a lot of impressive verifiable specific results — for example, find a counter-example to this conjecture — but we have not seen "come up with the idea of topology" kinds of levels of things, or come up with things like group theory.

And it seems like ML research has elements of both of these things, but the less verifiable thing of "come up with new ways of thinking about the problem" would be harder to induce.

二、Scaling Laws 作为例子：验证回路的长度问题

Take, for example, the idea of scaling laws. Obviously there is some end verification loop such that you can train GPT-4 better if you have the idea of scaling laws from like 2020. But there is a longer and potentially more compute-laden road to getting to inducing AIs to be like: "Okay, I got to think carefully about how I should be scaling my parameters and data. What are different kinds of investigations I could run to understand this? Maybe I can come up with the visualization in like an isoflop analysis or something."

But that does seem hard — that does seem like a longer verification loop than just "hey, let's get nanoGPT loss to go down."

三、回应：AI 已经能做"婴儿版新理论"

Yeah, let's talk about this.

So first of all, I think in the context of math, the thing I would say is that the AIs can do the equivalent of like "baby's first new theory" or whatever — where, for example, they can just prove interesting conjectures via making connections and producing new understanding of like: "Oh, there's this thing that AI — this construction AI — found which is pretty interesting," or "found this way of thinking about the problem that's a bit different."

And we do just see that. It's just that the examples we see are not as impressive as founding the field of group theory.

Yeah. But like, in part, you know, probably founding the field of group theory is one of — you know, it's like among the best, biggest mathematical accomplishments of all time — and the AIs just aren't, you know, they're not that good at math yet. And I think that from my perspective, there's a continuum between that and the things we're seeing now, that the AIs are continuing to march up.

四、核心论点：ML 相对于数学是一个"浅"领域

Second, I think ML is a very shallow domain relative to math. So I think in math there was much more of a "you find some true deep abstraction," and then if you really understand that thing — which is hard to understand — then you get somewhere.

Whereas I feel like the things that are the equivalent of that in ML are really dumb. Like — I'm like — scaling laws — like, come on guys, we can explain scaling laws really quickly. And I think the deepest and most important concepts in math, for example, don't have the property of "you can really understand the underlying thing and why it matters in a very short period of time."

五、2030 预言：低垂果实被摘光之后

But I feel like one effect will be that we will have gotten rid of all the low-hanging fruits by 2030. Like, I feel like scaling laws will have been in like what — math history — you know, finding the Cartesian grid and doing very basic mathematics was. And then eventually you want to keep making progress in the 2030s — it's going to be like doing whatever is happening at the frontiers of mathematics right now.

六、结构性差异：数学/物理 vs. ML 及其他领域

Yeah, that could be right.

My sense is that just like some domains are structurally different in terms of how they operate and how much they depend on sort of deep abstractions. And physics and math are much more on the side of being very far on the "very deep, hard to come up with ideas" side, whereas I think ML and most other domains are much more amenable to sort of hill-climbing. And that's my sense of how this will go in the future.

七、2030 年之后：真正的瓶颈不是"深刻洞见"，而是"实战品味"

And even in the regime where your AIs are like, you know, having to plow — like it's 2030, they need to — a bunch of low-hanging fruit and research has already happened, they need to make further progress — I still suspect that a bunch of the work will live more on the side of building increasingly complicated infrastructure, having really good intuition about what the experiments roughly look like.

And so I think I'm probably less sympathetic to the thing that "the AIs will lack is some deep insight," and more sympathetic to: they really need a bunch of taste about in-the-weeds experiments that they currently don't have, and need to have a bunch of intuition for what sorts of training approach would work and what wouldn't work, in ways that current researchers have.

八、案例：Chain-of-Thought RL 本可以更早出现

And even in cases where there's been some breakthrough in AI, oftentimes in retrospect it looks like a big bottleneck to making that breakthrough happen was sort of getting all of the micro details and munging intuition right.

Like, an example of this is when it comes to training AIs to be good at reasoning and chain-of-thought, and doing sort of RL and chain-of-thought training. It looks like you probably could have done RL and chain-of-thought on like GPT-3 and gotten kind of interesting results on math if you had really scaled it up and done a good job. But at the time there was low-hanging fruit, and also doing a good job with that training is kind of in the weeds on all the technical implementation and scaling it up and getting the hyperparameters right.

And so maybe you can demonstrate everything on like Qwen 1B or whatever, and get some sense that this whole thing is going to work — but people didn't demonstrate it as early as they could have because, you know, of all of these other munchy details and intuition about exactly how to tune the parameters and how to set things up.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.description:
## 一、"浅"不是贬义，而是ML能被AI自动化的根本原因
Greenblatt 说 ML 是"浅"领域，很多人会本能地把这理解为智力上的降级。但真正颠覆性的观察是：**正是这种"浅"，使得 ML 反而比数学更容易被 AI 自我加速**。
一个必须长期沉浸才能理解的抽象（如群论、同调代数），恰恰因为它需要"深度封装的直觉"才能操作，反而是 AI 短期内难以复刻的；而 scaling laws 这种"三句话讲完"的浅概念，因为其表面性，反倒可以被无数并行 agent 在实验循环里疯狂爬山。
**换句话说：ML 之所以是第一个被 AI 反噬的学科，恰恰因为它不够深。** 深度是护城河，浅度是加速器——这两者在同一学科中不可兼得。
## 二、隐藏的悖论：真正难以自动化的，不是深奥理论，而是"脏活里的品味"
这是整段对话中最反直觉的洞见。人们默认："AI 追不上人类是因为缺乏爱因斯坦式的洞察"。但 Greenblatt 反其道而行：AI 在 ML 里追不上顶尖研究者，不是因为缺少 deep insight，而是**缺少那种"在超参数、日志和 CUDA 报错之间摸爬滚打养出来的肌肉记忆

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on John Danaher: He creates champions | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、看似讲柔术，实则在讲"垄断性系统"的运行机制

Khabib表面上在夸John Danaher"制造冠军"，但真正被他点破的是一个反直觉的商业与组织真相：冠军不是被"训练"出来的，而是被"筛选留下"的。他明确说——进入那个"黑房间"的人很多，但绝大多数在一年半到两年内心理崩溃离开，"没人记得他们"。

这与硅谷顶级基金（如YC）、海豹突击队BUD/S、以及少林寺武僧堂的机制完全同构：这些系统的核心产品不是"训练"，而是"淘汰"。它们的竞争优势来自于"允许极高的失败率"——一个不敢让80%的人离开的组织，永远造不出冠军。这里有个让人不适的洞见：Danaher系统的"善"，恰恰建立在它对大多数人的"残忍"之上。

二、Khabib无意间透露了一个被现代人系统性遗忘的哲学：肉体的痛苦是治理能力的先决条件

注意他说了一句极其古怪的话——"2000年前，这样的人可以轻易统治整座城市"。这句话乍听是即兴发挥，但其实是整段访谈里最锋利的一刀。

他在暗示：古代精英选拔的底层逻辑是"通过身体苦难验证决策资格"——罗马将军、蒙古大汗、日本武士、斯巴达执政官，全都遵循这个规则。而现代社会切断了"身体承受力"与"治理权力"的联系，把它替换成了"信息处理能力"（考试、简历、KPI）。

跨领域连接：这正解释了为什么当代很多成就极高的CEO都痴迷于极限运动、马拉松、冥想禁食、冰浴——他们在潜意识里试图重建被现代性抹除的那条古老资格线。Khabib说的不是训练，是"权力合法性的身体基础"。

3、真正让人意外的观察："忠诚于痛苦"比"热爱训练"更能预测顶级成就

Khabib反复用"fanatical"（狂热）这个词，但你若细读，他描述的不是"热爱格斗"的狂热，而是对"不舒适的状态本身"保持狂热的能力——他说的是"stay there for a long time, endure"（长时间待在那里，忍受）。

这里藏着一个反鸡汤的真相："热爱你所做的事"这个流行叙事其实是错的。冠军不是因为爱训练所以留下来，而是因为培养了"与不舒适共处的亲密关系"——这是一种反常的、几乎是病理性的能力。

跨领域映射极其鲜明： - 写作：真正的作家不是"爱写作"，而是能忍受"面对空白页的羞辱感" - 创业：连续创业者不是"爱创业"，而是对"不确定性"上瘾 - 修行：禅宗坐禅的核心不是"入定"，而是"与腿疼共坐"

所以Danaher真正的秘密不是柔术技术，而是他构建了一个让"忍受"变得有意义的意义系统——这才是所有伟大教练、导师、宗教领袖、军事将领的共同技艺：他们不是教技能，而是重新分配了痛苦的语义。

📝 转录文本

关于 John Danaher 的训练体系

Well, look, I'm training with John Danaher. And they train like that too. They train three times a day. And it actually feels right this way.

I mean, of course, this is how you have to train.

冠军工厂：不是一两个，而是全部

— 'Cause of that, John has one of the best...

— Yeah, he makes champions.

— ...students in the world, and after all, they don't just take some random place. I mean, they're not somewhere in the middle. They're at the top, and look at their whole approach.

Some people... Look, a person with that kind of approach just can't be somewhere in the middle. It's impossible. If you have a fanatical attitude, the right attitude toward the training process, on top of that, you have to be fanatical about it. You love what you do, and in the end, there will be results.

Well, just look at John and look where his guys are. He creates champions. He finds a champion in everyone, across every category, right?

— He creates champions, not just one or two, but all of them. He finds a champion in everyone, across every category.

"黑房间"：一个系统如何筛选出冠军

— Look, the people who come to him, he has a system, let's say, right? Under this roof, under his roof, there is a system. People come here, and they become champions in this system.

So there are people there who are champions. These are specific established names. And there are other people who came and left. They entered that black room, so to say, an uncomfortable place. They went in, stood for a year, a year and a half or two, and left. Nobody talks about them.

These are the people who came in, broke mentally, and left, and there aren't just a few of them. There are a lot. Usually, most people give up. There are many who give up, but then there are the ones who come in and stay there for a long time. Long, long time.

And after some time, they achieve success. They become the best. They prove to themselves that once they enter the system, they could stay there for a long time, endure, and become the best.

从格斗场到治国之才

They prove that they are already capable of many things. They can be trusted to supervise big, important projects.

I would even say, for example, 2,000 years ago, they could easily rule entire cities. So a person who has gone through it physically, who has lived through it, who has faced challenges, passed the tests, they are capable of a lot, highly capable.

You don't just walk into martial arts and become the best. It's very difficult. It means that you go through pain, you make sacrifices, you give your time, you face setbacks and failures in training. The mental strength and capacity mean a lot there.

顶级学校的真正门槛：十年起步

And when I talk about his system, look, I mean those schools that became the best, let's say, in football or in freestyle wrestling or, let's say, in MMA, in grappling, or in judo.

It's really hard to enter one of the best schools in the world, to stay when they are breaking you, throwing you, choking you, to improve as a person and as an athlete, and to become a champion.

It takes at least 12 years, 10 to 12 years, maybe 15. For some, it took longer. And to get through the grind for these 15 years and then to break through and become the best is worth a lot.

item.title: [Latent Space] Simulating Humanity: from Generative Agents to 8 Billion Digital Twins — Joon Sung Park, Simile AI
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"逆莫拉维克悖论"：为什么"变笨"比"变聪明"难得多

June 反复强调一个反直觉的技术定位——Simile 的模型必须"as dumb as I am"（和我一样蠢）。这是一个几乎被整个 AI 行业遗漏的洞察：前沿模型（GPT、Claude）是在 Mercor 之类平台上用职业程序员、科学家的顶级推理数据训练出来的"超理性机器"，它们越强，越无法模拟一个真实的人在星期二晚上点披萨时的懒惰、偏见和情绪化。

这其实是莫拉维克悖论的镜像版：机器人做不了三岁小孩的动作，同理，超理性 LLM 也无法犯正常人那种"明知会后悔却还是点了甜筒"的错误。整个行业都在往"更聪明"的方向 scale，而 Simile 在悄悄地朝反方向做 scaling law——这是当前 AI 版图里唯一朝"人类愚蠢"方向扩张的严肃项目。

二、隐藏的产业依赖链：所有"个人助理"公司都在暗中押注 Simile 成功

June 提到那个"第二名"的时间机器候选——个性化 agent。他随口一句话透露了一个巨大的战略判断：没有精确的人类模型，就不可能有真正的个人助理。凤梨披萨的例子看似小，但推论惊人——ChatGPT Memory、Claude 的 markdown 用户文件、所有 AI wearable、每一个"AI copilot"，本质上都在用穷人版的行为建模来临时对付这个问题。

跨领域连接：这就像 1960 年代操作系统对编译器的依赖——你以为你在造应用，其实你在等一个更底层的抽象成熟。如果 Simile 的"行为基础模型"真的做出来了，它会变成一个所有 consumer AI 都必须付费调用的"人类物理引擎"，就像 GPU 之于图形、Stripe 之于支付。这是一个还没被 VC 定价的、隐藏的 platform layer。

三、社会科学的复现危机，意外地为 AI 造出了完美语料库

最让人拍案的伏笔藏在 OSF（Open Science Foundation）那一段。社会科学界过去十年因为 p-hacking 陷入"复现危机"，逼出了"预注册研究"制度——研究者必须在做实验之前公开假设。这个为了拯救科学严谨性的补丁，居然无意中为 AI 造出了地球上最干净的"因果机制"训练集：数万个高质量 RCT，带假设、带干预、带反事实。

这里的跨领域讽刺极其精彩：社会科学的失败催生了 AI 的解药。它类比于中世纪炼金术士为化学准备了纯度极高的试剂——他们本意不是这个，但历史选择了这份副产品。

四、painter/fractal 隐喻背后的深层世界观

June 的画家背景不是简历彩蛋，而是他整个技术哲学的密码。他说"最好的画从不完美，它只突出关键本质"——这解释了为什么 Simile 不追求预测未来（那是股票模型的活），而追求揭示走向未来的每一步。这正是 Asimov《基业》中心理史学的核心：不是"帝国会崩溃"，而是"把科学家流放到 Terminus"这种反直觉的具体步骤。

跨领域的意外连接：Schelling 1971 年那个红点蓝点的隔离模型，其实就是最早的 Generative Agents 论文——两者相隔 52 年，用同一个方法（简单规则 + 涌现）研究同一个东西（人类群体行为），只是从"红点"升级到了"有 markdown 记忆的 LLM"。而 Schelling 靠这个拿了诺奖。June 在悄悄告诉你他要什么。

五、被低估的观察：Facebook > LinkedIn 的数据学

被问到"如果只能拿一个平台数据"时他选 Facebook——不是 Twitter，不是 LinkedIn。理由是"人在 LinkedIn 戴着职业面具、在 Twitter 演一个人设、只有 Facebook 是 default state"。这直接对应社会学家 Goffman 的戏剧论自我呈现理论：数据的价值和"表演成分"成反比。

这句话对整个 AI 数据行业是个重击：Reddit、X、GitHub 这些被高价采购的"高质量语料"其实是表演性最强的，而真正有价值的"基态人类"数据反而被 Meta 独占且从未真正对齐外部。下一个真正的 data moat 也许不在文本质量，而在"表演系数最低"的语料上。

📝 转录文本

开场：8 billion digital twins 的愿景

Joon: Can we create a simulation of 8 billion people living on earth? I think that's quite interesting and that really is the vision. And once you get to that kind of state, the kind of questions that you can help answer for the society also start to change. From my perspective, for me it's questions like: can we help solve climate change?

If you look at climate change as a problem space, this is what social scientists would often call the "wicked problems" problem — where you have many actors with competing incentives trying to make a very complex coordination decision. Can simulation help us solve that?

主持人开场白

Before we get into today's episode, I just have a small message for listeners. Thank you. We would not be able to bring you the AI engineering, science, and entertainment content that you so clearly want if you didn't choose to also click in and tune into our content.

We've been approached by sponsors on an almost daily basis. But fortunately, enough of you actually subscribe to us to keep all this sustainable without ads, and we want to keep it that way. But I just have one favor to ask all of you: the single most powerful, completely free thing you can do is to click that subscribe button. It's the only thing I'll ever ask of you. And it means absolutely everything to me and my team that works so hard to bring the Inspace to you each and every week. If you do it, I promise you we'll never stop working to make the show even better.

Now, let's get into it. Today, we have Joon in the podcast. Excited to kick this one off. Very exciting company.

个人成长故事：从韩国到画家再到研究者

Host: I want to kick off and ask you the question — talk us through the story of your life. How have you gotten here?

Joon: Yeah, for sure. Really excited to be here. A story of my life… So I was born in Korea, and I lived there for a good 11 years or so. Then my family moved to Boston when I was 11. My parents were doctors — they were basically going through their post-doctoral studies. My dad was a surgeon, so he was doing his sabbatical years actually at the Boston Children's Hospital.

So I grew up there, not too close to tech actually. I was very much like a music, artsy, painting kind of guy. I actually got into painting a little bit later in high school, but that's what I used to do. And then I grew up mostly in the East Coast after Korea. So I lived a good number of years in New Hampshire, and then I went to college in Pennsylvania.

I got into more of this tech scene in college. So I was originally trained to be an artist. I actually thought that would be my professional career. It wasn't a hobby — it was actually like "hey, let's make a living out of this." And then gradually I got really interested in this idea that the greatest artist often creates their own medium, and the best medium that we had available today was actually in computation. So I decided to go deeper into that. And one thing led to another, and obviously we can go deeper into this, but I decided that research was something that gradually I got interested in. And here I am.

Generative Agents 论文的诞生

Host: So there's obviously a lot that you packed into the research component. You had one of the best papers of 2023 — the generative agents paper commonly known as the Smallville paper. Feel free to call back to anything else that you mentioned, but most people would have heard of you from this. Do you have any statistics of how many people have read it? Arxiv gives you something, right?

Joon: Yeah, it's a good question. How many people have read it? I'm actually not sure. I know that we do keep track of the number of citations, which is going up quite fast, but the readership…

Host: Google Scholar has 72,000. It made a bigger hit — it was a pretty instrumental paper. It was one that got cited so many times. It is frequently when people ask "what is the best paper of the year, best paper you've read recently" — it's this one.

Host 2: I thought the memory component was pretty underrated — a very good early memory system. But yeah, one of the biggest papers.

Joon: Yeah, yeah. So maybe I can talk a little bit about how this particular paper came together.

When I got into research it was back in 2020 when I started my PhD program at Stanford. That was the year we were about to get GPT-3.5, GPT-3 to be available. So we already had GPT-2, and you could sense that there's this new class of models that was just becoming available in the market. The team got very intrigued, and the general consensus was: well, is this model actually going to be useful for anything? It's really strange that these models are not trained to do any particular task. But we decided to take a bet.

So a large group of scholars at Stanford — and it was actually led by one of my co-founders Percy Liang — came together…

Host: …who coined "foundation models."

Joon: …who coined the term foundation model. We wrote this paper called "Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models," and during that process, the thing that I started to think deeply about was: here is a model that is fundamentally new in our ecosystem. The reason why this was new was — again — it wasn't trained to do anything in particular. Its premise was it could do anything and everything. It was like a stem cell, if you were to take a biology analogy.

I got really interested in this idea that: if we were to really think about what the killer applications of this particular technology would be, what would that be? Many of my colleagues were using this for simpler classification, simple generation. Interesting that these models can do that, but from an interaction perspective, not that interesting. We've known how to do that for many decades.

What we came down to was: these models are actually trained on this very broad data from the web — these are human behavioral data. It's social media, Wikipedia, all these kinds of data. So if you poke at the right angle, you could see human behavior that would just pop out — that's actually quite realistic. And we've never seen that before.

The "Time Machine" 思想实验

So that got us really interested. The exercise that we decided to do — this is something that we, this particular group of colleagues that I have, myself, Michael Bernstein, Percy Liang, who ended up becoming my co-founder at Simile — we sat down and we played this game that we call the "time machine game." Imagine we were to get on a time machine and fast-forward 10 years and look back: what would have been the single application that would have mattered, that would be the most interesting and inspiring?

Well, we thought: what if we can just recreate the world that we live in? I mean, it's really hard to get more ambitious than that. Like, let's just create a world. And that's where we started. Initially we had this paper that was a precursor to the generative agents paper called Social Simulacra.

Host: Before you go further — were there other candidates for the most ambitious thing in the time machine exercise? What was number two or number three, if you remember?

Joon: Okay. So there is a close second that we were considering, which basically ended up becoming more of these automation tools — but especially the vision around really personalized agents that actually do things for you.

Host: That's also happening.

Joon: It's also happening. But it was sort of interesting for us, in that the reason why we decided to go with the idea of simulation… one, I was a huge science fiction nerd, and this idea of creating simulation, I was personally really just fascinated. I love the idea. It's really cool to see a game town like this and just see these agents live in it.

But at the same time, my bet was: if you were to create a really amazing personal assistant out of this technology, what you actually need first is an amazing model of your users. For instance, I told the model "hey, can you go buy late dinner for me," and it orders Hawaiian pizza, and I do not like pineapples on my pizza — then it totally failed. The way for it to not make that mistake is only by having a deep understanding of who I am. I gave a very simple and dumb example here, but you can imagine how this core understanding of people is instrumental.

This is how, for instance, if we have our family, closest friend, they have a good mental model of who we are — that's the basis of our social connection. So our bet also was: this technology around simulation, creating accurate representation of people, ought to precede the more complex agents that would automate the world that we live in. So that was the bet.

That was a very close second, and I'm still very much fascinated by it. I think there's a lot of interesting work going around. My hot take actually here though is: I don't think we've actually seen a true personal assistant that's actually useful in ways that meet the ambition of that particular line of work. I think there are early applications that are obviously interesting, and if you talk to even ChatGPT nowadays or Claude, they obviously know a lot about us. So a lot of the generation it's doing, I do think it's much more tailored. But I think the ambition is quite large in that field, and I don't think we quite have all the right ingredients just yet.

个人助理的差距：从 markdown 到真正的人类模型

Host: So OpenAI, Claude — all these clients, personal agents — what do you want to see from them that they don't currently have?

Joon: I do think it's slowly getting there, but I generally want them to have a much deeper understanding of the person. Right now you look at the models — OpenAI, Claude — what it's basically leveraging is basically a markdown file. And I think it's quite clever.

If you look at the generative agents paper, this actually was the same intuition that we had. Initially, when we were creating the memory architecture for the generative agents — this is like back in 2022, so we didn't really quite have the idea of agentive architecture or the term "agent" — but the intuition that we shared with some of the work that's coming out today was: we initially thought, well, do we want to make the memory into let's say a knowledge graph? Do we want to train a bespoke model? All these kinds of things.

And what we decided to do was: no, no, just forget about all this. These language models are actually quite good at modeling text and understanding and reasoning about text. So just put everything in a markdown file or text file. You're done. I thought that was quite interesting that we could do that, and there's a lot of strength in doing that.

But also there is limitation. It's the way you retrieve and make sense of data that's extremely large — it takes a lot of work. So I think that technology is getting better. I also do however think there are certain things you just cannot shape just by prompting the model. So to some degree you do need to touch the parameters of the model itself. There are these kinds of work that I do think do need to happen, and obviously it is happening. The question is how far can we take it, how do we source data, and how do you also create an ecosystem where the people are continuously feeding data to this model so it's learning about them.

何时需要训练模型 vs 提示模型

Host: What's the intuition between why you need to do it in the model?

Joon: My intuition behind when do you train or even post-train a model versus just prompt a model is: if the model has to learn the underlying physics of the world that it's operating in — so it has to learn new social physics. The places where it doesn't have to train: it already has the physics. We trust the physics. It already has the base statistics, but it's just trying to react to an environment. Then I think you can just prompt your way into getting the actions out of it.

I don't think the model has yet — at least the models that are out in the open have yet — learned the complete mapping of social physics of humanity. And this actually is one of the core theses of Simile. One of the core reasons why that is the case is: if you look at the data that the model was trained on, these models were trained on the web data — whatever was available on the web. These are really interesting datasets, but they are fundamentally the self-exposed attitudinal data, with some behavioral data sprinkled around here and there. And it has yet to learn really deep behavioral nature of people — not just what people say they do online, but what they actually do in real life.

This is actually what I would consider to be the "dark knowledge" of humanity that we haven't quite captured. And it's these kinds of data that would also need to get factored into the model creation.

三类数据：Interview / Observational / RCT

Host: You call it "behavior foundation model." There's a good one-liner there, but outside of that — what type of data do you need? What are you changing on the model level? How do you go about actually building a behavior foundation model?

Joon: We think about data in three buckets.

Bucket 1 — Interview data. For instance, qualitative rich qualitative data is interesting. It's not behavioral, but we would literally ask people "hey, tell me the story of your life."

Host: Yeah, that's what we're doing here.

Joon: Exactly. The question that you all asked at the beginning of this interview literally is the question we also ask — and obviously we ask our participants to go a little bit deeper than how far I went. Maybe I can actually give more of my life story in lieu of this.

But the reason why that data is interesting is: by learning about this very long-tail information about people, you actually get a lot of texture around this model, like this person as a model. So even understanding their childhood memory or their trauma, their first love, these kinds of things — quite informative in ways that's really hard to predict. So that's one.

Bucket 2 — Observational behavioral data. These might actually be transaction data, or these might be data that you can get by scraping the web. You can imagine why these datasets would be interesting: they give you the base statistics of people's behavior.

Bucket 3 — Cause and mechanism data (the "why"). The last category of data — I personally think perhaps the most important — is the data that basically describes the cause and mechanism, the whys of people. Some of this is covered by the interview data, the qualitative, because people talk about why they made certain decisions. But really where you get to see the most behavioral aspect of this actually is in randomized control trials (RCTs).

Imagine you basically have the same setup but you have a few different variables that you're trying to tweak. Can you actually get realistic human behavior out of it? "Imagine you had this particular option. Imagine you're even trying to choose whether you're going to drink coffee or not. The day you drank coffee versus the day you didn't drink coffee — does your behavior change?" That's a dataset that describes a cause or mechanism.

This actually is quite important in modeling people. The reason why: oftentimes when people come to us — or not just to us but the reason why people are interested in simulation — actually isn't because they want to predict the future. If you're trying to win against the stock market, predicting the future is interesting. But most decision-makers, what they want to know is: how can we shape the future?

It doesn't really help you to hear that your sales is going to tank in two quarters. They're just going to say, "wow, that sucks." What they want to know is: what do we need to do now to avoid that future? That's cause–mechanism. And this is also very hard data to come by, because the world is our ground truth, but it happens once. So in a very controlled setup where everything is equal except for one variable, this kind of dataset almost rarely happens. So it's both hard to come by but also quite important if you're trying to model human behavior.

如何获取行为数据：虚拟实验室

I don't even have data for myself on… I want to analyze my own health or habits and I just don't log everything. So how can you have that data?

Joon: So we actually run a lot of randomized control trials.

Host: Yeah. But you put people in the lab, they watch them sleep or what?

Joon: We do actually care a lot about the consent process. So people know that we invite them to be a member of this community, to both share data and also have themselves represented in different forms. But we bring a lot of people to the lab, or virtual lab, where we design experiments that would actually pose them real behavioral decisions.

Often in these kinds of experimental setups, what makes the difference between what is attitudinal versus behavioral is: if the stake in your decision is real, that's ultimately what makes it behavioral. In these kinds of setups, we are inspired by our colleagues in social sciences, psychology and so forth. When they run studies, the kinds of techniques they utilize — imagine there's an online store that you're inviting people to come by, and whatever they purchase in this experiment, they actually get that item delivered. These are the kinds of things that make the stakes real.

So we run a lot of these experiments, and we also partner with firms. Right now we also have customers who are quite excited to at least give us a glimpse of the kinds of behaviors that their users exhibit, so we can get a little bit deeper understanding of how people behave in these different platforms.

Simulation ≠ Prediction：Foundation series & psychohistory

There's also another aspect here, which is: this is the reason why simulation is actually different from prediction. In the ideal-case scenario, what simulation is trying to show is each step of the way — each step that we need to take to get to a certain outcome. In the most advanced simulations, sometimes the next step that we're suggesting might actually be quite counterintuitive.

The analogy I sometimes give — as I mentioned, I'm a huge fan of science fiction — I don't know how many of the audience members have read things like the Foundation series.

Host: We've mentioned psychohistory a number of times.

Joon: Okay, fantastic. I might actually be talking to the right crew. If you read the Foundation series, literally the first act is: there's a group of scientists who have found out that the Galactic Empire is going to collapse, and we're going to have 30,000 years of unrest. They basically run psychohistory, the simulator that tries to teach them: okay, how can we keep this unrest to a thousand years? And they plan this out. And the first step of that plan is to get the scientists who say "okay, this is coming" exiled into this random place in the galaxy.

Host: Terminus.

Joon: Exactly. And that's so counterintuitive. What a strange move — that you literally sent the group of scientists who was raising voice around the potential collapse of the Galactic Empire into nowhere. How is that the right first move? Well, it turns out in this particular simulation that actually was the move.

It's these kinds of things. The reason why these kinds of reasoning are possible is because you're showing the step function — each step that results in a particular outcome. So really what simulation allows you to do in its highest form is: you give it not a problem or question like "what would people answer to the survey" — that's not what we do. What we tell it is: "here is a goal that we have." In the context of Foundation: we want to keep the unrest to a thousand years. What is the path we need to take now to get to that particular future? That's what simulation allows you to do.

Translating that into a real market: imagine you're an automobile company, and you're about to release an EV, and you're trying to understand how do we market EV to make sure that our stock price goes up. But what if the answer comes down that — well, you can market your EV in XYZ way, but that might change people's perception around the cars that's not EV and actually make your overall sales go down? Not very intuitive. Especially if all you're trying to optimize is EV sales and that's the only thing you're tracking, then that might actually result in a completely wrong solution — or at least a different solution than what you would have expected, whether it's right or wrong.

Host: Yeah, that's the power of simulation.

For listeners, we covered a similar topic with ML Parin from Shopify where they are working on SimGym. I don't know if he ever talked to you about it. It's very similar — the goal is increase conversion, but the journey is very unusual. He's actually trying to look for interventions on a shopping trajectory, which is similar to what you're saying: it's not about the attitudinal — that's your word for it — it's about behavior. And that's exactly the difference: it's not about the near-term direction, but more about how do you affect multiple turns of interactions.

如何验证 simulation 是 grounded 的？The 1000-agent paper

Host: You had a good quote at the start about this as well — it's not about people wanting to know the outcome. It's about how they can change it. But I want to take it back to: how do we know this is grounded? How do you run evals? How do you test that simulations come through?

Basically, if I was to do the same thing that you described with, say, your favorite LLM — Opus, GPT-5 — have some agent to map out these things, how different are the answers we would get if I give it the same goal, the same objective? You're saying that you need to change the model weights. You have your own solution to this — but how far off are we, and how do you check if it's grounded? You have some interesting stuff on your site that actually points to how you run evals. I think that's one of the big concerns that people have. They're like, "LLMs hallucinate — you're just hallucinating layer after layer."

Joon: The way we do this — and this is actually the paper we worked on after the generative agents paper — that really became, at least for Simile and also the field of simulation and synthetic panels, the foundation.

Host: Yeah, this is the paper "Generative Simulations of a Thousand People."

Joon: Here's what we've done for this paper. We actually brought a thousand people that's representatively sampled from the US to a virtual lab. What we basically did was: we spent two hours collecting fairly wide-ranging data. In this particular study, we focused a lot on this interview data, whose script was taken from a project called American Voices Project, and then we would also pair it with a lot of behavioral data and so forth — whatever we can collect within two hours.

Then we would actually send these people away for a couple of weeks, and during that time I would use this data to create their digital twins. And I would bring the human participants back after two weeks and have them complete a battery of surveys, experiments, behavior studies — the list includes things like behavior economic games, the Big Five personality test, General Social Survey. We would also run the randomized control trials that were published on PNAS. And we would have their digital twins predict how the source individuals would have acted in these studies and surveys.

This is where we basically could replicate people's behaviors and attitudes 85% as accurately as people would replicate their own. So that actually was the first paper that gave this validated result that we can actually model individuals in an accurate way.

Host: For listeners who are not seeing the YouTube — the headline figure is 85% accuracy, which is a big improvement over all the other methods that you showed.

前沿模型 vs Simile：为什么"太聪明"是问题

Joon: But the part that was actually particularly striking to us, especially as we improved this technology even further, was: the generative AI models like ChatGPT, Claude that's coming out — it does give you the right foundation, however what they do not consider is the true attitudinal and behavioral aspect of people, especially in the population that you care about.

What these models are really really good at today is: they're trying to basically become the super-rational objective machines. So you go get their data from places like Mercor Scale, you talk to professional programmers, scientists, to create models that's amazing at reasoning. That's what they do.

Simile actually doesn't care about any of this. The models we're talking about here — what we're trying to create are models that are as dumb as I am. If I make those mistakes, the model has to make the same kind of mistake.

Host: Oh, that's very hard.

Joon: That's very hard. You're solving Moravec's paradox.

Host: That's exactly it.

Joon: And this is actually a completely different kind of data and training objective. This is also where we actually see quite a bit of discrepancy in the performance in human behavior prediction between the frontier models and simulating being created in the space. In some cases the model performance of frontier models goes all the way down to 20–30%, especially if you go into that more niche population on topics that our customers would actually care about. On more gen-pop it might be around 50 to 60%. So it's not very robust — you wouldn't want to make your decision off of these kinds of findings. If you can bring that up to 85%, that is ultimately what people end up getting very excited about.

The OSF Paper：用 RCT 后训练模型

Host: Do we want to keep going on the paper route?

Joon: Yeah, for sure. So the last one was sort of an interesting one. This paper was the follow-up paper to the thousand agents paper, where the idea was: now can we augment the models even further and actually post-train a model based on a lot of randomized control trials?

The data is always the most interesting part of modeling in many ways. The data we got here — there's this platform called Open Science Foundation. Some of the audience might be familiar with this. Especially in the social sciences over the past 5 years or so, there has been this concern around replicability of studies. It's a bit of a crisis the scientists acknowledged: where we rerun the study and we don't actually see the same finding. It's tough.

The reason why that was often the case: there's basically the survival bias, where the papers that get published often need to maintain what we call the p-value of less than 0.05 in the experiments that we ran. That basically suggests that there's only 5% chance that the results we saw is a false positive. But the tricky part was: all the papers that were not published — and there's still a 5% chance that whatever we publish is actually totally just randomly generated. There's 5% chance that "hey, this effect is not real, but it just happened to be real because of the sampling bias."

Because of that, what scientists started to do was pre-register their studies. Before running an experiment, they would go to this platform and say "here is the data, here is the population we're collecting, and here's the hypothesis" — and they would just say "here is our hypothesis, this is what we believe" — and you cannot retroactively change those hypotheses. This is what actually gives us more scientific statistical confidence that whatever effect you ended up seeing is actually true.

So that ended up creating this really interesting platform where there's one platform that now contains tens of thousands of real-world experiments and hypotheses, and a lot of these are actually really high quality, professionally designed behavior studies and randomized control trials. So we actually got the data and the studies from this platform and basically used that to make a point. Obviously this particular model is not something we're serving commercially because this was a part of the open science. But this particular dataset helped us make a point: by collecting a lot of these well-designed randomized control trials, we can make significant improvement in a model's capability to predict human behaviors. So that's what this paper was about.

个体级 vs 群体级建模

Joon: So this particular model actually was trained… the data we actually had at the level of individuals, but this particular model actually was trained… we experimented with both. In this particular work, we've done the same here. The results we are reporting are much more geared towards individuals because we do actually think that is the harder task in many ways.
