Yeah, and I can tell you the exact reason democratic socialism is going to win, continue to win, and these far-left Democratic candidates are going to dominate. And it's, you know, it's the Republicans' fault. They had all three branches of government here really tightly in their control.

And if you look at what the podcast bros and the pro-podcast referencing stack is responding to — and I listen to them, you know, not every episode, but I dip in and out of Tucker, who is now making his own political party, Joe Rogan, Tim Dillon, all these folks who were all in for Trump — they cite Epstein investigation, which, okay, whatever, I don't think it's particularly material, but it is to them. The Iran war is obviously top of what they believe is the problem here because they were promised that wouldn't happen. And then it's, to your point, Freeberg, this inflation thing has not been solved and it just keeps going.

And we're going to be sitting here, I think, in another six months or 12 months talking about, my Lord, every investigation possible into the Trump administration. And we need to start looking at what would be things — to your point, Chamath — and I thought you summarized some of the broken parts of capitalism I think well, but we got to get granular about it.

And I brought up last week just the edge behaviors in capitalism, where we over-optimize. I felt the delivery providers, and Sax and I had a party debate about it last week, we're just being too clever, squeezing too much out of the last mile, quite literally. On Amazon's part, how we treat the people who are at the bottom of the employment stack is what's causing this. And not being able to solve the cost of homes, and not making that a focus, not being able to solve the cost of childcare, not being able to move the minimum wage — I think we have to look at all of these things and say: that's what Trump should look at all those things. And he should build the second half of his term just around those things.

No more crypto stuff, no more wars, no more attacking our allies. All of this performative stuff and just mistakes — they got to go away. And we got to focus on what he sold people on. People feel they were sold that this would be a populist presidency that took care of the working man and woman in this country. And it has been the opposite.

Sax：政府过度介入的地方通胀最厉害

Sax, I'm sure you have some thoughts, and we'll give you the final word on the inflation thing because you talked about — and Freeberg's talked about it — I mean, basically you're saying the cost of living is going to drive everyone to socialism.

I agree there's some risk of that, but let's break it down into a little bit more nuance here. If you look at where the most inflation has occurred, it's always in those sectors of the economy that the government's most involved. So healthcare and colleges and housing, where the government has massive amounts of subsidies and regulation — it only seems to make the problem worse. Kind of makes sense that if the government's paying for something, then the providers have a huge incentive to charge as much as possible. And in fact, a lot of them engage in fraud as well. So we know these areas are rife with abuse, but those are the areas that are most inefficient and where you see the price going through the roof. I mean, hospital services — man, that's just exponential just about.

And then if you look at the areas where we've had not just no inflation, but actually prices have come down — it's in all the tech areas. It's basically TVs or computer software, cell phones, things like that. The prices have come down a lot.

By the way, this chart is showing all the way from 2000 to 2026. So it's a 26-year timeframe. And during that time, overall inflation went up 96%. So the price level almost doubled in that 26-year period. Fortunately, on average, that's right. But like I said, with certain things like healthcare becoming 300% almost more expensive, whereas computer software went down by 67% in real dollars. Meanwhile, the average hourly wage grew 135%. So at least the average hourly wage grew by about 40% more than the inflation level. But obviously it's still bites that you have all this inflation.

I guess my point is just: how do you solve it? We know that you bring prices down through vigorous competition, not through more government interference in these markets. And unfortunately, what happens is that socialism causes the problem. And then what happens is that groups like the DSA argue that the way to solve the problem is through more socialism. So it's a disease that claims to be a cure. And then people take it and they take more of it and the disease gets worse and worse. And that is the spiral that I think we risk being in.

争论：这是不是"死亡螺旋"？

We're in a socialist death spiral now. All this spending now is going to be —

We're not in a death spiral. Take it easy. We're not in a death spiral. No, I mean, it's great for you to say — because it sounds like really like you got some real hot take. We're not there. America is doing fine. We are cranking. The economy is great. There are things that need to be fixed. I would say start with corporate America. Let's get our act together and let's start doing things that are honorable, interesting and aspirational.

Yeah, I think you totally missed the point. I think the real point here is: if he hadn't started the war, we wouldn't have the same inflation issues. We wouldn't have the same expense issues. And this would be a totally different picture. And it was his job, Sax, when he promised the American people he would focus on affordability. And he had control of both houses and the presidency, and he's willing to do any executive order on crypto, on wars, on anything, but he didn't do any executive orders on affordability. And that's the failure of this project.

Maybe you missed the point where Chamath said it'd be a tailwind to get out of this war. I think the kinetic part's already over, by the way. So it's just — let's hope. I mean, it just should never have been started.

But in any event, look, the president passed his economic program last year on Big Beautiful Bill, and I think it's working. We're seeing a huge investment boom. We're seeing small business confidence rise to its highest level in a long time. They are saying they're going to create more jobs over the next year. I think the economy is doing pretty well. I mean, we do have these issues. I'm not saying we don't. And spending is a long-standing problem, can't disagree with you there. However, I don't think Democrats have the solution to the problem. And the democratic socialists definitely don't have the solution to the problem.

Because that's my point. We are now incentivizing young people in the Republican Party to embrace socialism. Moderates are embracing socialism. They're all looking at it saying, "Well, that sounds better. If Trump won't be a populist, maybe these people are the populists." And that's what I mean by the death spiral, because they're going to just keep spending money. They're going to increase the velocity of spending. You may be right, which is scary, by the way. That's what — I don't think we're like in it now. We're risking going.

Sax：DSA 政策要花多少钱

Just one last point. They did a cost estimate of the policy platform proposed by the DSA — remember, we've talked about that before. And the estimate is that it would project new federal spending of between $71 trillion and $212 trillion, by the way, total, over 10 years. There's no hierarchy of the American population. $182 trillion. $182 trillion, yeah.

Okay, but I'm just saying that's how much the DSA program would cost if you guys believe that the root of our problems is overspending and basically too much government. Unfortunately, this is not that. The DSA is gonna — no.

But here's what's gonna happen, and I'll just let me just walk through the sequence of events. Sequence one: they enact a policy starting in 2028 with Comrade AOC in charge and the Politburo — Ro Khanna, Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, and the rest of the Politburo — organizing themselves to launch these new programs. Those new programs get launched and costs balloon. The bond market sells off 30 years. And so now the 30-year yield spiked 7%, 8%, maybe more. Things become more unaffordable.

So then the question is: okay, well, we can't bridge it from a fiscal perspective. We can't just get the Fed to start buying bonds. There's not enough buying power there to bring rates down, to bring inflation down. So we need more income. So now we need to pass a national asset seizure tax. And there's not enough money in the billionaire class or the $50 million class. The total net worth of all people that are worth over $50 million is only $23 trillion. You could take 10% of their net worth and it would only cover three months of fiscal spending today's fiscal spending. So at the end of the day, the only way to get there is to start doing massive taxation seizures.

And so seizures — seize. So this just came out this week, okay, by Cato Institute. And again, it shows the low end of the DSA spending, $71 trillion. The high end is $211 trillion. Now, you compare that to things like corporate profits or private sector wealth. Corporate profits are only $35 trillion. The Forbes 400, all the wealth of the Forbes 400, is only $6.6 trillion. So it's less than 10% of the low end of DSA spending.

Chamath：这不是数学，是愤怒

Guys, I keep telling you, this is not about mathematical realism. This is about anger towards a class of people that are increasingly odious and misrepresent.

Yeah, but people also can't afford to buy a house. People are 35 years old with roommates. And people go to the grocery store and they're shocked at the fact that they have to spend an entire paycheck or a third of a paycheck to buy groceries.

It's not that people want to buy a yacht. It's that the yacht class are just despicable.

Freeberg：Rene Girard 视角下的替罪羊

Well, no, I mean, look, in every socialist revolution, every revolution we've seen historically around this, there is always an elite branch of society, and they're typically classified different ways. It's wealth, it's Jews, it's some race, it's immigrants — there's some organizational assignment, some identity assignment, that says this is the cause of unaffordability.

At the end of the day, the dysfunction of the relationship between government and all the other organizations that make up that society — those organizations can be states, they can be private companies, they can be the NGOs — it is the dysfunction of the government's relationship with the other organizations that fundamentally causes things to become more expensive and dysfunctional. And the actual market for getting access to things for the individual fails.

And at that point you have to identify — and you don't identify the government, because the government is the aggregate of all the people. So the government — and remember the government is the system, the means of action. So for the people to organize, they have to organize the government to go, and then they have to have an alternative system to go and destroy. You have to point the finger, and you have to point the finger at somebody.

And if you're going to scapegoat somebody in 2026, the best class of people to scapegoat are the billionaires and, frankly, even better than them, the trillionaires. At the end of the day, it's all tech, right? The data center is the temple where the billionaires and trillionaires pray. It's where they go to make their sacrifices. It is their gathering spot.

So I think the data center is this like, you know, temple on the mountain. So that's why I think the data center gets tied up in all of this. There's no rational discourse about data centers. It's like, no, no, no. Look, if you take it through the Rene Girard lens, everything maps. It's like the billionaires will be scapegoated, and the trillionaires — I mean, even worse. And because that will allow the catharsis that will allow society to reset and realize, wait a minute — oh, my gosh, yeah. There's a generation of that, though. There's a generation ahead. And only then. Yeah. It is a long process. It is.

J. Cal：给特朗普一个建议 —— 造100万套房

Here's an idea. Next president, or Trump in his second half, just putting it out there: do an executive order that you're going to build like a million homes, two million homes. If you can have executive orders, if you can start wars without the approval of Congress, right — what's that? You know that that's not how it works. There are local laws, of course. But he pulled out all the stops for getting data centers greenlit. We know that, and he worked with the state governments.

I'm talking about him coming on saying, "You know what? We did a great job for the data centers, we did a great job for the crypto industry, and now we're going to do two great things. We're going to do two great things: we're going to make trade schools and we're going to make affordable homes. I'm just going to make that the next 24 months. We're going to figure out a way to mobilize the private sector, mobilize the public sector. We're going to make more homes, and we're going to get you a great education that turns into a job."

That would be a great thing for Trump to do.

The federal government does control the largest amount of land in the United States. So it could do something on federal land without the need for a bunch of other state and local gobbledygook. So there is — Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac.

Now, it may not be located in places that actually make sense for commerce and for people to live or that are already living there, because I don't think it really abuts most cities. So unfortunately, it's not in his control, even if you wanted to just kind of say, "Let's make this happen."

I think if the president can go spend a couple hundred billion on this war, he can go spend a couple hundred billion on homes that are affordable. And maybe you can't put them in Manhattan, but he could put them other places. And he should fight for the regulations to get — just like he fought for the regulations on data centers and energy. He made an appointment on this very podcast at the AI Summit: "Hey, we're going to clear all the pathways to nuclear, to nat gas, we're going to — they have a beautiful clean coal, federal, which is great." Now do it. Now do it for homes. Strong. Use that same energy.

They just passed a housing bill. They just actually just passed a housing bill. When's the last time we heard Trump — unfortunately, it was written by Elizabeth Warren, so I don't know how good it is, but yeah.

Anyway, I'm just giving him the solution to save his legacy.

结尾

All right, everybody. As always, you're looking out for everybody. I'm looking out for everybody. You're looking out for the audience. Nostradamus, thank you. Nostradamus is also looking out for you.

Okay, wrap, I got to go. Come on.

All right, everybody. It's been another amazing episode. Love you, boys. Nice to be back. Good to have the quartet back. Let's go. Bye-bye.

Rain Man, David Sacks. And it's said, we open source it to the fans. Love you, S. I'm the queen of kids. Besties are back! Oh man! It's like this sexual tension that they just need to release somehow. We need to get merch! Besties are back!

item.description:
## 一、Dario的"回应模式"暴露了权力结构的隐秘等级
最反直觉的观察：Dario一年半没回应Sacks，却对Gavin Baker迅速回击。这不是傲慢，而是**权力雷达的精准校准**——他回应的从来不是"论点强度"，而是"资本市场信号强度"。Sacks代表意识形态战场（可忽略），Gavin代表二级市场分析师的判断（会影响下一轮融资估值和LP心态）。这揭示了一个残酷真相：**当代AI CEO已经不是技术领袖，而是资本叙事的运营者**——他们的"透明度"完全由资金流的敏感度决定。
跨领域连接：这与中世纪教皇只回应国王、不回应神学家的模式完全一致——真理不重要，能撼动金库的人才值得回应。
## 二、"数据中心 = 现代神庙"——Rene Girard框架下的AI恐慌
Freeberg那句"数据中心是亿万富翁朝拜的神庙"是本集最被低估的洞见。真正惊人的是：**反对数据中心的运动本质上不是环境议题，也不是就业议题，而是一场宗教运动**——民众在寻找一个可见的、可捣毁的"圣物"来完成社会张力的献祭仪式。
这也解释了一个悖论：为什么Abbott和Shapiro这两个原本最亲数据中心的

item.title: [YC Root Access] Supabase: Cash Does Not Equal Success
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被冻结在模型权重里的"老树林"——一种前所未见的护城河

Paul 讲了一句几乎被采访者本人低估的话："2023 年之后训练模型用的内容，质量不会像更早期的那么高。"如果你把这句话往前推一步，会发现 Supabase 拥有的最深护城河，不在产品里，而在每一个大模型的权重里。

2020–2022 年他们在 Hacker News、Discord、Reddit、GitHub 上留下的每一行讨论，都被当时"干净的、人类写的、非 AI 生成的"语料吸进了 GPT-4、Claude、Gemini 的基础训练集。这些权重不会因为竞争对手今年融了多少钱而重写。竞对哪怕拿 10 亿美金去做内容营销，产出的也是 2024 年之后的"AI-slop 时代"内容，权重更低、被去重的概率更高。

这本质上是一种"时间性的训练数据资历"（temporal training-data seniority）——像老树林生态系统一样，一旦砍掉就再也长不回来。跨领域对比：这和中世纪教会为什么能垄断"神圣性"是同一个结构——它抢在了印刷术普及之前把自己写进了所有手抄本。谁在语料"清洁期"里发声，谁就永久地成了模型的"默认答案"。

二、把销售提成变成"随机对照试验"——最反直觉的商业模式创新

大多数人听 Paul 描述销售 comp 时会一带而过，但这里藏着一个真正颠覆性的东西：Supabase 的销售提成不是按账户价值算的，而是按"相对于对照组的增量"算的。

他们把 1000 个高增长客户切成两组：500 个上了电话（treatment），500 个没上（control）。对照组自然增长 25%，treatment 组增长 125%——销售只拿那 100 个百分点的增量对应的提成。

这在销售领域几乎是异端。传统销售 comp 假设"这笔单子是销售促成的"；Supabase 直接承认"这笔单子的大部分本来就会发生"，只为销售真正创造的部分买单。这是把临床药物试验的方法论（RCT）搬进了销售组织——同样的逻辑让 FDA 判断一款药有没有效、让政治竞选团队衡量广告 lift、让 Meta 决定要不要开一个新广告位。

这里最深的洞察不是"公平"，而是它悄悄改变了销售的心智：一个不能提高 lift 的销售，无论电话多漂亮、单子多大，都拿不到钱。它把销售从"关系艺人"改造成了"因果实验员"。

三、Clippy 的哲学——把失败"预先审美化"

2023 年初他们做出第一版 doc RAG 时，怕模型胡说八道，就故意把图标做成 Clippy——"如果它幻觉了，至少你能笑一下"。听起来是个笑话，但它其实是一种极其成熟的产品哲学：把不可避免的失败预先包装成体验的一部分。

这和游戏设计里"死亡动画要好看"、Duolingo 让猫头鹰在你不学习时哭泣、Netflix 把加载图标做成 loading 而不是"错误"——是同一个跨领域原则：当你无法消灭失败模式时，就把它变成风格。

再往深看，这背后是一个 Supabase 一以贯之的元哲学——他们不假装完美，他们让不完美变成品牌资产。开源许可给你无限制使用权（承认自己不是唯一供应商），公开定价（承认 Firebase 会让你 bill shock），承认自己是"open source Firebase alternative"（承认自己不是原创）。这条链条的另一端，是 Paul 在采访结尾那句极其少见的诚实："我不认为 AI 生产力提升已经被证明了——只要人还在 loop 里，就不算真正的收益。"

一家公司如果敢在采访里承认这个，说明他们内部的决策系统不依赖"我们赢了"的叙事撑着。这或许才是 Supabase 真正跑得比对手快的原因：它是一家不需要靠幻觉运转的公司。

四、一个隐藏的悖论作为彩蛋

Paul 说 60% 以上的数据库是 agent 创建的，但他"猜"实际接近 90%——因为 agent 通过 CLI 创建时他们根本看不到。这意味着 Supabase 已经不知道自己的客户是谁了。

这不只是度量问题，这是一个哲学时刻：当你的"用户"是一个由人类朦胧驱动的软件实体，"客户成功"、"NPS"、"用户访谈"这些 SaaS 时代的基石概念全部失效。Supabase 无意间成了第一批必须给不可见客户做产品的公司之一。他们的 dashboard 日活还在涨，但占比在跌——他们正在见证一个奇怪的现象：产品的表面被人类使用得越来越少，但产品的深处被使用得越来越多。

这个反转，在互联网历史上只出现过一次可比的：搜索引擎从"给人看"变成"给爬虫和 SEO 优化"的那几年。Supabase 现在站在的位置，就是当年 Google 面对 SEO 觉醒的那个前夜。

📝 转录文本

Supabase: Cash Does Not Equal Success — YC Root Access 访谈

开场

Host: Today I'm joined by Paul Kstone, the co-founder and CEO of Supabase. Supabase is a Summer 20 company, who started as an open-source Postgres as a service and has now become one of the fastest growing dev tools in this AI era — to the point that their last round put them as a decacorn. Thanks for joining us.

Paul: Happy to be here.

关于前两次创业

Host: So maybe before diving into this latest news — you started the company in 2020, but it's not your first company, right? I mean, you created two others before.

Paul: Yeah, this is my third venture-backed startup. So I've done — so also…

Host: How many you still?

Paul: Uh, I don't know. Um, I also helped a lot of people launch their startups, because I just really enjoyed that space, and in some ways that kind of is the genesis of Supabase. I mean, Supabase — people build startups on top of it. So it's kind of the thing.

Host: Yeah, it's full cycle.

Paul: Um, but in terms of my own startups, yeah, I did two venture-backed ones before this. Both in Southeast Asia — and both got acquired for a lot of money. No, they weren't as successful as Supabase. Um, you know, I still learned a lot and got a lot out of them.

Host: But how much did these first experiences influence what you are doing now?

Paul: Quite a lot. Quite a lot. I learned a lot. I think that's the thing — whether a startup succeeds or not — and in fact in many ways, if they fail you learn a lot from the failures themselves. So I think I would not have been able to build Supabase like we have today if it wasn't for doing those two startups.

起点：为农民做的实时数据库

Host: Awesome. And I think that's also how you got the idea. Is that fair?

Paul: Actually the idea started a long time ago, when I first started building. In my career I was doing contracting and really focused on the database side of things. So I've been building with databases and building databases since I was at university. I started contracting and working immediately. And funnily enough, one of the first jobs that I ever had was to build a real-time system on top of a database — for farmers, 'cause I'm from New Zealand.

Host: Okay.

Paul: But yeah, so again it's kind of full circle now. After what — 10, 15 years — now I'm building a startup that kind of has the primitives that I needed at the time.

Host: So you're building software you wanted to exist back — like 10, 15 years ago.

Paul: Yeah. Well, funnily enough, now that I think back to it, the technology existed but not in a form that you'd use today. I was using something called ColdFusion, which is a technology by Adobe — you know the one? Yeah, with the Flash charts and things. So that was actually very, very impressive. They were leagues ahead of their time. But unfortunately they didn't build on Postgres.

为什么押注一门 30 年的老技术

Host: Okay. So Postgres — when you started Supabase, Postgres was already like 30 years old or something. Why bet on an old technology?

Paul: So we knew we wanted to build a database company. We liked the problems that databases presented — big, hairy problems present good opportunities for a startup founder.

And then why did we choose Postgres? Mainly because I monitored Hacker News a lot and I could see this very nascent but growing groundswell of developers choosing Postgres. And I see Hacker News really as a sort of early-adopter mentality. And then, as we've gone on throughout the years, Postgres has now become the most popular database.

Host: So few…

Paul: Well, we would like to think that we contributed a little bit. But I think the 30 years of development from the community, and all the systems around Postgres, are really the main thing — and hopefully we just added a little bit of fuel to an already raging fire.

Host: You placed your bet on Postgres. You saw it as an old but upcoming — in some way — the right technology for the future. And then you decided to be open source. What was the intention behind that?

Paul: There wasn't too much thought. I think Ant and myself are very philosophically aligned to open source. I really like the community around open source — especially, you know, like Postgres. It's a community that is very distributed. Postgres belongs to no one. And so in this way it actually has some very interesting dynamics.

Not only is it 30 years old, but I expect it to continue being popular for the next 30 years, purely because no one company owns it. Because of this it has some very interesting dynamics: because no one owns it, everyone can contribute to it; because everyone can contribute to it, it makes it better. So you end up with this very interesting flywheel where all the hyperscalers have to offer Postgres, which makes it better; and then we as well will contribute, and everyone is contributing to the success of Postgres.

So for us, I really like that model where everyone can contribute and feel like it's not just developed by a single company. And this actually points towards one of the differences we have as an open source company: we try very much to contribute and give back to existing open source tools rather than build our own.

You know, a lot of database companies will come in and say, "I'll build a bigger, better database, and I'll make it look like Postgres." Our way of doing things is to build an ecosystem around Postgres — but find the tools that already exist if possible and contribute to them. If they don't exist, then we'll build them. But when we build them, we always build them open source.

Host: Completely open source?

Paul: All of our licenses are either MIT, Apache 2, or Postgres license.

Host: So it's real open source.

Paul: Completely free. Yeah. You can use it without restriction.

为什么不做开源核心（open core）

Host: And that was a choice from the get-go. A lot of open source companies have this kind of open-core model where they do features they sell on top to enterprises. You never tried that?

Paul: We never bothered. I think the main thing with the database is — it's difficult to manage the full database and you probably want to hand that off to someone. So I can see why many other open source communities might want to do it that way, where you can stand up a single instance. But for example, managing backups with Postgres and failovers and consensus algorithms and all these sort of things are actually a hard thing for an individual to do. So you probably want experts to be managing it, even if we provide all of the tools.

Host: And never worried about the big cloud providers taking over — like, pretty much making more money than you from the project by reselling Supabase, given the license lets them do that?

Paul: Yeah, I mean, that's always a topic of discussion, as you would know, in boardrooms. Um, Supabase is a little bit different in that: first of all, we're going all in on Postgres, and they already have their Postgres offerings. So in many ways we're kind of competing with them, rather than — what are they going to…

Host: Because they have their own version, own flavor…

Paul: Their own flavor of it. Yeah. That would be very weird for them to take another one with themselves.

Host: Yeah.

Paul: Exactly. And also that points to another thing: Supabase is an amalgamation of a few tools that center around Postgres. So for them to spin this up, it wouldn't be like standing up a Redis instance or Elasticsearch or something like that — it would be building an entire ecosystem around many different tools. So it would be a new model for these hyperscalers.

早期启动：从 "Realtime Postgres" 到 "Open Source Firebase Alternative"

Host: Okay. So not a big worry. But early on you did not have that kind of success. Did that take off right away? How did you launch?

Paul: So yeah, our initial launch — well, our very initial launch — was positioning ourselves as "real-time Postgres."

Host: But Hacker News, I guess? Yeah, given how much you were reading it.

Paul: Yeah. So what happened was: in my previous startup, I was developing the tech stack knowing that I wanted to launch a dev-tools company. I was using Postgres and Firebase. Firebase was great — we were using it for this chat application, but we hit some scaling limits and we had to find out how to solve these limits.

So I ended up building the real-time engine on top of Postgres. So one of the tools that I couldn't find in the ecosystem — I put that on Show HN, and it started getting some traction. And then I thought, "Oh, now's the time to build this database company." And I thought, "Oh well, the real-time engine — people like that, so we'll call it 'real-time Postgres.' That's our differentiator." And we kind of launched it. We applied for YC, we got into YC, but it wasn't really getting that much traction.

And then one day we changed the tagline from "real-time Postgres" to "open source Firebase alternative." And at that point — yeah, kind of actually someone else launched us. They put us on Hacker News and it went straight to the top for a few days. And at that point we knew we had something, but we were missing a lot of features.

Host: You were not yet Firebase.

Paul: No, no planner or anything.

Host: No.

Paul: Exactly. And that was kind of aspirational. I mean, Firebase is a phenomenal back end and it's very comprehensive. We knew we mostly wanted to be database-centric, and Firebase has much more than the database side of things. So we just decided on the few tools that we really wanted to get Postgres out there, and we started working towards those.

如何从 Firebase 手中赢下开发者

Host: That's awesome. How would you convince startups? I guess you started mostly bottom-up, with small companies first. How do you convince them to use you and not Firebase? I mean, Firebase was already backed by Google — kind of more reliable in the mind of people, I guess, than the new company just starting.

Paul: Yeah, definitely. I think the main things — actually, the "not Google" was funnily enough one of the positionings that worked quite well, for us at least, or for the developer audience.

The other differentiators with Firebase: really, Firebase is one of those tools that you both love and you might hate. It's phenomenally easy as a developer. The reason you might dislike it is you might scale off it, or you might not like the pricing. So we solved those by saying, "Well, it's Postgres" and "Here's our pricing." You basically could not get bill-shock from Supabase.

And then the other things we said were: it is open source — which I know James, the founder of Firebase, really wanted to do, but in the end they didn't pull it off after they moved to Google. So being open source was something developers really resonated with. And the Postgres side of things meant it was a relational database rather than a NoSQL database — and that ended up being a very important decision throughout the years as the shift kind of moved back to…

Host: So Firebase was actually NoSQL back end. Okay, that's super interesting.

Paul: Yeah. And so that open-source aspect — that community you build around yourself — was the first seed of that crazy growth that came after.

Host: Yes. Yes. And you know, it comes in waves, right? So the first one was that launch. Then, right before our Demo Day, we did another big launch for another product. And then after that we did another launch where we went from alpha to beta.

Host: So everyone was using you in your batch?

Paul: In our batch, no one was using us. So — well, we were the first remote batch, so we didn't have the same connection with everyone. But also I wouldn't have expected people to. You have to build up some credibility when you're a database company, so the founders are a little more conservative.

Host: They should be.

Paul: Um…

Host: How about today?

Paul: So today, now we've got — yeah, what — 10 million developers using Supabase.

Host: And at last, the YC companies use you?

Paul: Ah — so yeah, now every batch, I think on the last batch we had over 60% of the batch.

Host: 60% of a single batch. Okay, that's a show of confidence.

Paul: Yeah, that's much healthier.

Developer Experience 与 "time to value"

Host: That's awesome. And I think you speak a lot about the experience of people — you focus on the developer experience of using Supabase. Can you tell us a little more about what you're looking at?

Paul: Yeah. Developer experience can mean many things. The way we measured it at the start was a metric — time to value — and it was pretty basic. What we wanted to do was: we took another Postgres service (an AWS one) and we literally measured how long it would take for a developer to sign up, launch a database, connect to it, and then insert a row. And it was something like 8 minutes.

And then we wanted to do the same with Supabase and make sure that it was less than a minute. And today it's, you know, 5 seconds. We just wanted to bring the time to value right down.

Host: So it became a metric you were monitoring and optimizing for — whereas Amazon didn't. How fast is it on Amazon now?

Paul: Um, I'm not too sure. I know that they — actually, I've talked to the database team. We're actually quite close to the database team at AWS. And I know that they made that a priority last year.

Host: Last year. Okay. So until last year it was still 8 minutes?

Paul: Yeah, something like that. And then — of course that changes now. Time to value is important, but with the agentic move, maybe you don't care about time. You might kick something off, walk away for 20 minutes while the agent is building, and come back. And at that point the value is not so much the time but the ability to get to a result without further intervention. So, you know, time to value I still think is a key metric, but what that means is shifting.

AI 的三章

Host: Excellent. As you were sharing, it looks like the course of Supabase has some big jumps at some point of time. It feels like the AI kind of disruption also impacted you in a big way — starting with vibe coding applications using you?

Paul: Yeah, there were actually three chapters of AI in the database world, at least.

第一章：Vector databases 与 PG Vector

So the first chapter was when vector databases came out.

Host: Oh, I remember that time — embeddings. Seems like it's the distant past.

Paul: Yeah, yeah, yeah. It seems like that's the world now.

Host: It's crazy. And of course, now RAG — everyone saw RAG as this completely revolutionary thing.

Paul: I remember how vector DBs were the thing to look at.

Host: Yeah, yeah. And that was super interesting.

Host: But that actually impacted you — like people started using you because of PG Vector?

Paul: Yes, yes. So we were looking around for how to do embeddings, and it's actually quite a cool open source story. I received an email from someone and they said, "Oh, you know, I really want to use Supabase, but I need RAG." They wanted to build something, and I thought, "Oh, that's kind of cool." And they emailed in and they had created a pull request against our Postgres repo to add PG Vector.

Host: Oh, okay.

Paul: Which is developed by Andrew Kane — like a completely different person. So it's all open source. And then I got on a call with them and said, "Ah, what are you building?" And he explained it, and I thought, "Ah, that's kind of cool. But we need a way to demo it to our audience so that they understand it."

And so he developed for us this thing where we would embed all of our documentation, and then we added the ability to talk to our docs. And at the time, no one had done this.

Host: This was like start of '23, I think. What are we? What are we now — just '23?

Paul: Just. Yeah, I think chat GPT was just released — people were already used to chat.

It was super early in the RAG stage. And then we were really scared. Yeah. So actually it was the start of GPT — I don't know what model it was, but it was at the stage where everything was hallucinating, and so we were very scared that it would make up stuff.

So we released it as — do you remember Microsoft Clippy?

Host: Yeah, of course.

Paul: And Clippy would be completely unhelpful. And so we thought it would be funny to release it as a demo, but make the icon a Clippy icon — so that if it hallucinated, at least you'd have a laugh. And then since then, of course, as we know, everyone's doing RAG on their docs. But it completely came from this contributor.

Host: It feels like — yeah, it feels like PG Vector kind of took the whole market of Vector DB.

Paul: So we were the first to offer it, and of course Andrew had been developing it for many years. So it was really credit to him for leaning into it so hard. And then AWS as well adopted it, and from there it became the standard for Postgres. Actually, yeah.

第二章：Vibe coding 浪潮

Host: And so next chapter?

Paul: Next chapter — yeah, the next chapter was the vibe coding wave. Like Lovable, Bolt — they came in, I think at the end of '24. And we thought we were getting DDoSed at the time, because we saw some customer that was launching hundreds of thousands of databases, or tens of thousands at the time.

Host: Not your usual pattern.

Paul: No, no, very unusual. And, or, it might happen and we think, "Well, these people aren't going to be able to pay their bill." But they were incredibly successful from their launch. And so that was an interesting wave.

Even looking back now, it's kind of obvious: okay, all of these platforms will exist. But for us in that chapter, it was confusing. Should we support this type of profile? What is —

Host: Super small DBs — and you make money out of usage. So I guess most of these small databases were not really used?

Paul: Exactly. They might be doing prototypes, especially at the start — and now that's evolved so they actually are building real workloads. But at the time, we were thinking, these are very small databases. Do you really want to support them?

But the main thing is that we've always had this thesis since the start of our company: to build a generational database company, you need to be there at the start when people are getting started, and then make sure that they never want to leave. And so it was clear that people were building with this, and maybe in the future they would want to continue building in this model. So we leaned quite heavily into it, and then built out what is now this product that we call Supabase for Platforms — where other platforms like Lovable can build on top of Supabase.

Host: How many customers for that platform product?

Paul: Uh, I don't know — over 50, I would assume.

Host: But they're big ones, right? Each of them is actually pretty big.

Paul: Yes, and — yeah, even some enterprise customers want to adopt this internally for their own development.

Host: So that meant for you, in a way, some reacceleration of the business — the business starting growing way faster despite you being at a kind of already late stage.

Paul: Yes, yes. So yeah, at that stage it started growing even faster, when we thought, "Oh, well, this is a huge growth factor."

Host: All this graph — like the replot graph, like everything — sharpens, it gets steeper, the curve gets steeper. One of these…

Paul: So the more interesting one then was — because of course with this profile, we were considering, "All right, they're not getting to their growth stage as fast, we're launching a lot more databases, so as an average it works out." As a good — like the revenue, you could see it was sharpening up. But on an individual basis, it wasn't. It's more prototyping.

第三章：Claude Code 与全曲线抬升

But then came Chapter 3, which is the start of this year — or kind of Christmas last year, December release, Claude Code. And that's where things felt fundamentally different, because not only did our growth rate on the top of funnel increase (more developers pouring in), but basically every other chart started going up, which was unusual.

Host: What were the charts?

Paul: Activation — so getting to an active database. And then…

Host: People who would use Claude Code were doing way more than the people who would use Lovable?

Paul: Yes. And so they would activate faster, and then use more. They would get to a — let's take the average profile of someone using Claude Code: they would say, "Oh, I want to build this project." And then within a day, they would get to their conversion — as in, "It's a production database, and I want to start paying for it." And then they would put it out and probably be more successful. So the database grows even faster.

So basically every curve was going up and to the right. Which usually, when your top of funnel is going up and to the right — as in it's accelerating off the base — it's because you're pouring marketing dollars into your growth. We don't really pay much for marketing at all.

So the quality of our audience is getting even higher. We're not diluting our audience at all. It's just high-intent builders. And so because of this, Claude Code would get them more successful to a successful stage faster, and yeah, just our revenue would accelerate, our conversion would accelerate — everything accelerated.

Agent 已经是多数用户

Host: How many of your users are not humans anymore? Like, what's the agent? What's human?

Paul: Yeah, it's hard to say. I mean, of course they're all humans kicking off their agents. But from what we can actually measure, over 60% of databases are launched by an agent.

Host: Okay.

Paul: But more likely it's even higher. We just —

Host: Guess like 90, or…?

Paul: Yeah, yeah. Because if they're using Claude Code, they're just launching it from their CLI, and we don't have…

Host: Oh, you don't know when they do that.

Paul: Yeah.

Host: Okay. So you're undercounting.

Paul: Yeah.

Host: By a big margin. What does that mean, in this world where the vast majority of the situation is driven by an agent by AI? What does that mean for developer experience? I guess you're not really targeting the developers anymore.

Paul: I think the main thing is that the tooling will have to change so that it will work with agents. That's obvious, and everyone is doing that. So what that means for Supabase is that if you're using MCP or CLI, these have to be first-class citizens.

So in our earlier chapters, we were really focused on the dashboard experience of Supabase — because a human would come in and play around.

Host: They still come in?

Paul: They do. We still see our daily active users going up. But not as rapidly. They can get to a successful — so the percentage of people who spend time on the dashboard is way lower than…

Host: Lower.

Paul: Yeah, exactly. So once the tooling changes to focus on CLIs, getting everything down into code, then you have to have really nice Git workflows. So for us, we have a Supabase folder which should basically mimic what we have in the dashboard. And all of the surface areas should be able to work in lockstep. This is kind of the way that we're moving now. So if you do anything in the dashboard it should exist inside the code, and vice versa.

让模型知道你，比让开发者知道你更重要

Host: So it feels like, in a way, it's more important for you that models know about you than developers at this point — because I guess in a few years, people won't even care what's their back end.

Paul: Yeah. And that's true of any database, right? So — or any developer tool. We were very fortunate in that we started very early, 2020, probably the optimum time. And we had a huge community. So our community is on Reddit, they're on Discord, they're on…

Host: Like everywhere that models are training.

Paul: Training. And existing.

Host: And of course open source — the models know your code. So they're probably great at implementing on top of you.

Paul: Exactly, exactly. So getting recommended as a default was one of the things that was a huge tailwind for us. And it would be incredibly hard, especially now. I imagine that as we go along and people are producing a lot of content, the training of the models on content after 2023 is not going to be as high quality as things that are earlier on.

So we were very lucky, if I'm honest, on our timing, and doing it with the community that we had and the content that we had produced. So now we have to focus on — well, how do we retain that? But even if we don't, then, you know, let's say that the models all end up choosing AWS because that just defaults to be the same thing. Then, or us and every other dev tool are back on an equal playing field.

So how do you compete if the models already have their defaults? Then it's either partnerships, or you just have to win eyeballs of developers, and then they might have preferences that they guide the AI to use whatever they prefer. So it's still important to communicate to your community.

高速增长下的组织：从 order-maker 到 order-taker

Host: So three chapters where AI kind of had a big impact on you and accelerated growth. At this point, I mean, your course is insane. What does that mean operationally? Like, how do you actually scale as a company?

Paul: In the initial stages of Supabase, we had this really strict policy of hiring — and our policy was: you only hire when there is a hair-on-fire problem. So, something that a full-time employee could handle, and otherwise we just manage it.

Then as we started growing, of course, the amount of users pouring in, and the amount of support that we needed to give, and the amount of IP addresses running out, and all sorts of random things that you don't think about…

Host: Sounds like you don't think about that when you're small.

Paul: No. So what is like a planned roadmap ends up just being a lot of things coming in from the side, and partnerships coming in that you can't say no to, and all sorts of stuff that happen. So the shift goes from you pushing a lot to you basically being an order-maker to an order-taker.

And we have all these things coming in where we just didn't have enough hands on keyboard to solve them. And that of course means we've got to focus on reliability, and scaling up the meta processes of the company — managers, and hiring staff, and everything else. So you go through that second stage of: first you focus on your roadmap, then you focus on your business.

Host: How many people are you today?

Paul: Now we're about 360.

Host: Which is pretty small.

Paul: It's quite small for the scale of the business. But grown fast this year — I think we started the year at about 220. So we've had to add a lot of people this year.

Host: It's all mostly to pretty much support the growth. The business is going so fast.

Paul: Yes. All to — yeah, so that's where we switch.

Host: Can you give us a sense of how fast the business is growing?

Paul: I think maybe in terms of the number of developers — maybe in the past 12 months, at a guess, I think it would be six or 7x.

Host: Okay. So 7x at your scale is…

Paul: Yeah, of a base of millions.

Host: So we're already at millions of developers. And now we are, like, what, 10 million or something?

Paul: Yeah, we're at 10 million. Yeah, so I think we started this year with something like 6.5 million. And so the acceleration this year has been hard to keep up with.

Launch Week 与 Defrag：从交替到并行

Host: Wow. Okay. So you're just trying to keep the foundation working. So you don't have that much — how do you continue innovating then?

Paul: Yeah. I think we were very famous in the early stages for our launch weeks. And that was really a big focus on velocity, and getting the roadmap out, making sure that we've got feature parity with everything. And that was a good stage, and a lot of fun of course.

And then what we would do was: we would move from launch week — and we'd do this for 3 months — and then we would do a period afterwards which we would call defrag. And defrag is from the old computer term where you refactor everything and organize everything.

Host: So you'd alternate between these two things.

Paul: And then since maybe about 12 months ago, everything's felt like defrag, as we've had to grow and do a lot of initiatives. And that kind of points to a key change in the company — where we would previously work in lockstep as an entire company, and now we're having to move… so okay, you don't operate that way as an entire company. Some of you have to always be focused on defrag; some of you can, after you move past your SLOs as an engineering company, focus more on velocity. And we need to get to a more nuanced way where there's always both of these activities happening in parallel, and then making sure we have systems set up so that we can continue to do that.

Host: The success — this crazy success — actually has a cost.

Paul: Yes, it has a cost in the short term, and then you have to be very deliberate about how you can focus on both of these things.

分布式团队意外成为 AI 时代的护城河

Host: And does that kind of disruption from AI that helps you — does that change also the way you operate internally inside the company?

Paul: Of course, a lot of companies focus on flashy terms like "token maxing" and things like that. We haven't done that, but we also haven't had to. We've been very fortunate in one key thing: Supabase as a company is completely distributed. So we have 360 people and we're spread across 60 different countries — more than 60 countries.

So this means everything that happens is written down on Slack, on Notion, and…

Host: It's not like every other company that started doing that 6 months ago. You have done that for six years.

Paul: Yeah. And we've got the full history of Supabase written down all the way back to the start of the company. So if I want to find out what decision we made right at the start, I can ask Slackbot and find the answer.

Host: The context you have — like the complete context of the company, since inception, available to AI.

Paul: Yes, yes.

So when you use agents to help you in your job, they have — like, this couldn't have more context. Yeah, exactly. So new people coming in — or even they might not be new people, they might just be someone who is, let's say, a CFO or an analyst who wants to understand something — instead of coming to me and asking what the timelines are and how do I explain this product to an investor, they can actually ask a bot, and the bot will explain it better than I can. So that's nice.

And then from this point on, what I have traditionally thought of as just BizOps is now AI-enabled BizOps. So we're looking at systems that we can automate end-to-end, where we can introduce AI and automate the entire process — as long as it's an end-to-end process.

So things like — could be as simple as creating the AI notes, but also generating them, finding the action items, and feeding it all into a company operating system. Which hopefully at some stage, we're thinking of trying to move everything to Linear, including the non-engineering folk, so that we've got task management. And if we ever need to have bots solving things — of course the engineers are the ones adopting these tools now, but as we develop it with engineering, then it'll trickle out to non-engineering teams.

Host: So today you mostly will get a lot of productivity gain on the engineering side. But the next frontier is every other function.

Paul: I think — I wouldn't say productivity gain if I'm really honest, because I know a lot of people like to harp on about that, but I don't think it's proven out yet.

Host: That's what I think.

Paul: Yeah. I think, for a full productivity gain, you really need that full end-to-end process. So if you only unlock one piece of the puzzle, then you still need a full engineer stepping in. So the true gains will come from where you have no human in the loop.

We've seen some success in this actually on the data engineering team.

Host: So you mean like the human becomes the bottleneck here because they have to approve everything.

Paul: Yeah.

Host: And you already have some of these loops working with automation?

Paul: Yes, yes. So a good one was from our data engineering team. We now ingest everything into our data warehouse, and we use a tool called Hex — which is great, and it's got an agent — and we now opened up Hex to our entire company. So we kind of format the data warehouse so that the agent will understand the context. And this includes sales calls and things like that.

So now if anyone in the company — a salesperson, CFO, a product person — wants to understand something, maybe a metric, or our revenue growth, or even the history of a particular customer and what their needs are, they can go into this and they can ask a question. They will get a much more detailed answer than what a data engineer traditionally would produce.

And this is good because we now can measure: if a data engineer, in a traditional sense, could answer say 300 questions per month — we can see how many questions are being asked across the entire company. And it turns out that actually there are three times as many questions being asked, because of the way that they've engineered the data warehouse. So this is good — you can see that we're already getting some gains. Now what we want to see is that replicated out to other teams, where you very much have people focus on the systems part of it, and if those systems can unlock higher productivity, then that is great.

用"对照组"给销售发提成

Yeah, I think we've talked in the past about our sales team is another really interesting one.

Host: Yeah, where you can also…

Paul: Yeah, the sales team. So we traditionally operated on a PLG model. In fact, not even traditionally — it's all PLG. And then we thought, "All right, we want to introduce salespeople."

But what you would typically do, as you would know, is introduce some salespeople who kind of flounder around a little bit trying to sell something. But you know, we've got a bunch of data from our customers, and we also want them to be very helpful. So we can see that an account might have had a poor experience with the database — and so we can send, "All right, a thousand of these customers are growing very fast. They've hit some limits and they might be frustrated." So we'll send out an email to a thousand of them, and maybe 500 of them respond saying, "Yes, I want to get on a call." And then from there, the salesperson — or actually it's very much like a success or support person — gets on the call.

Host: But they still are getting commission?

Paul: Yes. So they get commission. But the way that we do this is: instead of compensating them on the entire account… so let's say a customer was spending $100 a month. If we measure the thousand — we take the entire cohort of a thousand — we take 500 who didn't respond. If at the end of the month their uplift is 25%, then that's our control group.

Host: Yeah.

Paul: But then if we take the cohort of people who actually chatted to the salespeople, and we know actually the uplift on that is 125%, so there's a 100% gain compared to the cohort who did not actually get on a call — and that's what the commission is based on.

Host: And then the commission is based on that.

Paul: So their input is actually quite measurable. And this is quite a different model from a sales-led motion.

Host: Mhm. And so they are compensated on the improvement from the default behavior that's already growing.

Paul: Exactly.

融资：现金不等于成功

Host: Awesome. Let's go back to maybe funding as the last topic here. Because, as you said before, you've gone through that hyper-growth a few times lately. I mean, that acceleration which led you to raise a lot more money — like in the last two years you did three rounds, and the last one was 500 million at over 10 billion valuation. And all that in less than two years. What does that mean for the company? Like, how do you stay grounded?

Paul: Yeah. Well, it's a lot of money. But of course, as you become bigger, you need a lot more operating cash to float you between two different periods — the period where you can launch a database and someone can build on top of it, and then they start paying you. So we of course want to have that operating capital to make sure that we can float between these two. And as long as we know the economics stack up, then it's very reasonable for us to continue doing that. So that's great.

Having the cash in the bank is basically to give us that operating capital.

Then from there, staying grounded is largely a factor of just remembering that the cash actually doesn't mean that you're successful. I think actually YC drilled this into you — where the fundraise itself is just a meta process.

Host: It's a means to an end. It's not…

Paul: It's just a — yeah, exactly. And if having more cash was the thing that made you successful, then by all rights Supabase would not exist. There are many of our competitors who have far more cash — huge companies — but still, we exist because we did things that they don't, and we should continue focusing on those things that we do very well as the way to continue to grow our stake in the market.

Host: How about the team itself? I mean, being grounded as a founder is the first step. But when the team sees these numbers, it's easy for them to probably get a little lost.

Paul: A lot of it spills out from the early founders. I mean, our way of operating is very much like a YC model, and then you hire in a bunch of people who are also of the same mindset. We've got a bunch of YC founders that work there, and a lot of ex-founders, and this trickles out into the rest of the organization. And then yeah, we try to treat our employees very, very well, but also be very transparent with them that, you know, we want to continue doing it in a way that we can look back and be quite proud of.

给 Dev Tool 创始人的建议

Host: To conclude — what kind of advice could you give to other, maybe dev-tool founders, who are starting today in this kind of unseen, unprecedented world they are navigating today?

Paul: The most generic advice that I can give — which they should already be doing — is: you have to be quite relentless and prolific. So you have to try many things, and when you find the things that work, then you have to relentlessly push on that thing to see where it can continue to grow. And then you try many things around it as well.

So as long as you have those two mindsets, then it basically translates to a grind mindset. And then, hopefully with a bit of luck, you should find some success. And luck is a very component — a very component of a successful startup.

Host: Awesome. Thank you so much, Paul, for joining us today and sharing your story.

Paul: Thank you.

Host: Thank you.

## 一、被冻结在模型权重里的"老树林"——一种前所未见的护城河
Paul 讲了一句几乎被采访者本人低估的话："2023 年之后训练模型用的内容，质量不会像更早期的那么高。"如果你把这句话往前推一步，会发现 Supabase 拥有的最深护城河，不在产品里，而在**每一个大模型的权重里**。
2020–2022 年他们在 Hacker News、Discord、Reddit、GitHub 上留下的每一行讨论，都被当时"干净的、人类写的、非 AI 生成的"语料吸进了 GPT-4、Claude、Gemini 的基础训练集。这些权重不会因为竞争对手今年融了多少钱而重写。竞对哪怕拿 10 亿美金去做内容营销，产出的也是 2024 年之后的"AI-slop 时代"内容，权重更低、被去重的概率更高。
这本质上是一种**"时间性的训练数据资历"（temporal training-data seniority）**——像老树林生态系统一样，一旦砍掉就再也长不回来。跨领域对比：这和中世纪教会为什么能垄断"神圣性"是同一个结构——它抢在了印刷术普及之前把自己写进了所有手抄本。谁在语料"清洁期"里发声

item.title: [Lex Clips] Does Khabib hate Conor McGregor? | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、情绪即战术：冷静不是修养，而是"武器化的自我"

大多数人把 Khabib 的冷静理解为"高情商"或"东方式克制"，但仔细听他的原话——"你会更快疲惫、更容易上当、更容易倒下"——他谈的其实是能量经济学。情绪不是道德问题，而是热力学问题：愤怒会以极高的功率消耗有限的糖原储备。这解释了一个被忽视的悖论：在八角笼里，最"冷血"的人往往是最诚实地对待自己身体极限的人。McGregor 的挑衅之所以危险，不是因为它侮辱人，而是因为它试图让对手替自己燃烧燃料。Khabib 拒绝上钩，本质上是拒绝为对方的战术做免费的代谢劳动。

二、跨领域连接：交易员、狙击手、外科医生的共同秘密

Khabib 描述的那种"press conference、weigh-in、媒体面前全程压制"的状态，与顶级期权交易员在市场崩盘时的心率数据、狙击手扣扳机前的呼吸控制曲线、以及心脏外科医生在术中意外出血时的语速变化——三者在生理指标上高度重合。共同点是：他们都必须在"情绪回报最丰厚的时刻"选择延迟满足。有趣的是，Khabib 自己承认"打完之后我让情绪全部涌出"——这暴露了一个反直觉的系统真相：极致的自控不是压抑，而是精确的情绪时序管理。他不是没有仇恨，而是把仇恨排程到了对结果无害的时段。这才是"冷静"的工程学定义。

三、意外观察：八年后的"惊讶"，才是这段访谈真正的深水区

大多数人会聚焦"他有没有恨 Conor"，但真正的爆点被埋在最后一句："looking back, I'm a little surprised… it wasn't easy." 这句话泄露了一个更深的秘密——当年的 Khabib 自己也不完全相信自己能做到。也就是说，那种传奇般的冷静并非天生的性格特质，而是一次高风险的自我实验，一次他事后才敢承认"其实很悬"的走钢丝。这里藏着一个反常识的领导力真相：外界看到的"稳如泰山"，内部体验往往是"勉强扛住"。这与创业者、总统、宇航员在事后回忆重大决策时的语言模式惊人一致——当事人越是事后表达"惊讶自己做到了"，说明当时的心理裕度越薄。真正的强者不是没有裂缝的人，而是知道自己裂缝在哪里，并把战斗安排在裂缝扩大之前结束的人。Khabib 打完就退役，某种意义上，也是这套系统性认知的延伸：他知道那口"冷静的井"不是无底的。

📝 转录文本

关于内心的愤怒与仇恨

Well, when you look into your heart back then and now, did you have anger? Did you have hatred for him?

Back then and even now, I'd still keep a cool head. Nothing has changed.

情绪失控的代价

When you let your emotions take over, when they're off the charts and you completely lose control, that's a very bad place to be. So you'll tire out faster. You'll fall. You'll fall for any kind of bait and so on.

I just knew that I needed to stay calm, composed, to stick to the plan no matter what happened, and not go beyond my emotional limits. This is a very, very dangerous moment when you give in to your emotions. You have to control them. Every single detail, every little thing has to be perfectly in place. The second you let it all slip, everything becomes a total mess.

比赛结束之后的释放

So once the fight was finally done, I just let all my emotions out. I had to step right in and prove it, and punish him, and show them I'm better, that I'm better than him, and put a final end to this whole bitter rivalry. When all of that was over—

Your emotions came out?

…that's when my emotions just went over the edge.

But until the fight was completely finished, starting from training, you know, at the press conferences, at the weigh-ins, everywhere, in front of the media, everywhere, I kept myself completely under control, and I was very good at it.

八年之后的回望

Honestly, looking back it's been almost eight years now. Looking back, well, I'm a little surprised. At that point, I was a very emotional guy, too. Over these eight years a lot has happened in my life, but I'm surprised that I kept it together.

And well, you know, it wasn't easy for me to keep myself within my limits, to keep myself under control like that.

item.title: [Business of Sport] Walter & Boehly’s Rumoured Chelsea Exit, the PFA Takes on the EFL, & The Meteoric Rise of Padel
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个故事，一个隐藏的主线：当"体育资产"被当作"金融工具"使用时会发生什么

一、LIV Golf：不是财务失败，而是"声誉套利"的反向清算

表面看，LIV 拖欠奖金和供应商账款是流动性问题。但如果你把 PIF（沙特公共投资基金）进入 LIV 的初衷理解为"用金钱购买声誉"的套利交易，你会发现一件出人意料的事：这笔交易正在以极高的杠杆倒挂。

沙特一开始的隐含逻辑是：即便烧掉 20 亿美元，只要能"洗白"国家形象、让世界习惯 Saudi = Sport，投入就是划算的。但现在的局面是——每一美元未支付的账单，都在以 5–10 倍的效率反向摧毁那笔"声誉投资"。这跟 WeWork 崩塌时的机制完全一样：叙事型资本一旦叙事反转，估值会以非线性速度归零。

更狠的一个观察：主持人提到的"付大 V 不付小供应商"的分流策略，在金融机构处置有毒资产时是标准操作（想想 2008 年雷曼破产时的债权人分级）。体育行业正在被迫学习投行的"声誉三角"——先保住能上头条的债权人，再牺牲沉默的多数。这是体育史上第一次，一个赛事组织公开采用了华尔街的破产分选逻辑。

二、PFA vs EFL：这不是劳资纠纷，是"谁承担系统性风险"的哲学之战

主持人拿 Arthur Scargill（1980 年代英国矿工工会领袖）来比喻 Maheta，已经是一个漂亮的类比。但真正被忽视的一层是：PFA 的"更大傻瓜理论"（bigger idiot theory）——总会有更蠢的下一个买家接盘——跟加密货币牛市末期的心态一字不差。

这里有一个跨领域连接非常尖锐：72 家英足联俱乐部中 47 家在挂牌出售，卖方远多于买方——这是流动性衰竭的经典信号，在房地产、艺术品、乃至 SPAC 市场都出现过。PFA 押注的是"接盘侠永续存在"，但接盘侠是利率环境的函数，不是体育情感的函数。当全球利率不再零成本，"社区情怀 + 亏损运营"这个商业模型的定价基础就崩塌了。

更让我震惊的洞察：足球俱乐部第一次要面对"没有下一个买家"的存在性问题——而 PFA 用的是 1960 年代 Jimmy Hill 反抗最高工资时的思维框架来打 2025 年的仗。工会用一个"稀缺型经济"（球员被剥削）的斗争剧本，来对付一个"过剩型危机"（俱乐部无法出售）的现实，这在结构上注定错位。

三、Mark Walter：体育行业刚刚发现自己变成了"影子银行"

Walter 的故事是本期最深的一个信号。他被指控用保险公司浮存金去买 Dodgers、Lakers、Chelsea——这个模式听起来很熟悉是吗？这正是 Warren Buffett 的 Berkshire Hathaway 模型：用保险浮存金作为超低成本长期资本去投资优质资产。

但这里有个惊人的反转：Buffett 投的是有稳定现金流的"经济护城河"企业；Walter 投的是没有现金流、只有资本增值故事的体育队。这本质上是把"影子银行"和"数字艺术品"嫁接在一起——保险监管的红线（10% 单一敞口）遇到体育资产的估值狂热（4 年翻倍）。

跨领域连接：这跟 2021 年 Archegos 爆仓、以及 Greensill/GFG Alliance 崩塌的机制几乎完全同源——将高流动性负债（保险赔付义务、供应链应付款）与低流动性资产（体育股权、钢厂设备）错配。SEC 现在盯上 Walter，其实是在向整个行业释放一个信号：当体育队的价格达到 100 亿美元级别时，它们已经不再是"玩具"，而是必须按金融资产被监管的"系统重要性物品"。

未来 3–5 年最不被讨论、但最关键的变化：大型体育资产的买家池会从"富豪个人"永久性地转向"必须接受金融监管的机构资本"。这将改变所有权文化——想想 Todd Boehly 与 Clearlake 的内斗为什么会公开化：私募基金 vs. 富豪 clanky 家族办公室，是两种不兼容的治理哲学。

四、Padel 的隐藏悖论：唯一一个"网络效应为负"的运动

关于 Padel，播客的分析已经很扎实，但漏掉了一个反直觉的结构性问题：

Padel 是唯一一个"稀缺时最赚钱、丰裕时最健康"的运动。

  • 球场稀缺 → 每小时 100 英镑 → 投资回报好 → 但精英层培养不出来（没有场地练习）
  • 球场丰裕 → 单场收入下降 → Sweden 式的商业崩盘 → 但精英层能起飞

这在经济学上叫"网络效应反转"——大多数运动（篮球、足球、跑步）随着参与者增多，每个参与者的效用都上升；但 Padel 的商业价值和竞技价值是反向拉扯的。

跨领域连接：这跟精品咖啡产业的困境几乎一样——第三波咖啡馆越多，单店利润越薄，但整个品类的品味培养和从业者水平却提升。Padel 想成为一个全球性的观赏运动，必须先经历一段商业上的"下沉痛苦期"——而目前的资本方（大多是把它当作房地产 + 会员制生意做的）根本不愿意支付这个成本。

最出乎意料的预测：Padel 会先在印度或东南亚（而非美国）实现真正的爆炸性增长，因为那些市场的中产阶级密度 + 土地成本 + 社交型运动偏好，恰好是 Padel 商业模型的最佳温床。而当这一天到来时，欧洲的 Padel 泡沫可能已经破了一轮。

贯穿本期节目的隐藏主线：体育资产正在经历一场"金融化的成熟"——它不再是富豪的浪漫玩具，而是被利率、监管、破产法、劳资关系等成人世界的规则同时压迫的资产类别。LIV 的账单、Walter 的保险、EFL 的成本控制、Padel 的场地经济学——它们都是同一个故事的四个切片：体育终于长大了，但相关方还在用小孩子的规则思考。

📝 转录文本

开场：LIV Golf、EFL vs PFA、Walter/Boehly、Padel 的四重叙事预告

If you think about where this all started out as being the thing that was going to eat the PGA Tour, was going to totally reshape the future of golf, it's one of those situations that ends up becoming not just a financial failure, but a colossal reputational disaster.

Of the 72 Football League clubs right now, 47 of them are up for sale.

The key point is they've picked on this because a change has been made without them being consulted. That's the party line.

It is now strongly rumoured within the media that Mark Walter and his business partner, Todd Boley, are entering discussions about selling their stake in Blueco, the owners of Chelsea, to their partners at Clearlake. $20 billion is reportedly what he needs to earn by the end of the year.

Let's blitz paddle. There's two parts of this that are fascinating. One is a participation sport that is absolutely booming, and the other is a professional sport which is struggling to match the interest and attention that has been given to it from a participation level. Charlie, do you see it as having a serious future as a spectator sport?

Fantasy Football League 推广

Before we start, who doesn't love a fantasy football tussle? The Business of Sport Fantasy Football League is up and running and looking super competitive. And why wouldn't it be when we put the football mouse of our esteemed audience to the test?

For your chance to win football tickets to a team of your choice and your very own personalised Business of Sport football shirt, sign up today before the deadline at 6.30pm. The link and the sign-up code are in the description below. We'll see you there.

开场闲聊：康沃尔的四人球赛

Good morning, Charlie. Hello, Charlie. I'm extremely well. May I say how much I'm missing you down in Cornwall since you've gone back up to the big smoke to put your nose to the grindstone. But it was a very happy little weekend we had together, wasn't it?

Oh, it was brilliant, wasn't it? I mean, there was... Should we start with the main news?

The main news. I think the main news is... Well, the main news is, for those of our listeners and viewers who are golfers, which will be many of you, I don't doubt, and who have played fours golf as opposed to singles golf, is when a new partnership is formed in golf, it's always with a little bit of trepidation. You never quite know whether the whole thing is going to come together and whether it's going to end up being fist bumps around the green or cold death stares shot as yet another mishap lands the other one in terrible trouble.

But in this case, thankfully, Charlie Senior and Charlie Junior managed to hold it together really quite well, I thought, Charlie. I mean, we won, didn't we?

We won a very important match for me as well against my father-in-law and a partner of his who's a very capable golfer. And as I mentioned, I think the last time I played with my father-in-law in Spain, I took a bit of a beating. So it was really important. Not just that we got this kind of breakdown partnership off to a good start, because let's be honest, for the amount of rubbish we talk, we need to actually be able to eventually put our money where our mouth is when we actually compete.

We have to walk the talk. We have to walk the talk. And when it came to performance, I have to say, we hold an awful lot of six-foot putts between us.

That's how you win them, isn't it? It's where the millions come from. They always say you can have the biggest, sexiest driver in the bag, but that putter has to be hot.

Anyway, it was really good to get out. I loved it. It was great fun. A tidy little pairing. And look, everyone just thinks our sub stacks for extra content and a bit of fun. No, no, no. If you want to come and have some participation in events with us, like little golf matches, that's where you've got to be. We will absolutely be taking challenges from anyone in the audience. All proceeds from these challenge matches to go to help top up live tour prize money.

As anyone who knows their golf, well, let's get straight on to that.

第一幕：LIV Golf — 从"吞噬 PGA Tour"到无法支付账单

But as anyone who knows their golf is, the arrogance and confidence we seem to show right now is only as good as backing it up and so we've got to win two in a row before we get too confident. But on LiveTour prize money, Charlie, I don't think we'll just be topping up LiveTour prize money. I think we could be paying some of their invoices because if you believe what you've been reading recently, and by recently I mean in the last few days, and there's more and more of these stories coming out, it seems like there's not just the players that have some outstanding payments to be made, but also a huge number of their vendors.

未付奖金与供应商账单

Yes. So just to bring people up to date, this time last week, Charlie and I did a segment on Live Golf and noted that the thing that we had predicted back in January had finally come to pass and that the tour had basically run out of money and would not be holding their final event of the season, which was due to be held in early September, which was their doubles event, team, so their team championship, and that the team championship effectively would be rolled into the last singles tournament of the season that is, I think, happening pretty much now.

But effectively what has since come out is that even the prize money for that tournament, which is the final tournament of this season on LIV, has been cut and that there are vendors who still have been unpaid and that as yet payment has still not been made to the golfers of the prize money from the previous event. Whereas normally, of course, in golf events, prize money gets paid pretty much on the nail and the tours have all the golfers' bank account details and it pretty much gets wired across the next day. 10 days after that previous tournament the prize money had still not been paid across.

新投资进来后要先填哪些坑？

So you've got all of that happening on the one hand at the same time as, you know, we were being told two weeks ago by the chief executive of Live Golf that apparently new investment is coming in to safeguard the next two years. But the question I asked, Charlie, is, you know, when that new investor looks at this entity, how much of that money is going to need to be paying unpaid bills and particularly contracts with the golfers, which have yet to be fulfilled?

I mean, they talk about converting that into equity in the new entity. But what happens with those golfers who say, no, I just want to have my contracted money? I'm sorry. That's just the way it goes. Are they going to need to go into a form of administration or Chapter 11 and effectively create something totally new?

谁被优先偿付？"声誉分级"的破产策略

It looks like that, doesn't it? I mean, it looks like if they're not going to pay it, it's the only way to do it. They have to restructure some of the debts they've got within the business. And if they can do that effectively, then they'll take some of those liabilities away and the people that get burned will get burned.

I wonder if it is going to be a situation where they pay, and this may sound weird, they pay some of the biggest debts to the individuals, the players, the ones that I would say could do the most damage to the reputation from an optics perspective. And the people that are owed a few hundred thousand, which in the context of some of the bigger checks is not a lot of money, get left behind. And they will have to file their lawsuits and they will have to go through processes. And it's almost a game of, well, you know, take it as far as you want. But it's going to be a lot of cost attributed to some of these cases to get back what is not going to be a huge amount of money based on where the legal fees could go.

"声誉投资"的反向清算

The reason I say that is because, Charlie, when we've spoken about this from a financial perspective before with PIF and LIV, the critique and the pushback that we've had from people has been, but guys, don't forget, this wasn't just a financial play from them. This was about reputation and branding and media exposure. Well, let's flip that on the other side. That may be true. But what this is also now is a significant amount of their reputation exposure branding that is now being pulled back and dragged in the way that they wouldn't ideally want it to be.

So I wonder how much of that will influence some of the decisions that are made in the coming months, whether they look to protect themselves in some ways by optically paying the John Rahms, let's just say, right, the people that will get the most news coverage around it. And those people that would be classed as the smaller liabilities, the smaller debts to be paid, they're the ones, the 100,000 service provider, they're the ones that could get left behind.

If you think about where this all started out as being the thing that was going to eat the PGA Tour, was going to totally reshape the future of golf, you've been reduced to a situation where even having cancelled one event, even to get the previous event on, having to sort of do so by robbing Peter to pay Paul, you know, sort of managing cash flow and all this type of stuff. And meanwhile, with all the sort of, you know, noise out there being that John Rahm is going to leave the tour, etc. It's one of those situations that ends up becoming not just a financial failure, but a colossal reputational disaster.

And I think you're right. I mean, logically, what needs to happen here is there needs to be a halt called and there needs to be an assessment made about the bills that do need to be paid to make sure that the reputational damage isn't lasting.

沙特实体的付款声誉问题

I have to say that this wouldn't be the first time that people within the sports industry were left trying to chase bills from Saudi entities. There have been rumours in the boxing and Formula One undergrowth in the recent past about a difficulty in getting invoices settled and this type of stuff.
