item.title: [YC Root Access] How Olivier Pomel Built Datadog By Refusing Every Shortcut
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、court-martial 与信任的悖论：对手关系里藏着最深的合作契约

最令人意外的细节，是 Olivier 与 Alexi 相识的方式：Alexi 因入侵校园网被"军法处置"，而 Olivier 正是执行"断网判决"的人。26 年后，他们共同创立了 800 亿美元市值的公司，并保持了极其稳定的合伙关系。

这与常识直觉相反——通常我们以为共同创业的密友源于"惺惺相惜"，但这里恰恰是"对立初见"孕育了终极信任。深层原因是：两个人在第一次接触时就在同一层"元规则"上相遇——一个执行判决，一个愿赌服输，都尊重系统规则本身。这比任何情感认同都更牢靠。

这个模式在跨领域反复出现：免疫系统的成熟依赖早期病原暴露、司法制度里资深检察官和辩护律师私下常是好友、围棋高手在对局中比在酒桌上更容易识别彼此。真正的合伙关系不是从"喜欢"开始，而是从"验证对方在压力下如何处理边界"开始。他们后来定期共进午餐、在重大决定（如出售公司）前反复对齐，本质上是在延续那次校园冲突所建立的"元协议对齐"机制。

二、CEO 作为自己直觉的 RLHF：采样式管理背后的贝叶斯先验

Olivier 描述他每天读客户工单、销售对话、产品简报，偶尔回复一个问题——他称之为"训练数据"、"fine-tuning my own data"。这个比喻远比听上去精确。

传统 CEO 收到的是"向上管理过的信息"——层层筛选后的高层摘要。这类信息的问题不是失真，而是方差被系统性压缩：所有异常（anomaly）在向上传递的过程中都被平滑掉了。Olivier 的采样机制专门保留"高方差样本"，用来校准他的先验分布。当高层汇报的故事与他的采样样本不一致时，他能立刻检测到"分布漂移"。

更妙的是那个"jolts people"的副作用——他只需偶尔回复一封邮件问"这是怎么回事？"，中层管理者就会自发地开始"向下看"。这是量子测量式的管理：观察行为本身改变了被观察者的行为。同一原理出现在：流行病学的哨点监测（不测全部人口，只抽样关键节点）、生态学的相机陷阱（稀疏采样反而比密集监控更能捕获稀有事件）、审计学的意外抽查制度。共同规律是：在大型系统中，感知反馈的价值不来自完整性，而来自不可预测性。

三、Usage-based 定价的隐藏进化优势：为什么同一波 AI 浪潮，是他的顺风、别人的逆风

一个被严重低估的观察：Olivier 提到 AI 时代 seat-based（按席位收费）公司必须重构商业模式，而 Datadog 因为 usage-based（按用量收费）"doesn't really matter"——反而随 AI 生成的海量代码、GPU、模型基础设施而爆发。

这不是运气，是商业模式与技术底层耦合方向的问题。Seat-based 的假设是"人的数量 = 价值创造单位"，而 AI 正好在解耦人和产出。Usage-based 的假设是"计算事件的数量 = 价值创造单位"，而 AI 正好在指数级放大计算与事件。

跨领域对照极其惊人：在资源突然膨胀的环境（如寒武纪爆发、菌丝爆发）中，基于"细胞级事件"计量的生物（单细胞、菌丝网络）比基于"个体数量"的生物扩张得更快。收费单元的颗粒度决定了商业模式的可扩展维度——正如代谢单元的颗粒度决定了生命形式的可扩展维度。

更深的洞察是：Datadog 从来没有押注 AI，它押注的是"复杂性会持续增长"这个更底层的元趋势。云、微服务、Kubernetes、AI——每一波技术浪潮的共同点都是"生产更多需要被观测的事件"。他不需要预测下一个 X，只需要确定"世界会更混乱"。这是元层博彩策略：不赌哪匹马赢，赌赛马场会扩建。同样的哲学出现在：卖铲子给淘金者、AWS 卖 primitives 而非解决方案、Bloomberg 卖数据管道而非投资建议。

四、拒绝的复利：三次否定塑造的公司基因

反直觉观察：Olivier 反复强调 YC 拒绝、200M 收购拒绝、10x 收购拒绝、安全事故——这些"负面事件"是公司基因的主要塑造者。他明确说："everything that was very traumatic had a positive impact on the company"。

真正的机制不是鸡汤式的"打不死的更强"，而是：每一次拒绝或创伤都强迫组织做出一个不可逆的架构选择。YC 拒绝 → 必须建立自给的商业模式；早期无 VC → 必须直接对客户负责；安全事件 → 必须重构安全体系。这些选择在顺境中永远不会被主动做出，因为顺境奖励的是延迟决策。

跨领域对照：进化生物学中的"瓶颈事件"（population bottleneck）反而加速演化，因为它强制筛选；建筑学中"约束越强，设计越优雅"（日本 4.5 张榻榻米的茶室美学）；心理学中的 post-traumatic growth 机制正是"强迫重新组织意义系统"。

Olivier 唯一的后悔——"decide faster"——恰恰印证了这个模式：他希望自己更早地把"拒绝"应用到人员决定上。拒绝比接受更能塑造系统。

意外收尾观察

三个看似无关的细节合起来揭示了一个隐藏模式： - Alexi 被断网的故事 - 采样读支持工单的习惯 - 工程团队增长速度封顶在 2x/年

它们的共同点是：Olivier 系统性地选择"低带宽、高保真"的信息与增长通道。他不追求信息量，他追求信息的可验证性；他不追求团队规模，他追求组织的可整合性。这与今天所有公司追求的"数据驱动 + hypergrowth"背道而驰——他实际上是采样驱动 + 匀速增长（sampling-driven, sustainable-pace）。在一个信息过载、AI 生成一切的时代，这可能是最被低估的领导力配置。

📝 转录文本

How Olivier Pomel Built Datadog By Refusing Every Shortcut

Today, I welcome Olivier Pomel, the co-founder and CEO of Datadog. He created Datadog with Alexi back in 2010 just to help engineers figure out what was happening in their cloud. Now, he's built that company in the defining company of the cloud era. Welcome Olivier.

Great to be here.

The First YC Application (2010)

Great to have you. So, we're chatting before about your first YC experience actually. It was not today. It was back in 2010. Tell me, what happened then?

Yes, so we actually applied to YC in 2010. We got to the interview and we got rejected.

I'm sorry to learn that.

So, I still have, you know, the email from PG at the time. And you know, it turns out — so, he was saying at the time that we were building a platform, but the platform was only as successful as its first product.

Mhm.

And you know, a little revenge on life has been that we did make the platform successful in the end.

[laughter] Do you think it actually helped you in some way to show us — to show him — wrong?

Rejection as Fuel

I think so. First of all, I think many people who start companies go through a lot of rejection initially. I think that's normal. I think it's good, you know, to give you reasons to prove people wrong and to put a chip on your shoulder. And also, you know, I think the fear to fail that you feel initially, at least in our case, it helped really build up the culture of the company — making sure we were so obsessed about building something that was valuable. We were so obsessed about building a good business, a business that could be self-sustainable in case we couldn't raise money. And so, all of that, I think to this day remains the culture of the company, and we owe that to the difficulties early on.

I'm so happy to learn that we actually helped you in the end. [laughter] That's awesome.

From France to New York

Let's go back to the early days because you were born in France and then you moved to the US after — was that after college?

Yes, so I had an internship at the end of college in New York in research at IBM at the time. And I thought I would stay for 6 months and I ended up — and I'm still there.

How long have you been living there?

So it's been like 26 years now. It's been a while.

The Dot-Com Era

So you pretty much moved there just at the time of the bubble — the dot com.

Yes. So I lived through the end of the dot com boom and I actually worked in startups during the dot com boom.

Which was — was it an experience?

Yeah, it was super — it was weird, you know, because you could tell that things were happening that didn't make complete business sense. So, for example, the CFO of one of the startups every day went to the most expensive pastry shop in town and bought pastries for the engineers.

[laughter]

I think that was a red flag maybe, thinking about it.

I guess you don't do that today.

Yeah, we don't do that.

That's not the thing you learned from them.

Yes. But so I think the world was full of promise then. Then of course the dot com boom turned into a dot com crash. We've been through all of that. There were few years after that where it didn't look like technology would be worth anything ever again. So I stayed in New York and my co-founder for Datadog Alexi also stayed in New York.

But I guess you worked elsewhere.

Yes, we worked elsewhere. We started working for an educational software company. It was a tiny company — it was not our company but it was less than 10 people when we joined. And I ran the development team there and Alexi ran the tech ops team.

How He Met Alexi

And so did you meet Alexi there?

No, we knew him from before. We met actually briefly in school in France.

Okay.

And the funny story here is — I was part of the team that ran the campus network. And Alexi was caught hacking on the campus network. And so he was court-martialed by the student body and he was sentenced to disconnection, and I carried out the sentence.

That's a great way to get to know someone.

Yes. So, we didn't really interact all that much, you know. I thought he was this black hat guy. And then we ended up finding each other again at that IBM internship, basically. So, he was there too. And then you worked again together at the next company you joined. And then we worked together in a total of four or five companies.

So, you never worked in any place without him.

Yeah, basically. I mean, we always bring the other — like, you know, maybe one of us would go somewhere and then two or three months later we'd bring the other.

So, that's a strong relationship.

Yeah, yeah.

Sustaining a Founder Marriage

And then you co-founded Datadog together.

Yes.

And you're still working together there.

Yes.

Any secret of keeping that kind of marriage lasting like that?

Yeah, well, I mean, look, it takes effort. For one thing, before we started a company — because starting a company is pretty hard — before we started a company, we had known each other and worked together for more than 10 years. And so, we had tested a lot of the different ways the relationship can go. And we're also good friends. And that helped quite a bit.

After that, I think as we've grown Datadog, we've made sure we kept a lot of space for talking to each other. So we have these regular lunches and things like that where the whole point is just to talk.

No agenda, just open-ended conversation.

Yes. And there's one extra thing which is very important, which is anytime there's a big decision to make. So, for example, sell or not sell. As you grow a company, you're going to have folks every now and then that will try and buy you out. These are big decisions.

Deciding Not to Sell

And did you decide after getting a real offer, or did you decide to not even open the conversation?

We had those conversations when we had offers or when folks were pretty serious with us. And it's very important in those cases to make sure that you're on the same page. Because that's what can cause companies to blow up. One of the founders kind of wanted to sell and the other one didn't. But, you know, one maybe didn't really tell the other, or they told them what they thought they wanted to hear, but then it turns into a problem later on. So, it's very important to spend a lot of time talking at those points to make sure you really understand what each other want.

You bet. It's very easy in hindsight now to say, yes, of course that was the right decision not to sell. But I guess at that time it's a lot of money you leave on the table.

Yes, and there's no guarantee that your company is going to be successful. And you know, when I started Datadog, I remember seeing companies that refused an offer for 200 million. And I thought, well, who refuses 200 million? And then we refused that, and then we refused 10 times that, and then refused more than that even.

Going Public

When you became public, what was the first cap of the money?

So, we went public at sort of the go-public price was around 7 and a half billion. And we very quickly traded at 10, 12 up from that.

And then the roller coaster —

And then roller coaster.

To kind of like a much more today.

Yes, today we're around 80. But at the time it was around that. And we've refused large offers along the way, and again the thinking there is always — what's the upside? How do we think about the business? Are we done with what we wanted to do? Is there 5x, 10x more we can do? Do we believe in it? Do we want to do it? Is it exciting enough for us? And that's what I usually do.

With your life after —

[laughter] Yes, yes.

You retire.

Yes, yes. But that's the consideration. These are very full-time jobs. So, you have to be really into what you're doing and you also have to believe into the outcomes that come after that.

The Early Days: Pre-Cloud

You bet. But before being that successful, I mean, the early days were not that easy, right? I know when you started it was nearly pre-cloud, the very early days of the cloud, right?

Yes.

How did you approach that?

Yeah, so it was very hard from an understanding-market perspective. Alexi and I didn't come from systems management. So, most of the people who started companies in our space used to work for a vendor that made software, that sold software for that. We didn't have that. We also didn't come from a hyperscalar. So, we didn't come from a Google or one of the places that was operating at super large scale where maybe folks had some glimpse of the technology that can run that or the technology coming for the rest of the world.

So, because of that, it was very very difficult for us to convince investors initially. So, we mentioned YC, but pretty much every single other VC also passed on us at the time. So, it was a very humbling experience.

A lot of people will regret today, I guess.

Well, I mean, some of them invested later, right? So that's the thing with investors. There's always a next round. Maybe not for YC, but for everybody else there's always a next round.

Being at the Center of the Cloud Wave

The other part of it though is, because we didn't come from the space, we sort of saw things a little bit differently. Our starting point was not, "Hey, let's take that existing product category and make it better." Our starting point was, "Hey, there's this huge problem. Dev and Ops don't talk to each other and they fight all the time, and can we bring them under one roof and into one platform?"

So, we saw that in a way that I don't think the rest was seeing it — on the user side. What we didn't really fully understand was the importance of the cloud and the fact that what we were doing was right at the center of it. So, disintermediating, bringing Dev and Ops together — that actually is a big part of the cloud adoption. And of course, we at the time in 2010, Amazon or AWS was the only game in town and it was a toy. Companies — real companies — were telling you that they were never going to use that.

Nobody was ever going to move to the cloud, right?

Yes, exactly. And of course it happens. It was extremely broad, extremely deep. And so that was a big part of our success.

It took a — when I compare that to how fast people are adopting AI, for example, cloud took 10 years to get to full adoption.

Yes.

And in a way you were lucky — I mean lucky, you are smart, but you cannot like end up at the center of that revolution. And that's probably gave you a unique advantage compared to all the incumbents who didn't see it coming. Is that fair?

Yes, definitely. I think — and look, anytime you build a successful company, yes, there's a ton of hard work, there's probably talent too, but there's a lot of luck.

You have to create your luck. You need to try as many things as you can so that you expand that surface where you can be lucky.

Yes, but timing in particular is luck. Whether something is going to catch now or in two years — it makes the whole difference for a company, and it's really hard to predict really.

Culture: Looking Down, Not Up

Yeah. So one thing that came back often when I was discussing with ex-Datadog — I have had quite a few founders who came from Datadog or got acquired by you — mentioned the culture and how you as the founder are still very much heavily involved in like some product decisions. You are not at the strategic whatever PowerPoint level at all. Can you tell us a little more about how you see that and how you make these decisions?

Yes, so there's something that's very important, which is that I and the rest of the management team have to understand what really happens on the ground. The problem you have as the company grows is that you develop these beautiful stories and then people tend to manage up. They want to be able to tell good news to management, and that's human. That's just the way people are wired.

And so everything I do there in terms of the systems we put in place is to force people to look down instead of up. To look at what's actually happening. What's happening with the customers? What's happening with the product? What's happening with the technology? What's working and not working?

Sampling as Management Practice

And concretely what does that mean day-to-day?

So day-to-day what I do is I sample a lot of the stuff. I'm going to read support requests. I'm going to read sales conversations. I actually read all of the product briefs — like all of the product releases and everything we do — to make sure I understand exactly what's going on there. And what I will do is occasionally I will reply and I will ask questions like "what's going on there?" or "I don't understand this part." And very often the first thing that happens after that is the person who wrote that email, putting that conversation in the system, says: why is he looking at that?

[laughter]

And what it does is it kind of jolts people a little bit and also forces the local management chain to look down and better understand what's going on there because I maybe asked about it. And on an ongoing basis it forces people to understand exactly the reality under them as opposed to just reading a beautiful message. And on my end, it sort of trains the machine — I get a sense of reality, a sample reality, and then I can also figure out what agrees and doesn't agree with the stories I see at the higher level.

That's your own training data.

Yes.

You're fine-tuning your own data.

And I think that's why also, when you deploy AI in particular, it's not good to automate everything — like it still has to go through your brain at some point for you to get an understanding of what's going on.

Yes, you cannot delegate decisions like the driving of the company.

Yeah.

How do you make these product decisions then? Like it feels like you could also become the bottleneck here if people need your opinion on everything.

So we try to set up in a way where feedback — or executive feedback in particular — is possible but not required. So things are going to move along anyway.

Okay.

And they're going to move along with a number of communication points where you see what's happening, you see what's going to be released or you see what has been released. Feedback can happen at any point there but people don't wait for it.

There's a few specific hard changes — for example, when you change the pricing and packaging of some products, or things that can have a large impact and that are hard to back out of — where you have some pre-approvals. But for pretty much everything we build, people just push it out. Maybe there's feedback, maybe there's no feedback.

So if it's life-threatening for the company, of course you have — you are like a feature. But if it's like relatively low-stake decisions, nobody's waiting for anyone.

Or high-stakes but you can reverse them easily. In B2B, it's very easy also to test some products with some customers, make some changes for some customers, see how it works, and that's actually how we build in general — we see at a small scale with some customers how it works, whether it improves things for them a lot, and then we roll that up more broadly.

Product Decisions: Three Sources of Innovation

So you started with just infra monitoring — I think you were not even calling that observability yet — and then you expanded to many other aspects of observability as a high-level term. How do you decide to build a new product? What's your process here?

Yeah. So mostly we see what our customers do with our product. We see what kind of situation they put us in and what kind of extensions and scripting and other things they build around us, and that gives us an idea of the problems they have and also where they think we belong.

So, for example, when we expanded from infrastructure monitoring at the time to APM — tracing applications, basically — we were seeing our customers build simple versions of that themselves on top of our platform. And so it was pretty clear that they wanted us to do that.

Instead of doing it yourself.

Yes. And we saw the same thing when we saw customers doing security automation with us — instrumenting their security posture and doing security automation with us. So it was pretty clear there was something we could do for them in that area. So that's really what drives most of the new [products].

And does that come from the teams who are seeing that today when they interact with customers? Is that some top-down approach here?

So there's actually three parts.

One: customer feedback. Customer feedback is the majority of the changes we make. The good thing about customer feedback is that you're generally right — you have enough customers, you have enough feedback, and usually it's right. The bad thing about customer feedback is that it's often very incremental. "I want fix that button, please," or "I need another integration."

We want the faster horses.

Yes. And that's great, but you do all of that. But then in addition to that, there's the more top-down — which I regrettably call strategic.

It's not the word you like to use.

I hate that word. But basically: hey, we know that we're going to new areas that are a bit different. There's less direct feedback from customers about it, but we know it's going to be important and we have proof points that it would be relevant for us. So you do some of that. You'll be wrong more often when you do that, but you need to do it.

And then the last part is completely bottom-up. The engineering teams or the product teams solved a problem that they thought needed solving, and are building products out of that. Could be an internal need. We built an internal platform for something and we want to productize it. Could be somebody saw something interesting with some customers and they want to try and build it. It didn't come from me, it didn't come from anybody in leadership. We don't have a lot of data from customers saying that it's needed, but somebody wanted to build it.

I mean, they experienced the pain, they solved it, and in a way that's validation.

Yes. And it's important to keep all of those. Of course customer feedback — you need to act on it. Of course you need to go in very deliberately into new directions. But also you need to keep room for internal innovation.

Scale: 25 Products, 8,000 Employees

So, how many products do you have today?

We have about 25 that we charge for.

25 products publicly released. Can I buy?

Yes.

And how many employees?

We have 8,000 employees.

8,000. Okay, so that's kind of like a complex organization to get right here.

Yes, but the way the products are adopted is somewhat similar to what you might see in a cloud provider like AWS.

I believe better.

Yes, well, that's the whole point. But the point here is you don't have 25 different sales processes and sales teams and everything. So, that's much simpler from that perspective.

Public Life and Market Volatility

That makes sense. And then there was that AI kind of complete disruption of the business and the market, right? How did you go through that? I guess — were you taken by surprise? Did that affect you? Once you're public, of course the market is more volatile. How did it react?

Yeah, I mean market volatility, I think we're kind of used to. We went public in 2019.

Mhm.

Pre-pandemic. Before — you went through ups and downs there.

Yeah, I mean our lockup expired the day of the lockdowns. So huge market crash the same day our lockup expired. The stock was down like crazy. Everybody was watching in horror at the time. Also, I mean the world was pretty scary too at the time if you remember.

Yeah. Nobody knew what would come next.

And it probably ended up being worse than what we thought at the time too, like in terms of how long it lasted.

But maybe business-wise it was not as bad as you —

No, business-wise it was actually a seesaw. The market crashed and the market went back up very quickly, and then we've seen more gyrations like that over time. So markets going up and down, I think we're used to.

We actually educate the company quite a bit on that. So every quarter we have an all-hands where we go through all of the results. And we always end up with a slide that says: in the short term, the stock market is a voting machine. In the long term, it's a weighing machine. And so, hey, what happens today doesn't matter. What really matters is we build enough of the right things, we find enough of the right customers for it, we deliver the right service, and then everything will be fine.

The AI Disruption

Okay, makes sense. How about the AI impact? Like I guess the market reacted to you being the incumbent. Earlier on you were kind of the disruptor, but by now you are the incumbent yourself.

Yeah. So, two things. One is — yes, technically we lead the observability market, but we only have 13% of it according to the measures. And that market is going fast, so the bulk of the opportunities is still ahead of us there.

On the AI side, I think it's difficult for public investors to understand who's winning and who's losing in the long run because it is fairly disruptive. It's changing a lot of the product needs, it's changing quite a few things. It's also disrupting business models. In our case, it doesn't really matter — in our case, we're usage-based. But many companies that are seat-based, for example, have to rethink how their businesses are going to be structured.

So on our end, we're actually quite busy building products both for the AI builders, I would say — like, so, yes, customers.

Yeah, AI companies as customers.

Yes. And also for all the other companies that are starting to consume AI. And then in addition to that, we're also building AI into our own product for automation. So we have these two big initiatives that initially we called them Datadog for AI and AI for Datadog.

AI as Tailwind, Not Headwind

In a way from kind of a scare of the market because you are the incumbent that was going to be disrupted by AI, you became a winner of the AI change. Because that's more customers, bigger customers, new products.

Well, on the one end, there's so much more demand — there's more software, more infrastructure, more everything, and it's getting —

Business now is AI companies.

So, we stopped disclosing it, so I can't give you the exact number because we choose which metrics to disclose. But we serve like the top 10 AI companies in the world.

Okay.

And they're growing fast. But we also serve all of the other startups — or not all, but a good fraction of the other startups — that are building and scaling fast.

Did you reaccelerate then?

Yes. So, we saw substantial reacceleration of the business. And if you zoom out, if you look at just the sheer amount of complexity there is in terms of the build-out, the GPUs, the models — the models themselves are really hard to manage and monitor and secure and everything else.

But in addition to that, the crazy amount of code that is being produced with coding agents — the fact that now the code when it's written, you actually don't know it. You don't understand it.

You can't even read the code anymore.

No, you haven't written it. You don't know what it's using. You don't know what the components are behaving like. So a lot of the value is actually shifting from the writing of it to the validation and the operations. And that's where we are. We live in production. We live in contact with the real world.

So the great news is there's tons of opportunity there. The painful news is it's actually a lot of work to add everything we need to add to make sure that we can shepherd the code and the applications every step of the way and keep up with everything that's going on on the AI side.

You better not, I guess. But that's probably very exciting to have a complete new space of potential products to build.

Yes. And look, the whole space has been chasing AI automation ever since the first infrastructure monitoring product came out — like I think there was maybe something about AI in it even 20 years ago, 30 years ago. It never quite worked. Today, at least, there's actually a lot you can do that can work. So the dream of — instead of waking you up at 2:00 a.m. so you can fix your software, having the machine do that —

Machine gets woken up.

And then the following day it tells you, "Hey, by the way, I fixed it. You want to check it out?" That's a much better experience, and that's actually within reach now. So that's pretty cool.

Internal AI Adoption

How about your own internal use of AI? Did you transform the company? And what can you share today?

Look, the biggest impact is on the development side. I think most software companies —

Everyone is using code guard or —

Yes. I mean everybody across the company is using it and it's helping every single side of the business. But there's much more upside on the engineering side right now than there is, for example, on the sales side. You can improve productivity a little bit, but you're not going to multiply productivity by two, three, four, 10 — like maybe you can at least in some parts of engineering.

At least we are not there yet, but who knows?

Yes. But there I think the killer apps have been invented for engineering. They haven't been invented yet for some other areas.

And so, my co-founder actually stood in front of the whole team a couple of months ago saying that within two quarters, we mostly don't write code anymore.

Was that two quarters ago?

It was a few months ago. So I think we're on the same schedule as most companies — almost tech companies — where we had an epiphany in December.

New model capabilities kind of like step change.

Exactly. New models and also maybe a little bit of free time for some people to experiment.

I think it was the Christmas holidays.

Yes. And then everyone could tinker.

Yes.

And discovered how powerful the models had become.

Yes. And so, look, it's not completely there yet. There's still a number of open questions about what truly works, what doesn't really work, how it works in the long term — because nobody has a lot of look-back on that yet.

There's still quite a few open questions on what the appropriate team structures should be. How many to produce a piece of product — how many product managers, how many designers, how many engineers, how many security engineers do you need? Are those roles coming closer together? We think they are, by the way, which is one of the big things we're building for. We want to bring everybody into one platform and bring those roles together. So we think from that perspective, the transition to AI for development is actually an acceleration of the trends we've seen before with the cloud. But there's still a lot that's up in the air.

Advice to 2010 Olivier

What would you tell 2010 Olivier when you were just starting? What kind of advice could you give yourself?

Yes, I would tell 2010 Olivier that it's going to be tough, but it's okay.

Okay.

And actually, I believe strongly that all of the hardships we've had — they've really helped us survive, get stronger. Whether that's the rejections initially and a lot of the culture came from that, or — like, 10 years ago we had a serious security incident also. And that also completely transformed our approach to security.

We're pretty much better today because of that incident.

Yes, exactly. So everything that was very traumatic, I think in the end had a positive impact on the company. So that's good.

That being said, moving faster — always decide faster. I think the advice I would give myself is decide faster.

On Hiring Speed

Yeah. Is that faster on product and people?

Product, people. Usually — product, I think you get better at deciding faster over time. People is really hard.

I have this path where —

Yes, and that's always like hiring, firing. Those are two things that in general you should be faster. Whatever your instinct is is too slow.

Did you hire enough people? Or do you think you took your time to hire? I'm thinking about team size because one advice we always give is don't hire anyone pretty much before product-market fit. Do you feel you should have hired faster there?

We — I think we're always on the slower side. Even when we were growing like crazy on the business side, we were not doing more than doubling the size of the engineering team every year, for example.

That's very conservative compared to your goals.

Yes, and mostly we didn't want to break everything. We saw some companies — many of them are customers — that had pretty dysfunctional engineering teams because they 10x'd the size of the team over 18 months. And we thought it's not helping anyone, because what you do when you do that is you — first of all, you lose all short-term productivity because all you're doing is hiring and ramping up new people. And then you have a huge risk that things are going to blow up. And then you'll be set back for another year or two after that.

So we thought, "Hey, maybe we'll leave a little bit of business on the table because we'll be undermanned, but we're going to cap the growth rate of the engineering team."

It's probably even more fruitful today. Like, you can do so much more with the same team.

Yes.

Awesome. Olivier, thank you so much for joining us today. It was awesome to have you.

Well, thank you for having me. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、court-martial 与信任的悖论：对手关系里藏着最深的合作契约
最令人意外的细节，是 Olivier 与 Alexi 相识的方式：Alexi 因入侵校园网被"军法处置"，而 Olivier 正是执行"断网判决"的人。26 年后，他们共同创立了 800 亿美元市值的公司，并保持了极其稳定的合伙关系。
这与常识直觉相反——通常我们以为共同创业的密友源于"惺惺相惜"，但这里恰恰是"对立初见"孕育了终极信任。深层原因是：两个人在第一次接触时就在同一层"元规则"上相遇——一个执行判决，一个愿赌服输，都尊重系统规则本身。这比任何情感认同都更牢靠。
这个模式在跨领域反复出现：**免疫系统的成熟依赖早期病原暴露**、**司法制度里资深检察官和辩护律师私下常是好友**、**围棋高手在对局中比在酒桌上更容易识别彼此**。真正的合伙关系不是从"喜欢"开始，而是从"验证对方在压力下如何处理边界"开始。他们后来定期共进午餐、在重大决定（如出售公司）前反复对齐，本质上是在延续那次校园冲突所建立的"元协议对齐"机制。
## 二、CEO 作为自己直觉的 RLHF：采样式管理背后的贝叶斯先验

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] 川普ALL IN，加密貨幣瞬間暴漲20%，但週期數據還是悲觀？【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直覺的訊號：不是「開會」本身，而是川普那句「已經討論過」

大家都在興奮川普把 SEC、CFTC、Coinbase、Kraken 全叫來開會，但真正炸裂的其實藏在一句幾乎沒人細品的回答裡——當記者問政府會不會下場買幣時，川普沒有拒絕，他說的是 "It's been talked about"。

這句話的權重被市場低估了。因為在政治語言的譜系裡，「已經被討論過」其實是一個極高等級的預告動作——它介於「沒這回事」和「即將宣布」之間，是華盛頓典型的「試探性放風」（trial balloon）。美國政府這種量級的機構從不會用隨口一句話回應這類問題，除非幕後真的在推演某種預算路徑。

換句話說：真正該關注的信號不是白宮的燈開了，而是川普用了一個「委員會語言」而非「總統語言」去回答一個本可以一口否決的問題。

二、四年週期為什麼可能第一次被打破——這其實是「生物節律」被政治強行倒時差

比特幣的四年週期不是玄學，它本質上是礦工經濟學 + 散戶情緒 + 流動性循環三者共振出來的自然節奏，就像人體的晝夜節律：晚上該睡就是想睡，硬撐能撐但代價是後面反噬。

過去三輪熊市之所以精準到「52 週、54 週、59 週」，是因為週期裡從來沒有出現過一個體量足以逆轉盤面的外生變數。而現在多了一個變數叫「美國財政部」——它的資產負債表比整個加密市場的市值還大好幾倍。

這裡有個跨領域的類比很有意思：這就像央行在 2008 年之後永久性地改變了美股「均值回歸」的統計特徵。QE 之前，美股的熊市平均長度是可預測的；QE 之後，熊市要嘛不來，要嘛短到讓所有技術派懷疑人生。如果美國真的啟動「戰略性買幣」，比特幣的四年週期就會進入類似的「後 QE 時代」——歷史統計學會失效，但不是立刻失效，而是滯後一到兩個週期才會被市場承認。

所以邦妮的判斷其實非常克制且準確：不能死守四年週期等年底，也不能一頭熱把子彈全打光。

三、被嚴重低估的隱藏戰場：Clarity Act 卡關的真相不是政治，而是銀行在保衛自己 300 年來的利差商業模式

大部分人以為 Clarity Act 拖延是政治鬥爭，但真正的阻力來自一個聽起來完全無關的地方——銀行不想讓穩定幣的收益率跟活存利息公開比較。

這件事的深遠意義遠比幣圈自己想像的大得多。因為銀行的核心商業模式從美第奇家族以來，本質上就是一件事：吸收廉價存款、放出昂貴貸款，靠中間的利差活著。穩定幣把「儲蓄的收益權」直接還給用戶，等於繞過了銀行五百年來的護城河。

你可以把這個場景類比成 2005 年左右Craigslist 對報紙分類廣告的降維打擊——當時報紙不是敗給新聞網站，而是敗給一個「把本來就該免費的東西還給用戶」的產品。分類廣告一夜之間消失，直接抽掉了美國地方報紙 40% 以上的營收根基。

所以 Clarity Act 遲遲不過，不是議員在鬧脾氣，而是美國銀行體系在打一場自己都不敢明說的存續戰。而這一戰的結果，比比特幣今年會不會創新高重要得多——因為它決定了未來十年美元的分發權到底歸誰。

一個留給你的問題

當一個資產類別的「週期」開始被一個國家用政策去干預的時候，它就不再只是一個資產，而是一個準主權工具。這意味著你手上的比特幣，從此的漲跌邏輯將越來越像黃金——受地緣政治驅動，而非減半日曆。這是好事，但也意味著幣圈熟悉的那套「四年一次抄底」的舒適區，可能正在悄悄關門。

📝 转录文本

開場：市場突然活過來了

crypto crypto crypto，bitcoin bitcoin bitcoin bitcoin bitcoin，加密貨幣市場突然整個沖起來了。比特幣向上拉了長長一根，拉回 7 萬美元，以太幣一天直接漲了 20%，幣圈相關的美股像是 Coinbase、Circle、MARA 也全部一起噴了。

原本幣圈的市場還是一副死氣沈沈的樣子，突然一下子全部活過來了——還得是川普。他把 SEC（美國證券交易委員會）、CFTC（美國期貨商品委員會）、Coinbase、Robinhood、Kraken 全部找來幫加密貨幣站台，連 SEC 的主席都說會全力以赴。

"We at the SEC are delivering on your agenda."

幣圈的大佬開始喊說：「好高興，底部已經過去了，我們回來了，最差的時候已經過去了。」

但這就是最吊詭的地方了。因為回顧比特幣歷史的週期，比特幣最低點高機率不應該在此時出現。看完這一集，你就會知道到底該怎麼做。

頻道介紹

Into the crypto world we go wild. Bonnie Chang, she's the queen of the game. Stacking crypto like it's her claim to fame. If you want success, then take a look her way.

Hello，我是 Bonnie。現在網路上的資訊很多，這個頻道過去幾年每一集都在幫你把市場上重要的消息跟背後的邏輯整理清楚。剛剛路過的話，歡迎你訂閱。

一、比特幣的四年週期：歷史劇本

比特幣最有名的四年週期告訴我們：比特幣大概每四年會發生一次產量的減半。歷史上的產量減半分別是發生在 2012、2016、2020 跟 2024 年。

那比特幣的價格，每一次的週期大概四年就會很規律的重複一次牛熊的循環。一個完整的週期會長怎樣呢？會先從熊市主底，然後進入牛市創下新高，之後再進到下一輪的熊市。

那如果我們用前幾輪來看，比特幣從牛市最高點一路走到熊市，大概通常都花一年左右： - 上一輪的熊市是 54 週 - 再前一輪大概是 52 週 - 2014 年那一輪大概是 59 週

也就是說，整個四年週期裡面真正從高點一路往下殺的這熊市，大概就只有一年。剩下的時間就是築底，然後慢慢復甦，再進到下一輪的牛市。

舉例來說：2013 年的牛市到頂了，接著 2014 就進入熊市嘛，在 2015 年初附近就到底了；2017 年再次創下牛市的高點，2018 年進到熊市；2021 年再創新高，那 2022 年又出現了下一輪的熊市大底。

尤其是從牛市最高點跌到下一個熊市的底部，大概歷史上都是一年左右的時間。所以我們如果還相信比特幣的四年週期，那市場原本的預期就是：2025 年比特幣價格到頂之後，2026 年底大概十月、十一月的時候會出現這一輪熊市最低的底部。

而且歷史上 8 月跟 9 月本來就是比特幣相對弱又很無聊的月份。所以如果按照歷史的劇本，幣圈現在應該是正處於一個非常非常無聊的時間。

二、大轉折：川普的白宮幣圈會議

但這故事的大轉折來了，就是川普「川投顧」。他搞了一個幣圈高層的會議，這個是以前週期沒有的東西。

比特幣呢，突然就這樣一根直接噴上去。那是不是就代表這次熊市提早結束了呢？美國政府是不是親自把比特幣的四年週期提前打破了？我們是不是已經開始要從底部爬上去了呢？

下面資訊欄連結點進去，開一個幣安的帳戶。如果頁面問你推薦人的話，記得要加上 HELLOBTC（H-E-L-L-O-B-T-C），確保領取的資格。

之後下載幣安的 App，你可以加入官方的 Line@，參加即將開辦的免費新手線上課程。主題是很難得——四年一遇的比特幣抄底訊號。完成任務之後送你 15 美元的 USDT。

另外幣安 App 左上方三條線點進去，獎勵專區裡面你可以按領取任務，之後入金就可以得到特斯拉的美股代幣 15 美元。下方資訊欄影片會附上所有手把手操作的教學。

如果你有任何問題，歡迎到那新手課程或者是到 Telegram、Line@ 詢問，會有專人回答你的任何問題。幣安它是全世界最大的加密貨幣交易所，目前的用戶超過 3 億個人，美股產品也很齊全。現在就到下方的資訊欄連結，去領屬於你的 30 塊美元獎勵。

三、白宮會議最關鍵的一刻：政府會買幣嗎？

川普這一場白宮的幣圈會議，SEC、CFTC、Coinbase、Kraken、Robinhood 全部都找來，高喊著要讓比特幣、要讓加密貨幣、預測市場、永續合約這些新的金融科技全部都留在美國發展。那川普他也直接擺明了呼籲國會下一步就要把 Clarity Act 趕快往前推。

整個會議裡面最重要的地方就是在這裏，一個記者問川普說：欸你們美國政府到底花不花錢買幣？

"Does the administration have any plans to accumulate sizable amounts of Bitcoin or other crypto?"

"Well, it's been talked about. I think I'd probably rely on Paul and the whole group for that. They'll make a decision. You guys will make a decision. And you'll let me know, but certainly it's been talked about. It's taken a lot of pressure off the dollar. It's been very, very good for the dollar. And I think if you came in with recommendations, two of you, if you came in with some recommendations, I would certainly listen. It seems to be a pretty big subject."

川普說：這件事情我們討論過，如果 SEC、CFTC 這些官員拿個具體的建議來給我，他很願意聽。

這就超重要的，因為美國現在雖然已經有這個比特幣戰略儲備叫做 Strategic Bitcoin Reserve，這個儲備目前有將近 33 萬顆的比特幣，但是這所有的比特幣都是美國政府過去查扣沒收來的，美國的財政部並沒有花錢跑到市場上主動去買幣。

那現在這個記者問的是：你們政府願不願意掏錢來買比特幣？如果這一步真的跨出去，這個事態完全不一樣，因為美國政府它的量級是有能力把四年週期提前打亂的。

四、財政部同步出手：美債回購加倍

幾乎是同一時間，美國的財政部也突然出手要來穩定債市。美債的殖利率剛剛衝到 19 年的新高，所以美國財政部長 Scott Bessent 就在 8 月 19 號宣佈，要把美國長期國債的回購規模直接加倍。

那這消息一出來，殖利率馬上就掉下來了，表示市場認為這個利率壓力稍微鬆了一點，借錢的成本也稍微低了一點。那這個時候大家就比較敢把錢放回股票、比特幣這些資產裡面。

"In a short period of time, a year and a half, we've had 80 days where the stock market hit all-time highs."

川普他也公開喊話，希望利率降低：

"We would really like to see interest rates come down. You know, in the old days with interest rates, many of you are too young to know this. But when we announced good numbers, interest rates would go down, and the theory was because the asset value became so good, it became so prime. But now when we announce good numbers, which we're doing all the time, they keep driving the interest rates up because they're so afraid of inflation. And they shouldn't be. They should allow interest rates to go down. When you announce good numbers, you shouldn't drive them up. They keep thinking that we'll drive them up to stop inflation, because success and growth does not cause inflation."

川普覺得說：數據都很漂亮，市場不應該因為這種數據漂亮就升息吧，應該要下降才對啊。

"Interest rates should be allowed to fall with the success of our country, not rise because of the success."

五、Clarity Act：為什麼川普一直點名它？

這一場白宮的會議裡面，川普還一直點名 Clarity Act，希望趕快通過，他想要簽。這又為什麼重要呢？

Clarity Act 就是美國想要把加密貨幣市場的遊戲規則正式的寫清楚。比如說： - 哪些代幣算是證券，哪一些是商品 - 到底是要歸 CFTC 管呢還是 SEC 管 - 交易所怎麼樣合法經營 - 加密貨幣的公司又可不可以合法的募資呢

這也是為什麼幣圈非常想要 Clarity Act 通過。因為過去最大的問題就是規則一直都很不清楚，政府只要換一屆，監管機構只要換一個主席，很多公司規則就要重來。那這樣反覆來回，美國就沒辦法在這個領域獨霸領先嘛。

"We're ensuring that America remains the undisputed leader not only in Bitcoin and crypto but also technologies like prediction markets, artificial intelligence, and much more, and we're leading in every single one of them."

原本市場是預期 Clarity Act 可以順利的通過，結果參議院是一路拖、拖、拖。現在下一個重要的時間點是 9 月 15 號，需要足夠多的跨黨派支持，法案才有可能繼續往前走。

其實這一陣子比特幣在 6 萬的美元附近晃、晃、晃，就是市場已經沒有那麼多期待說這個法案會短期順利通過了，就大家原本很期待，可是現在失望了。

六、Clarity Act 為什麼卡關？兩大爭議

但是為什麼一個把規則講清楚的法案可以拖這麼久？這聽起來都是正向的啊，要把規則寫清楚不是才對嗎？喔，因為他們在吵的是細節的方面兜不攏。

爭議一：銀行 vs. 加密貨幣公司錢包

第一個爭議就是銀行不爽——銀行跟加密貨幣公司錢包的戰爭。

現在有很多加密貨幣公司讓用戶把穩定幣放在平台裡面就可以拿到利息收益。加密貨幣公司的邏輯就是說：這個利息收益本來就該歸你，那理所當然就是要給你。

但是銀行不開心，因為他們給的定存利息一直以來都滿低的，那這利息就是銀行很重要的收入來源。所以他們擔心用戶一比較之後，欸可能覺得這個穩定幣的收益更好，用戶的存款可能就會從銀行流出去。

"Some of the big banks that don't want the competition from crypto companies."

爭議二：川普家族的加密生意

第二個爭議就是川普他自己。民主黨現在很在意川普家族有很多加密貨幣相關的生意，他們想要限制政治人物在幣圈獲利的這些細節。

不過川普身邊的高層像這個 SEC 主席 Paul Atkins，他本來就是幣圈友善的主席，他看起來是義無反顧支持這個法案通過：

"You've committed to making the United States the crypto capital of the world. And yesterday, the SEC, I'm proud to say, took another significant step to deliver on that. Our proposal, the crypto assets rule, would provide crypto entrepreneurs like those here in this room and job creators the certainty to raise capital in the United States using digital assets. This action is consonant with our belief that the most important priority is for Congress to send the Clarity Act to your desk for your signature. And the SEC is doing everything we can to support that work."

七、結論：四年週期還在，但要開始警覺了

那現在最麻煩的地方就是：你看這個四年週期目前還是準的，但是也不能埋著頭就只看這一個訊號嘛，不能就乾乾的等到年底。

怎麼說呢？因為如果四年週期的歷史重演，現在我們這一波反彈可能並不是熊市立刻結束的訊號，因為畢竟熊市裡面出現比特幣突然衝 20% 甚至 50% 的反彈都看過。

但是美國政府如果真的開始買比特幣，或者是真的資金輪動變得超樂觀，那一直把資金等等等到年底想要熊市底的時候再買，可能也等不到。

歷史告訴我們四年週期現在是還在的，但是市場開始出現一些值得注意的訊號了。

我甚至覺得說 Clarity Act 通過都不會造成什麼很誇張的買壓，市場可能會小慶祝一番，但是真正要有很大的突破的，會是川普突然說「哦，美國會花錢買比特幣」的時候。

反正我們永遠抓不準最底部的那一天，最好呢就是永遠待在場上，但是手上要留子彈，隨時注意這個趨勢。總之這是非常好的消息，因為我們看到底部今年不遠了，大家可以慢慢開始回來關注幣圈。

社群資源

你知道嗎？總計已經有幾萬個用戶在我們各個社區享受官方資源了。資訊欄的官方 Line@ 有專人一對一幫你回答市場的問題，還有美股代幣跟幣圈的新手專屬七日陪跑課程，教會你所有的基本功，群裡面也有很多福利可以領。全部的好康都在資訊欄，快去看。

💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：基础设施的匮乏，是一种被伪装的护城河

最容易被忽略的一句话是 Angela 说的："在美国你可以在每一层拿到 as a service，但在拉美你没有 fraud-as-a-stack、KYC-as-a-stack，所以你必须自己造。"

大多数人把这理解为"落后国家创业的负担"。但真正的洞察在反面——这种"必须垂直整合"的强制性，恰好制造了美国 SaaS 生态很难复刻的深度壁垒。美国的 fintech 创业者是在乐高上拼装，拉美的创业者是在浇筑地基。当 AI 让软件层的差异化变得越来越薄，谁掌握"没法被 API 抽象掉的那一层"，谁就赢。

这和生物学里的"岛屿演化"惊人相似：加拉帕戈斯之所以孕育出达尔文的独特物种，正是因为主大陆的"物种服务"进不来。"资源匮乏 = 演化压力 = 独有形态"——New Bank、Rappi、AI 之所以出现在拉美而不是硅谷，本质上是生态位效应。

二、跨领域连接："AI 奥林匹克"揭示的其实是"国族叙事从体育向科技的迁移"

Gabriel 提到 11 Labs 成为波兰"参加 AI 奥运会的选手"，波兰政府亲自下场投资。这不是简单的产业政策，而是一个更深的文明转向：

过去 100 年，国家用足球和奥运奖牌牌位建构民族自尊；未来 30 年，这个角色正在被 "unicorn / foundational model" 取代。

这解释了几件表面不相关的事： - 为什么法国总统亲自站台 Mistral； - 为什么沙特把整个国家改名叫 NEOM 来招募工程师； - 为什么"美国排名前 X 的独角兽"变成外交语言。

创业公司正在成为主权国家新的"外交筹码"——这一层被 a16z 的策略敏锐地捕捉到了。他们卖给创始人的其实不是资本，而是"如何把你变成你家乡的国家代表队"。这和体育经纪人签约天才少年的逻辑一模一样：赢一次，母国的所有资源都向你倾斜。

三、一个几乎没人说破的暗结构："中间失败者"才是生态系统的真正枢纽

注意 Gabriel 反复提到 Voi 的创始人 Fredrik——一家"看起来像 Lime 的滑板车公司"，退出规模不大，但几乎投中了瑞典所有 AI 新星。

大部分人以为生态的中心是那些超级 winner（比如 Spotify 的 Daniel Ek）。但真相是：顶级赢家太忙也太高，反而是"中等成功、心中不甘、还有 5–10 年精力"的第二梯队创始人，才是网络里带宽最高的节点。

这个模式在其他领域都有对应： - 学术界推动学派繁荣的往往不是诺奖得主，而是那些"差一步就是诺奖"的博士导师； - 好莱坞真正推新人的是"曾经很红、现在做制片"的中生代； - 硅谷 90 年代的 PayPal 帮，也不是从最成功的公司衍生，而是从一次"被迫卖掉、心里憋屈"的退出裂变而来。

"未竟之志"是最好的燃料，而不是"已经登顶的荣耀"。 Borderless 生态选中的 luminary 之所以准确，是因为他们捕捉的不是"最高分创业者"，而是"最高 δ 创业者"——那些"世界还没给到他应得位置"的人。

四、Bonus——被埋在细节里的一个反转

对话里被一带而过、但极其重要的一句："Cognition 早期收入的很大一部分来自巴西。"

请重读一遍。硅谷最热的 AI 编程公司，早期最好的客户不在硅谷。

这颠覆了"新技术永远从硅谷扩散到全球"的旧模型。真实情况是：新兴市场的 CIO 比硅谷 CIO 更饿，愿意用没跑通的产品换取压缩时间。这意味着未来 5 年，最聪明的美国 AI 公司会把"第一批客户"放在东南亚、拉美、中东——不是因为价格便宜，而是因为决策带宽更宽、试错代价更低。

这是一个"技术扩散反向"的时代信号。谁先看见，谁先赢。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open — Three Signals

"Anyone international — whether you're building primarily in your home country to start but that you have global ambitions — you're a borderless founder."

"They tend to have a chip on their shoulder — the desire that they want to become the benchmark and prove something to the world that regardless of where they were born, they can still achieve greatness."

"Unlike in the US where you can get everything as a service at every layer of the stack, in many other markets you just can't do that. There's no fraud-as-a-stack, KYC-as-a-stack — so you end up having to build everything."

"There's this interesting dichotomy in this technology: it's very democratic — it distributes the ability to get it anywhere in the world, it opens up other markets — but then it also concentrates the epicenter of where things are moving the fastest to the Bay Area."

"10 years from now, what do you hope to see in the global topology of startups everywhere in the world?"

Introduction

Welcome back to the a16z Podcast. Today we're here with Angela Strange and Gabriel Vasquez, two of the architects of a16z's global investing strategy.

So, today — on the day that we're publishing this podcast — we're also running a piece on this idea of borderless founders and who borderless founders are.

Q: Venture historically has been really situated in Silicon Valley. So what makes borderless founders interesting, and what is the story of international investing?

The Origin Story: A WhatsApp Group and a Wide-Open Market

Angela: Very early in my career at a16z, I was investing primarily in financial services or fintech, and one of the first articles I wrote was around just how to get distribution in financial services. It can be very difficult — you need to find a consumer at exactly the right moment in time when they're ready to change from their incumbent services. There's just a lot of inertia.

At that same time, my brother had just joined Nubank down in Brazil. And I remember him saying that David had said: "Yeah, you know, you could compete to be the fifth financial services for every customer in the US. Or you could go to a wide open market with five fat, happy banks that only serve 20% of the population."

Yes, it's much more difficult to get things going — you've got to get licensed, you've got to build all the infrastructure — but there's just these wide, wide open markets. And that is what initially got me interested in looking at Latin America.

The first check I ever wrote at a16z was actually into Santiago Suárez, the CEO of Addi, which now serves a quarter of the Colombian population for banking and payments. That kickstarted our international strategy, which initially focused on LatAm.

Not long after, I get a WhatsApp from Gabriel — who had joined a16z totally on a different team. And he's like, "Hey, you haven't met me yet, but I just see this huge opportunity in Latin America. I've gone and met 25 of the most important CEOs. I've got them all in a WhatsApp group. Like, we should probably do something here."

Q: At the time, Gabriel, were these all fintech founders, or were they working in every single industry under the sun?

Gabriel: Every single industry — but historically in LatAm you see more fintech founders than you see in other regions. The premise was: at the time that I did the mapping, there were only 30 unicorns in Latin America. So the thesis was, you can put them all in one room — and get them to connect, because the Brazilian unicorn founders weren't talking to the Colombian unicorn founders or the Mexican unicorn founders. There was this opportunity to bring them all together.

We ended up doing that. We created a WhatsApp group with Angela, with Marc Andreessen, Alec Rampell and a bunch of other people at the firm, and we put them all together. One of the interesting things is — they were discussing topics about the region, but they also started exchanging deal flow, because they were all prolific angel investors. So that gave us a great opportunity to not only see early deal flow but also participate in that community and help them out.

What Early Borderless Founders Have That Others Don't

Q: What did early people in this community have, do you think, that a Silicon Valley founder wouldn't have?

Angela: Some of the best founders there grew up in their home markets, spent some time in the US, and then came back.

Take Santi from Addi. He grew up in Colombia, went to Yale, spent some time at a bunch of financial services companies — both large and small — in the US, and then came back home. So it's a combination of: saw the models that worked in the US, but then deeply understands his home market. He recruited one of his childhood best friends who was very technical.

The other thing you have to know is — unlike in the US where you can get everything as a service at every layer of the stack, in many other markets, including Latin America, you just can't do that. There's no fraud-as-a-stack, KYC-as-a-stack. You end up having to build everything, which requires a much deeper local market knowledge — but it's very helpful to be able to borrow from around the world.

The AI Inflection: From "Come to Brazil" to "Come to the Bay"

Q: This finds its origins in a WhatsApp group and now suddenly is an entire strategy that you two are leading at this firm. What was the moment where you were like, "This needs to evolve past what we're doing right now"?

Angela: We had very active communities across regions, and then really what happened was AI.

There's this interesting dichotomy: this technology is very democratic — it distributes the ability to get it anywhere in the world, it opens up other markets — but then it also concentrates the epicenter of where things are moving the fastest to the Bay Area.

So it changed. Versus Brazilian founders, Colombian founders wanting us to come down to Brazil and Colombia and connect — they all wanted to come to the Bay Area and get integrated a lot faster.

What Founders Bring, What They Find

Q: When that happens, what kinds of problems were they negotiating? What are the challenges — and what are you bringing with you from your home country?

Gabriel: One of the things we noticed about these groups is that if you are, for example, from Brazil, you end up mapping the top talent that is in Silicon Valley from Brazil. We started seeing this trend in pretty much every country — you can extrapolate to Europe or Asia. The question is: where are the smartest people from my country, because they're going to understand where I come from?

The things you bring in are less about local knowledge (because now you're going to play at the global stage) and more about the connectivity you can have with somebody you don't know. And the fact that they're in Silicon Valley — Angela and I discussed this a lot — is this culture of giving. People help you a lot even before they know you. But there's a closer affinity if you're from that same country, because people can see themselves through that journey.

The Borderless Dinners

That led us to organizing this — what started as a small community — the borderless dinners. We called them "borderless" because at the beginning it was very niche, very focused on only Latin Americans. We mapped out the most successful founders from Latin America, and every time we had people coming to visit, we would create a dinner for them — 20 to 30 people. They would get to see what the journey of a person from Latin America was in Silicon Valley.

A big part of this was Guillermo Rauch from Vercel — a persona that has obviously succeeded and done really well in Silicon Valley, but was very excited to meet people from Latin America and help them out in that journey. We had the founder of Brex, Pedro Franceschi, do this as well. And a lot of other founders came along.

The other interesting thing is that the group has matured. People who were early attendees have now graduated into unicorn founders — and now they're speakers. Victor Cárdenas from Slash, Andrés from Foundry — this has created an amazing connectivity.

The Diaspora as the New Alumni Network

Angela: The relatable American version of this is — if you think of the top schools, the alumni networks around them are incredibly powerful. I might argue that the international, country-specific diasporas are even more powerful — they just often lacked the sort of organization.

Lots of these diasporas are now organizing. We're not the only people that help here. But what we saw was: if you came from a country and landed in the US — figured out how to get your visa, figured out where to live, made yourself into the network, got your customers — you have this desire to pay it forward. But there's not really an easy way to do that in the same way that you can just go back and speak at your college.

So we're like: what if we made an easy way to go back and speak at your college — but your college is all of the smartest kids who graduated from college or dropped out of high school, who really want to build global companies? The power of that is really exciting when you get in the room.

Defining a "Borderless Founder"

Q: For someone listening — what is the difference between a borderless founder and an immigrant founder, or a borderless founder and someone who just happens to be an international person starting a company in the US?

Angela: I like to take the most inclusive view ever — which is just anybody who's trying to build a global company. Americans technically could be borderless founders, but they tend to be connected here anyway. So anyone international — whether you're building primarily in your home country to start, but you have global ambitions — you're a borderless founder.

Gabriel: There's something unique about these people: they tend to have a chip on their shoulder. They either grew up in a country that was overlooked — my story, I grew up in El Salvador, a small country. When you come to the US, nobody's like, "Hey, I met this other great guy that came from El Salvador." You're creating the benchmark on your own.

We backed a German founder that grew up in a really small town in Germany. Germany is well known and everybody has respect for the country, but the fact that he came from this small town — it's like, "I'm going to make the most of this opportunity." Even in the US, we've seen people that grew up in small rural areas, and that's what drives them.

It's the desire that they want to become the benchmark and prove something to the world — that regardless of where they were born, they can still achieve greatness. That's the mindset these people have who want to go and dominate globally.

Finding the Community — And the Canadian Precedent

Q: How do founders find both the a16z borderless founder community and other communities? And how do we find them?

Angela: There is an interesting history of countries doing this. Part of the reason I became so passionate about working on this with Gabriel is: I'm from Ottawa, Canada originally — very much not far from Silicon Valley, but also a country where lots of companies were started, and very few got to scale.

Maybe 15 years ago, a group of me and several other Canadians in the Bay Area started an organization called C100. It was 100 Canadians in the Bay Area who had founded very large companies or were in influential positions where they could help. It was a forum for them to give back, and by that, help Canadian companies scale.

Really two things: one, helping them find design partners — obviously the startups had to be good enough to land the contract, but we would open the door. And two, helping them find executives that would help them scale. That's one of the tougher things — you can have very smart people, you can land your customers, but then when you look around for who's my sales leader to take me from $50M to $500M, you probably have to find them in another market until your market gets to be more mature.

Now there are lots of unicorns around the globe started by Canadians — Shopify is a big one, but OpenEvidence's founder was Canadian. These markets start to go, and those diasporas become easier to break into and easier to find.

Which Ecosystems Are Ready?

Q: Are there places that are where Canada was 15 years ago now? Or has AI and the allure of Silicon Valley proliferated that narrative faster?

Gabriel: The maturity of markets is very relative. Some of the markets we spend the most time in are the UK, Sweden — Israel is very well known for this, because historically on a per capita basis, these countries have produced a lot. AI has enabled them to grow exponentially in some cases.

But there are other countries where — because of dynamics — you still don't see it flourishing. And this is where we see a lot of founders actually moving to Silicon Valley. There's an interesting tension: these local ecosystems that are fruitful — people feel very prideful. In the case of Sweden, "we want to make Sweden great." UK — "we want to make it an independent ecosystem." Versus other ecosystems that might be a little bit earlier — they feel like the best next step is to come here first.

To be fair, there are a lot of founders that want to dedicate their life to build that ecosystem in their own countries. Sometimes we see this father-figure in earlier ecosystems who built a really hard business, and all these AI-native founders go to them first — like a lighthouse — and then they illuminate them about what Silicon Valley is, direct the path of who they should connect with.

Angela: The interesting thing happening now — we're investors in a company called Taqe, which does payroll HR workflows across Brazil, but their bigger mission is cutting down bureaucracy in Brazil. One of the founders was previously the founder of RappiPay, teamed up with another founder Fernando — this is his second company. They've been able to recruit Brazilians back from the US. They grew up in Brazil, they understand these bureaucratic problems, and they think with the right talent, the right AI, they can help their country. This talent flow has become really interesting.

Three Native Advantages: Talent, Brand, Customers

Q: In the piece you wrote, you talk about three native advantages borderless founders have: talent, brand, and a strong customer base. We've touched on talent — let's talk about brand and customers.

Brand: The "AI Olympics"

Gabriel: In terms of brand — an example in our portfolio is ElevenLabs. This company started out of Europe, in the UK, but has Polish founders. For Poland, ElevenLabs has become such an important name to be their representative. There's a founder we know who calls this the AI Olympics — every country wants to have their own candidates winning medals. For Poland, ElevenLabs is that candidate. The Polish government just invested in ElevenLabs and is going to do a bunch of initiatives with them.

In Sweden, the Swedish government has supported Lovable and Legora a lot. When this happens, it gives you such a jump start in validation with all the large enterprise companies of your country — and even countries ancillary to it — because everybody sees the support of the government and thinks, "Wow, that's a stamp of validation. I want to work with them."

Customers: The Design-Partner Ladder

Gabriel: On customers — we've had companies at very early stages start with a design partnership that eventually converts into a multi-million dollar contract. We invested in a company called Factor Labs — they started working with the largest conglomerate of all of Latin America, owned by the Slim family. That introduction has led them to other workflows.

We also see this playing out — if you're a founder born in Spain, like the case of Supersonic: who's the smartest person that went to my university, and what are they doing now? In their case: someone who used to be the CRO of Salesforce is now the COO. They connected with him, and Salesforce actually became their first design partner and eventually a customer.

These advantages are not very obvious. It might seem random, but it's all connected to the same root.

Brand → Global Talent

Angela: Global companies need to recruit global talent. Addi scaled very quickly, and then — how do you find a credit officer that can do billions of dollars of GMV? The best credit people tend to come from Capital One. How do you attract somebody from Capital One in Virginia to want to work in Bogotá? You become the hottest company in Colombia. Versus joining one of 50 companies that kind of look the same in the US, why don't you join the winner that by brand is very clear?

Another element of brand: you can build relationships with the government. Jeeves has done a lot with the central bank in Brazil — they're helping corporations move money internationally via stablecoins. They're getting that reputation with enterprises as being the most trusted, compliance-speedy way to do that. As a result, they attract more talent, and that compounds.

Preferential Attachment — With More Levers

Q: This compounding loop — the idea of preferential attachment — Marc first introduced this idea. The next incremental person, the next incremental customer, becomes that much easier to attract. Do borderless founders have an easier or more differentiated time with this?

Angela: In some ways, all of a16z was founded to accelerate our founders' preferential attachment — how do you get that flywheel moving as quickly as possible? I would argue borderless founders have more levers at their disposal.

Talent: This is the fiercest talent market I've seen. They have insight and access to differentiated pools. We have an AI insurance company in Brazil. You might think the best talent is at the top well-known universities. Actually, for AI talent, it's at a university you haven't heard of. How do you find it? You go to the scholarship programs that scour the country for the best students. It's these robotics competitions. If you get 10 incredibly smart people really early, the 11th you're trying to recruit — who has 100 other offers — meets your team and is like, "Holy — how did they get people that good there?" That starts the flywheel.

Customers: Anytime you want to land a large customer, the first question they'll ask is: "Who else is using you in my industry, at my size?" Nobody wants to be the first bank or the first insurance company. Via the borderless founder network, you can get a large bank and a large insurance company in another country much more quickly — and that accelerates the US.

Reverse Bridge: US → Emerging Markets

Gabriel: We've also seen the case of really hot companies in Silicon Valley like Cognition — where their early go-to-market was actually Brazil, and it represented a really high share of their revenue early on. These enterprises really desire to adopt AI as quickly as possible, and they don't get as many providers to do that. Cognition built a really strong network in Brazil to do that.

Q: Does that mean you can also pursue a borderless strategy by selling into markets that might not necessarily see this?

Gabriel: The best way to think about it: there's the bridge to Silicon Valley — and that same bridge can be used in the opposite direction. That's how we position it: borderless founders come to Silicon Valley, but obviously have global ambitions. They might have a strong network in Germany, but no knowledge about Brazil or Japan — and those are things we can be very helpful with.

Angela: We started this by connecting diasporas amongst themselves, and now almost the bigger power is the intra-diaspora — the German company's first design partner is the largest Spanish conglomerate. That's amazing — not super intuitive that it would have happened.

Gabriel: Something is very unique about what we built here — there's probably no other investor that can cross-pollinate across different ecosystems and geographies from the get-go.

Mapping a New Geography: "Local Luminaries"

Q: At the beginning, Gabriel, you mentioned your first market map of Latin American unicorns was 20–30 companies. When you approach a new geography now — what is that process like?

Gabriel: We have this term we use — local luminaries. It goes back to what we alluded to before: people highly respected in the local ecosystem who have built companies. The scale and success of the company doesn't really matter — but they're people who try really hard to make their ecosystem valid.

In the case of Sweden, we met the founders of Voi — Fredrik Hjelm and Adam Jafer. Looking from the outside, you wouldn't think — because what they built was a company very similar to Lime, a scooter company — you wouldn't have thought they'd be in the middle of the AI boom in Sweden. But if you look at all the angel investments Fredrik did, he's pretty much in all the relevant companies that came out of Sweden. Because he's very well connected with the younger groups of founders, but also the experienced ones — and he brings them all together, makes a case for Sweden, going back to the AI Olympics analogy.

You see this persona across every different market we mapped out.

Step 1: Understand and Validate the Luminary

Our first job is to understand who these people are and how to help them. One way is validating their message — when you've been an evangelizer and get validation from a firm like us, that helps them prove their point. They get closer to us; we start working with them, doing events, helping their companies recruit — and that gives us access to the best people within their network.

Step 2: Map the Rising Stars in the Valley

Then you map the equivalent — the rising stars who are luminaries in Silicon Valley from that country. One of these in Sweden is Gabriel Petersson — a high school dropout from Sweden, came to the US with no education, got a job at Midjourney, then became one of the youngest researchers at OpenAI, and now started a company. Every time a Swedish founder wants to move to Silicon Valley, they want to get in touch with him.

If you build this network — mapped out when they are in Sweden, and when they move — helping them connect with successful people from their country — you're pretty much in the flow.

The joke people usually tell us: "Gabe, you're so well known in Sweden, or Germany, or Brazil." The joke I tell them is: in every country, I make them feel like it's the only country I look at — because we try to derive at a very local level where the luminaries are.

Step 3: The Mission-Driven Executive Layer

Angela: As ecosystems mature — the executives at the rising next set — what makes it powerful is that it's really mission-driven. They saw how hard it was, and they see heads of sales, founding engineers with a little bit of liquidity, who now want to pay it forward to the next generation of founders. We have a global scout program where we recruit the rising stars at the companies to be part of it, and that helps create the ecosystem.

Gabriel: When we find enough density, we do events just for that community. About a year ago, Angela and Ben Horowitz did one where he was a speaker — we brought the best Nordic founders to Silicon Valley for a week and hosted them.

Q: It's funny — we just released a podcast with Will Gaybrick from Stripe, and the parallels between how Stripe works and what you're describing — you start really early with individuals or teams, very small companies, and grow with them. You're there for every single generation, every step of the life cycle.

Gabriel: 100%.

Angela: If you think — all of us remember the people who helped us when it wasn't obvious. In our role — you've got to be really passionate about meeting people, paying it forward, generally raising your ecosystem. Some will become great founders you get to invest in. Others become broader parts of the ecosystem. But you've got to be there early.

Repeat Founders: The Second Wave

Q: I'd love to talk about the repeat founders you've identified — how do you think about that?

Gabriel: It was pretty much continue to execute on the WhatsApp strategy, funny enough. These local ecosystems had a first wave of entrepreneurs that got to meaningful scale — usually within the $1B to $5B range — but they didn't get to see it all the way through. Because it was the first time around, because the ecosystem was really hard, there were lessons they couldn't fulfill their vision on.

That gets them thinking: "I'm going to do a next business, and this time I'm going to apply all the knowledge I have, all the network I built, and go build something even bigger." That's how we identify these people — because of their drive: "This $5B exit wasn't enough for me. I want to do something greater from my local ecosystem."

We track them very closely. We help them come to events. What they usually want is to reactivate their network — especially in AI, they want to get connected with the smartest engineers at Stanford. They want to be in the flow of talent, and we give them that bridge.

We're very intentional when putting it all together. In the case of Pipe.com — Fredrik G's new company — when they were coming to Silicon Valley, we put them in touch with the top XX from DoorDash, the top XX from Lyft, top XX from a bunch of our portfolio companies. We helped them ideate. After they came back from that trip, they had a pretty clear vision of what they wanted to pursue — and they decided to go with us. Despite them having pre-existing relationships — because a lot of investors want to invest in them — we differentiated on the ideation side.

Angela: The other opportunity to close the gap for repeat founders — they probably don't have a network of the smartest 18-, 19-, 20-year-olds all in AI. These are amazing engineers who probably want to be founders but might want one job in between. Sometimes these repeat founders are — especially the really hungry, going-it-again ones — they've learned so many lessons, and it is great CEO school to come work for their companies for 2, 3, 4 years.

The Journey of a Seed-Stage Borderless Founder

Q: If I'm an early-stage, seed-stage founder, what is my experience like coming into this ecosystem, and how do you grow with these companies from Series A to growth?

Gabriel: The first thing we focus on is visas. This might not sound like a big deal, but it's the most stressful process when moving to the US — what is the right visa, what do I qualify for, who's going to write a recommendation letter?

We're actually investors in a visa company — an AI-native visa company called Extraordinary. Through Extraordinary, we partner a lot on helping founders come to the US, making sure they have the right qualifications.

The Hacker Houses

There are a lot of hacker houses that started abroad but now have campuses in the US — to use Angela's analogy — where they offer free rooms for people to stay for a short amount of time. We sponsored one called Palo House. We met them at Slush, the big event in Finland. There were four really smart students from CDTM — one of the best programs in Germany — and they had this idea: "We want to have a house in Palo Alto and bring the smartest people we know to stay with us and ideate."

Over four months, they crowded the house too much. Through dinners and everybody who stayed, it was like 1,200 people who ended up staying there. Through that, we met really exceptional people we stay in touch with. They really were running a small liberal arts college. Now they want to find a way to keep that alive independently.

Through our borderless communities: "Hey, you're here for a couple of weeks — why don't you come to this dinner and meet other really smart founders and operators that just went through a similar journey?"

Family Enterprises as Design Partners

Angela: As founders start their companies — often very technical founders have an idea and are looking for which market, which use case to go after. Particularly interesting internationally: many countries have several powerful families that control a lot of the enterprises, and the next generation is very motivated to become AI-native. We've brought them into our borderless founder group. If you want heads of operations, finance around the world to ideate with, talk about their problems — they're very willing to talk to the smartest people in our community about what they should build. That can be a really interesting connection.

We've had actual contracts for portfolio companies land from those initiatives.

Advice: Should You Move?

Q: If I'm an international founder listening — thinking about moving to Silicon Valley — what should I know? Should I come for a month, 3 months, or move altogether?

Gabriel: The answer varies for everyone, but one thing that's very common: definitely come and spend time in Silicon Valley. Even if you're going to go back, you go back with a lot of insights. I never met somebody who came to Silicon Valley and was like, "This was such a waste of time." Everybody goes back excited, and it helps them calibrate on the level of speed.

This is one of the things Silicon Valley continues to be ahead of every other ecosystem on — the level of speed at which people operate. Calibrating on speed is really important. I'd personally recommend at the very least 3 to 6 months, so you can immerse. A couple of weeks isn't as influential — you have to go through the depth of the network. In a couple of weeks, some people get discouraged because it's really hard to connect. But people who spend a little bit longer come back with the right connections, even if they decide to go back or finally decide to move.

Angela: Lean on your diaspora — either via us. We've posted about a lot of the things we can do. It is way deeper than probably you think in the Bay Area, and very much primed to help you build your company.

Ten Years Out

Q: Ten years from now, what do you hope to see — not just in a16z and our portfolio, but in the global topology of startups everywhere in the world?

Angela: This trend is just going to continue. We actually ran the stats — out of our apps, 40% of our investments were in international founders. Half of them were based here, half were based in other countries. All nationalities internationalize mix — a more diverse set of minds builds bigger and bigger companies. It's great for consumers, great for enterprises. We are just 1% scratching the surface of what we can do with AI.

Gabriel: I'd second that. There's a statistic a lot of people in Silicon Valley used to frame — that 90% of the returns in venture capital come from Silicon Valley companies. If that share goes from 10% all the way to 20–30% — that's something I'd like to see, because that builds the case.

The other thing — I never really quite liked that statistic, because it doesn't fully tell the story. A lot of these borderless founders are based here, but a lot of the engineering team might actually be back in their home country. A lot of these advantages were never really told. There are a lot of these companies that are actually claimed by two different countries — and that story was never really told. You've seen that historically, and I think it's going to continue — but hopefully now from this perspective: "We're a global company that has headquarters in — at the very least — two different countries."

Close

Host: Angela, Gabriel — thanks so much for joining me today. This was a ton of fun. When this episode releases, everyone will also be able to read your piece on the subject — so check it out on Substack and the a16z blog.
