item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：安全护栏正在制造"防御者盲区"
大多数人以为 AI safety guardrails 只挡住坏人。视频揭示的真相恰恰相反——**防御者和攻击者在向模型提问时，措辞几乎无法区分**。"这段代码里哪里可以被利用？"从红队和蓝队嘴里说出来是同一句话。Hugging Face 在应急响应中被自家 OpenAI 模型"拒绝服务"，只能回退到 GLM、Kimi、Qwen 这些开权重模型——**开源在这里不是意识形态，而是 incident response 的救生艇**。
这暴露了一个更深的悖论：**模型的对齐机制建立在"意图不可知"的前提上，于是把语言形式当成了意图的代理**。这本质上是一场反向图灵测试——模型必须仅凭措辞判断人类的道德立场，而这在语言学上根本不可能。对齐越强，蓝队越残废，这是护栏设计者从未在白皮书里承认的税。
## 二、Honeypot 的自噬：当"太乐于助人"变成攻击面
蜜罐十几年来一直是主动防御的皇冠——撒一堆假 AWS key，谁碰谁曝光。视频里最黑色幽默的一幕：**销售代表让 agent 部署一个 demo，agent 尽职地扫环境，

item.title: [Business of Sport] “Padel participation will be ahead of tennis in 10 years” | Team GB’s Nikhil Mohindra
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"英国税"悖论：稀缺套利如何战胜纯粹实力

Nikhil 无意间揭示了一个反直觉的市场规律——一个排名远低于西班牙同行的英国球员，商业收入却可能高出对方数倍。原因不是他打得更好，而是他"更稀缺"。当西班牙的顶级人才池像一个过饱和溶液时，任何单独的水分子都无法结晶；而在英国这片相对空旷的溶液里，他就是那颗最先析出的晶体。

这与学术界的"小池塘大鱼理论"惊人吻合——三线大学的博士常能获得比一线大学同行更多的教职机会，因为竞争密度不同；也解释了为什么很多好莱坞明星去中国拍烂片的酬劳，反而高于在美国主演大制作。能力的市场价格，是"能力密度 ÷ 市场密度"的比值，不是能力本身。这意味着体育经纪人未来应像基金经理选股一样，主动寻找"低估值高稀缺"的地理套利机会——去非西班牙、非阿根廷的国家扫号码位。

二、可及性悖论：世界上"最平民"的运动，正在变成最贵的运动之一

板网球的整个设计哲学是降低门槛——球拍小、球场玻璃兜底、发球必须下手、70 岁的老人也能对打。它的技术 DNA 里写满了"人人能玩"。但英国的现实：伦敦球场每小时 £100，教练课 £70–90，David Lloyd 甚至出现了机器人抢位脚本 + 场次倒票的"二级市场"。

这是一种极其罕见的错配：产品是民主的，基础设施把它变成贵族的。类似错配在别处也能看到——比特币号称"人人的钱"但矿池被少数矿场垄断；MOOC 号称"人人的教育"但完课率与家庭背景强相关。当"精神民主性"和"物理稀缺性"冲突时，几乎总是后者胜出。因此 Nikhil 提到的瑞典泡沫破裂，几乎可以看作英国 5–10 年后高租金球场倒闭潮的预告片——市场自我校准是可以被定价的事件，唯一未知的是时点。

三、职业球员的 Catch-22：这不是体育问题，是"创作者经济"的通病

最让人意外的洞察藏在 Nikhil 讲自己的两难里——训练越多，商业曝光越少；商业曝光越多，训练越少。英国一号 Christian Medina 全职训练但赚不到大钱；Nikhil 抓商业机会拓宽收入但排名上不去。

这不是运动员的独有困境，而是所有"创作者-从业者"的通病：播客主想做深度节目就得停止接广告，接广告又没时间做节目；独立开发者想做产品就得停接外包，接外包又养不起产品。板网球职业圈提前撞上了后来所有创作者经济都会面对的核心问题——你的注意力单位不能被两个市场同时消费。真正跳出这个陷阱的人几乎都走了第三条路：把训练本身变成内容（Nikhil 已经在做的 vlog 化训练日常），让过程变成产品，让"练球"和"赚钱"共享同一份时间。

四、Federer 的 54%：微观胜率与宏观胜率之间的巨大杠杆

对话里一带而过但极其锋利的一个数字——Federer 职业生涯只赢了 54% 的分，却赢了约 82% 的比赛。这是一个几乎跨越所有高风险领域的通用真理：结果不是过程的线性累加，而是"关键节点表现"的凸函数。

在投资里，这就是 Buffett 说的"一辈子只需要打对二十个洞"；在创业里，这是 Peter Thiel 的幂律法则；在写作里，这是"90% 的书没人读，10% 的书塑造时代"。所以顶级职业选手真正在训练的不是"打好每一球"，而是在 40:40 的金球时刻不崩溃——这正是 Nikhil 的心理教练教他去感受手指纹凹凸的原因。这是一种典型的"降维应对"技术：当宏观压力过大时，把注意力锁定到无法承载压力的微观感受上。类似的技术在冥想、外科手术、狙击训练里反复出现——它们都在解决同一个问题：如何让 54% 的努力变成 82% 的结果。

五、被忽略的"沉默变量"：为什么顶级明星反而在向他学习

Nikhil 提到 Ronaldo、John Terry、Shevchenko 在球场上向他"请教"时，最令人意外的不是他们的谦逊，而是——这些人已经在自己领域达到过顶峰，他们对"如何达到顶峰"本身有一套元技能。他们不是在学板网球，他们是在演练自己"从零到熟练"的能力。Ronaldo 早上 7 点做拉伸不是为了 8 点的球课，而是为了永远保持那个"能吸收新东西"的身体状态。

这暗示了一个反直觉的选人标准：如果你想学任何新领域，不要找那个领域的一流选手，而要找任何领域的一流选手。因为"如何变强"是一种领域无关的元能力，而具体技术是领域相关的。这也解释了为什么中年转型的顶级人物成功率异常高——他们带过来的不是知识，是学习知识的操作系统。Nikhil 的真正财富，也许不是他和 Ronaldo 打球的关系，而是被这些"操作系统"反复扫描后，他自己的操作系统也被无形升级了。

📝 转录文本

Opening Hook

Within 10 years, participation of paddle will be over tennis. I mean, in Spain a few months ago, paddle was played more than football cuz everyone can play paddle.

I've been playing for team GB for about 6 years, traveling the world, competing, having amazing opportunities, meeting the likes and coaching of Cristiano Ronaldo, John Terry, the Beckhams. If you told me this 10 years ago, I would have been like, I'm just a West Ham fan. Like, I played with Mark Noble and I was over the moon. Like genuinely, like he's my hero.

In paddle, you're spending what you're earning because you got to travel, you got your coach, you got your physio. Just like tennis. For winning the P1, you get €25,000 each. And where SA picks up 5.2 million, you got number one's Tapin Kua picking up €25,000 each. Some coaches have literally just transitioned from tennis to paddle to charge more money. And I've seen some of the coaches, they can't coach paddle. They're just doing it because they can charge double.

How do you get the call to go to Dubai and play paddle with Cristiano for a week? So, business of sport. Fascinating.

Welcome & Introductions

Aquil, welcome to the business of sport. Welcome paddle to the business of sport as well. It's ridiculous uh that it has taken us 135 shows. One of the most popular things demanded by the fans, but now we're finally doing it and I couldn't think of a better person to do it with. So, thank you so much for coming in and joining me.

Oh, thank you so much for having me, Charlie. I mean, I I've always see all your stuff on Instagram, YouTube, and I love it. So, when you when you dropped me the message, I was like, I've got to go on.

Well, I had firsthand experience of you having you actually gave me a little bit of coaching with another business of sport alumni, Benjamin Kaiser.

Yeah.

I can very very pleasingly say that it massively helped my game. Uh, which needed it.

No, for I don't know. You're getting better. You're getting a lot better.

Yeah. Low bar. Low bar.

Being Inside the Paddle Boom

Um I I mentioned to you that when we came in here I did say it's one of the most requested topics that we have. You were surprised about it but the demand for paddle is just off the chain. What's it like being in the heart of that?

Well sometimes you don't actually get to see it because I'm in it. I'm so involved in it dayto-day training few hours a day traveling. So I don't actually get to experience some of it but I did for the first time at Olympia at the Premier Paddle um last week which was an amazing event. You got to see the true fans, the people who are watching your content, the people who are dropping your Instagram messages, supporting you. So, it was it was a phenomenal experience and being able to see the world number one obviously compete in the heart of London is something it's such a rarity to see. So, it was amazing.

Was that one the f that was one of the first major events

That was the first in London. So, it's yeah, great experience.

Why Has the UK Lagged?

Why has it taken so long?

Well,

Or has it taken so long?

It has taken quite a while. I mean, you see the other European nations like Germany, Belgium, Holland, all having these events already, but that's cuz their infrastructure is so much far developed than ours. So, we we've just passed 1500 courts and all of those nations passed that a long time ago.

One of that is due to the planning constraints. I mean, I'm building a club in Surrey at the moment and that's taken almost 6 years uh just to just to start construction because of I mean here you've got animal ecological surveys then you've got construction issues and you've got to talk with a landlord about X Y and Zed it's so ridiculous where's where compete in Sweden there's no change of use for anything you see a warehouse you agree a deal you get your courts in it's a lot more straightforward.

So this I mean you some of the best clubs you've got in Canary Warf in in Raketer North action. They've been taking years just because of it's so so many political things going on behind the scenes.

So we actually played and we in Rakateeer probably what end of June hot it was it was literally the hottest day wasn't windows were open, doors were open

But that's I mean guy if you haven't seen this by the way I mean it is incredible. It is a huge I mean hanger type big warehouse.

It is the club to go to. I mean they've done it very nicely

But that takes them years to build.

Oh yeah. I mean I speaking with the owners like 3 years just to get the heads of terms all completely sorted cuz they had to make sure the old tenant had to leave and I mean size of that warehouse Amazon are coming in for it and that just kicks out any paddle operator right so it was good to see that paddle is absolutely booming at the moment with all these amazing clubs and foreign investment coming in and is just making the sport bigger and bigger.

Who Is Nikhil? A Brief Bio

I'll come back to what you're doing in there because I think it's interesting and is a huge part of the business of the sport but first of Let's just give anyone that doesn't know like give them a brief kind of overview of who you are and what you are really doing within the world of paddle.

Sure. So I' I've been playing paddle for about 8 years now. Um I've been playing for team GB for about 6 years traveling the world competing. Alongside that I'm an ambassador for Paddle India. So traveling there to help grow the game and off the back of that I started something called the Pad Foundation which is a organization. And it's a charity, registered charity which helps people from underprivileged backgrounds get into sport because as you know paddle is super expensive and paddle is the most fun, social, accessible sport when it's not 100 quid in London.

So we approach schools from deprived areas and kids who have never had the opportunity. We get them in get all of my best friends who are part of the team GB paddle as well. So very rare you've got the national team coaching kids for free and we sort them out food and everything like that and they have the best day ever and we make sure it's a reoccurring thing for them. So that's been a big part of what I want to do and been achieving.

And then also the content side which I think is really cool. So being in team Chibi being having amazing opportunities, meeting the likes and coaching of Cristiano Ronaldo, John Terry, the Beckhams, it's I mean if you told me this 10 years ago, I would have been like I'm just a West Ham fan. Like I mean I played with Mark Noble and I was over the moon. Like genuinely like he's my hero. But then when I'm with these guys it's like wow I'm very fortunate.

So off the back of that as I said creating content copied what James Cordon was doing when he was doing the carpool karaoke thing. So filmed quite a few of them already. So very unique position paddle and uh very fortunate.

How He First Picked Up Paddle

Okay. You've literally done the schedule for the show and it's brilliant. Let's let let's pick out the first thing you said before we get into all the rest of it which was you started playing paddle 8 years ago. How do you even begin to to play paddle?

Sure. So I I left school at 17 um to go into the family business which was clothing like Asian clothing. And I figured after 6 months I was like oh I don't know if this is me. I was always into sport and I had to stop playing football because I was sever asthmatic. So anytime someone kind of barged me over, I was having asthma attack saying to the manager, I need my inhaler and nebulize or whatever. I just need to start breathing again.

So at this point, David Lloyd had just put in three courts out of nowhere and all the tennis people were just like a this is terrible. What is this? What's going on? And I was like, I'm not very good at tennis. I'll give this a go. Started playing with 60, 70, 80 year olds. And I was loving it. Like playing every single day. used to go to your family office, come back and then just hit on the wall. Anyone that was free and all my friends were like, "Mate, what are you doing? Like this sport is just a rubbish tennis like just cuz you can't play tennis." I was like, "Yeah, I can't really play tennis, but this is fun as well."

Fast forward a few years and courts start to grow, etc. And I start playing some local tournaments, but these tournaments like the same 20 people enter, so you know every single person. And the reason I actually started playing was cuz my my friend in school moved to Spain at 16. His name's Sam Jones and we're paddle partners now. And I was like, "Oh, that looks quite cool." And so that's why I first got into it.

But it wasn't with a name of going, I'm I want to lock into this because you saw an opportunity to

Especially I'm I'm from a quite a Asian background, right? So it's very much you're going to study and then you're going to just get a secure job. And paddle is by no means a secure job. Even to today to earn money. We've gone on to that the prize money and stuff like that is very low. But I was as soon as I started playing a bit more got got recognized by some of the the heads of the uh GB team got selected at at 19 going on 20 years old and very fortunate to now still be competing for them traveling the world Qatar Dubai Marba it's it's been amazing.

The Brutal Economics of Being a Pro

Tough

Very fortunate life the business though you did touch on it the life that comes from being a professional paddle player is hard if you're just looking at it from a financial perspective

100%. I mean in paddle you're spending what you're earning cuz you got to travel you got your coach you got your physio just like tennis. Like in tennis if you're not in the top like 100 or whatever is I don't think you're making money that's why making that grand slam where you're making that £30,000 first round is everything. But in paddle first round of the P1 you get €1200 so it's a very different kind of ball game.

So so for winning the P1 you get €25,000 each and that's that's winning almost. It's essentially a grand slam of tennis and where SA picks up 5.2 million. You got number one is Tapian Kua picking up $25,000 each, which is obviously not a lot of money when you're trying to fly everywhere, train everywhere, and pay for your coach's food and drink. Um, so it's it's extremely tough, but the money comes from the sponsorships.

I mean, they're all the top 10. I will be on minimum like £800 900,000 a year from head adidas all these brands which is just blown up paddle now like for example AP and uh Rolex are getting into the game by sponsoring the number ones so it's definitely becoming a a household sport.

The Tournament Pyramid: Majors, P1s, P2s, FIPs

You said a P1 there P1 is a tournament that you'd be playing in like an ATP 1000 cuz the slams you have you have four slams

Same as paddle yeah

Exactly the same as tennis

Then you have the P1's am I right in Those that's the rest of the tournaments.

So slams in PA they're called majors. Yeah. So they're held in Mexico, Qatar, Rome, and Italy. Um and then one under like you said, the HP 1000s would be the P1s. And then under that is the P2s. So I can't even play in P2 yet. I don't have enough points. So I'm playing in the division under which is this is almost like the championship football. It's called the FIP. FIP uh bronze, silver, gold. So that's the championship. Then once you have enough points, you go into the Premier League, which is P2, P1, and major.

So Louis Harris, who's British number two, right? 272 in the world, he played a tournament in Portugal, a P2 tournament a few weeks ago, and the prize fund for the whole tournament was €10,000 for 32 players.

Sure. Yeah. I mean, it's nuts. And that's split like equally men and women. So yeah, so it's it's not a lot of money there at all.

Why the £3–4B Industry Doesn't Reach the Bottom

And yet we have all of this come back to the attention um the interest in the sport where you've got millions of people a global industry that reportedly is worth about 3 to four billion pounds but that hasn't quite made its way down to the professional end yet.

No exactly it's still drip feeding way through. I think it will still take I think at least another generation to be honest. I think it will take quite a while because a lot of people who the money this is just going to the people who are going to be on TV, right? Like the sponsorships are great for the top end and for the bottom end is not that not that lucrative at all.

I mean um I've been approached by quite a few brands fortunately just because of my uh access to the celebrities and content. It's not really for my playing level cuz if they want that they'll just go straight to Spain or Argentina. It's a waiting game to be honest um for it to drip through to the bottom.

The Player's Catch-22: Training vs. Commercial Work

Okay. Okay. So, how do you do it? How do you make this a successful career for you?

So, this is like a catch 22, right? So, the British number one, his name is Christian Medina, and I've always talked to to to him about this, right? So, he has just gone full mode pro. Like, so he's spending every bit of money. He's got to train and be the best and he is a phenomenal player. And I've always looked at it as like this sport's very short, right? So, every time I've kind of done well in a tournament, I would try to get awareness for that on social media and build myself a a club or something like that and get involved in a commercial venture somewhere.

So, that kind of spins round, but that also has a impact because once I'm doing this commercial things, I'm not training for that week. And so, that's so Christian's amazing on the playing side and playing fantastically well, but then I'm doing uh better on the commercial side when I'm involved in the UK clubs. So, it's really a catch 22 in like how you do it. For me, sponsorships is a big thing and also very fortunate to have um a family that's backing me, but a lot of the British players don't have that. Whereas they're coaching a lot of the time, Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday they fly out to tournaments and they're back by the end of the weekend and it's just a cycle. So, that it's everyone's got a pretty different situation.

Is it a problem for the sport when the commercial opportunity doesn't come from the professional angle to make money really said you you're not going to do it by focusing purely on your performance at a tournament every single week which means at some stage something has to give

That's quite it's quite a unique opportunity right so I just played a tournament in Belgium and the prize money to win it was €600 for the winning pair and I spent €400 getting there so you're taking a loss. So, I think it's so it's so important to try and create something outside of that. And you're seeing so many more players now vlog and uh video their journeys to these tournaments because then that's getting traction then sponsorships come in.

But, and honestly, unless you're the top I mean the top 10 are making very good money, I believe, but unless you're in the top 80 in the world, you're not making that that much money. And to be honest, cuz it's very saturated with Spanish, Argentinian, Argentinian players, you you've got to be top of that nation to earn that money. If you're number 60 in the world and you're Argentinian, there's 50 people better than you from your country. So, you won't be getting the the big prize pot there.

Spanish Dominance & the Olympic Question

So, talk to me about this cuz this is this is fascinating, right? I always knew from going on the occasional holiday to Spain, right, and seeing paddle courts long before I probably paid too much attention to what paddle courts were. Spanish dominance in this sport is ridiculous. I was having a look at the um the the number of players at the event in Olympia in in London a few weeks ago. So over half of the men's draw was Spanish. And I mean literally the women's draw when I had a look it was just Spanish flags everywhere. I looked at the official number. I think it was 42 of the 56 competitors.

I mean

Were Spanish

And that's Yeah. And that's because the British got wild cards as well. So if this was a tournament in Spain, the British players wouldn't be in it. It's crazy because this is actually quite good. A few years ago it was even more saturated with the South Americans and the Spanish. So you're starting to see like the Portuguese and the British and the Dutch and all these different countries come in. So now you're starting to see a bit of a change, but that's also one of the reasons for the Olympics.

I'm pretty sure they don't want to have a sport in there that's so dominated by one country. So I think they're playing a waiting game a little bit as well to make it a bit more fair cuz there's no there's not really another sport where well I might be incorrect here but a country wins every Olympics, right? whereas Spain or Argentina they they dominate the gold medals there. So I think on the Olympic side that's what they're waiting for as well.

What has to change to make that happen? Is it infrastructure play and embedding it in a grassroots level making it available and accessible?

100%. I mean it's in Spain it's how we treat football, right? I mean they're good at every sport in Spain but it's annoying. But we we start football like anyone that plays tennis or or paddle like we all can kick a ball pretty well. But we started Raet Sport so late and there they've got over 20,000 courts. Here we've got 1,500 and as as I just touched on, it's so hard to build a club here. We've got such a fantastic federation in the LTA, one of the richest in the world. So, it's just about getting them more involved in the sport and that's just only going to take time.

The LTA's Role

So, can you tell us how that works with the LTA? Have they got um a well they have a program right which has been focused and geared towards the development of paddle. How does it work from you the individual versus how it builds and supports the game as a whole in the country?

Sure. So, it's it's been a huge positive the LTA taking the sport. So, someone called Tom Murray, he founded British Paddle quite a few years ago and that's how I first got into it. Um, he then spoke with the LTA. I'm not sure who approached who, but the LTA then adopt it as an official sport in 2019. And there's so many benefits that happen with that. Like it bypasses a lot of things. Then when you're applying for planning for a club, you get a letter of support from the LTA. It carries a lot of weight and it accesses a lot of uh clubs for grants and funding to improve the infrastructure and for players.

Now it's a lot more uh professional like we get um scheduled funding, we get um IDP to individual development plans and all these things which is fantastic but it's still so small. LTA is huge. I mean they get nearly I'm guessing nearly 70 80 million a year from Wimbledon and so if if paddle can unlock a bit more of that funding because honestly within 10 years participation of paddle will be over tennis. It's so much easier to play and it's just so much more fun.

I mean it's never going to have the rich heritage of tennis. I mean I went to see Jovovich play s in Wimbledon and the aura that they have honestly is second to none. But the point's over so quickly and they spend 30 seconds getting the ball and so you spend that 30 seconds speaking to your to your friend that you've gone with and then you're watching for 10 seconds whereas paddle for me maybe I'm biased here but you see them running out the court you see them smashing jumping reaching it tapping it out the court for me I'm like like tennis athletes are the best in the world alongside many other sports.

A lot more I think if you're a good tennis player you can be a good paddle player not necessarily the other way around cuz paddle is a lot easier than tennis. I mean, I'm very skinny, right? I'm not a very strong uh player or in any way, but the reason I can be good at paddle is because of the technical and the tactical awareness of it.

Physique & Style

But it's all about all about timing and yeah, just technique really. I mean, you see SA, he's not very big,

But then as opposed to Nadal who was quite big, it's all about timing, technique, and just yeah, just training that up really. What's the What's the perfect physique, would you say, for a paddle player?

Well, I I don't think there is to be honest cuz I mean, for example, you've got someone like Louis who's in the GB team, right? And he isn't your traditional He's a very good friend of mine, so be saying this.

You're about to say he's fat.

Definitely not cuz I'll end up on the floor if I say that, but uh he's not the traditional uh physique, but he's got one of the best smashers in the world and technically he's amazing. But then you've got someone like me who's like skinny, not much power, but I'm a lot faster around the court. So, I don't think there's really a perfect kind of physique.

And it just makes me feel so good. makes me want to do it more because just like helping other people like if it's not getting better but is give them 10 minutes of escape from anything they're suffering from which was what I which I had when I used to watch the side men or niclan or any of these guys I like that 20 minutes is like my escape like I'm in this own world where nothing else matters and I'd have the notifications on so whenever it's released I just watch it and that's I'm like I hope I'm helping people like that as well cuz That's how I felt when I was younger.

The Niko Omilana Story

You did one with Niko, didn't you?

Yeah. I mean,

That must have been cool.

Niko is the best guy. Like, honestly, the nicest, most the funniest guy, like the sweetest guy. I nothing but love for him because he's helped me so much. Not only just like coming on my channel, but advice as well. Like, he knows I've told him, opened up to him a lot, and he's just so like has time for me. And you can see that that's why for me, he's the best content creator like definitely in the UK and in my opinion in the world. Like just the stuff he comes up with is phenomenal and he's just he loves his paddle. Um, and I've been fortunate enough to know him.

I mean, that's how he started everything to be honest. I got an Instagram message from my favorite YouTuber, Nicol Milan. I'm like, "This is a scam." He's like, "Brother, I need you in this video tomorrow." And I was like, "Okay, this is a scam." He was like, "Give me your phone number." So, what have I got to lose? Anyway, I give him my phone number. 5 minutes later, I get a phone call.

Was like, "We're going to scam Mr. Beast for $100,000." I'm like, "I'm in." So then next day I and I'm in Spain for a for a training camp. I'm like, I've got to go back for this. Like, it's it's Niko. So anyway, I get a flight back and uh Stormy shows up. I'm like, "All right, this is pretty nuts." My first real exposure to anything kind of contentwise and uh he's like, "Niko said to me, you're going to be my little brother." because we got similar names, similar skin complexions, like it kind of works out. Anyway, first kind of yeah game I I throw it away. So Storm's just like I got £10,000 in the bag. Like we bet £10,000 on the game and I'm like this is £10,000. This is pretty nervy. But anyway, I go to Nick like, "Okay, should we should we turn it on now? We do it. We beat them very easily."

And that for me was just the start of everything. Next day, next week, I get a message from Talk Sport like, "Do you want to come in?" Since then I've been in talk sport more than 10 times and on the way there people like you're Niko's brother even to this day people like you're Niko's brother and that honestly was the start of everything.

What are you going to talk about on talkport?

Growth of paddle uh the Asian community how it grows and just yeah generally just all things paddle.

Do you enjoy it? I mean you're saying sitting in the chair here right now under serious pressure right so give the right answer but

I absolutely love it to be honest. It's just given an insight to what people don't really know about the sport. A lot of people have already like presumptions like, "Oh, it's expensive. These people uh don't want to play the sport, whatever." But it's actually really nice to be able to give another point of view, someone who's been in it for pretty much the start of when it was here and still fairly young, 25 years old, so still a lot more to see in the sport. So, it's really nice and to be able to experience this.

Balancing Player, Content Creator, Business Owner

So, we've talked about a lot, right, that you do. You've got first and foremost professional player and I'd imagine at the heart of everything you want to be as successful as you possibly can as a professional player.

That's number one. Yeah.

Yeah.

But how do you coming back to now now we've got the information you know I come back to that point of that's the dream but the reality of the life that it creates still relies on you being very active in all the other areas. How do you look ahead? How do you look to balance all of this so that you can achieve that ultimate goal but still make sure that you're doing what you need to do behind the scenes to support yourself?

I mean balance is probably the hardest thing. I mean when you're training then the content drops and when you're doing the content the training drops and then the GBT status gets impacted. So keeping a balance is super difficult.

And at the moment it's like I wake up super early in the morning to try and get my training done in the morning and then I'm going to the meetings and then I'm going all around to kind of build up my kind of reputation. And you've got to be super careful with that because your reputation can go like that like in anything. It takes years to build trust in the moment for it to break right and to build it back. It doesn't happen.

So training fulltime in the mornings and but it's not just training, it's also eating the right things. Like when you're traveling, and any sportsman will know this, it's actually pretty hard when you're abroad. Like it's fast food's always there. It's the easy option, but you're not eating your healthy pastas or your meats, whatever. So it's super tough and to balance it at the moment. I I'm finding it hard because not only that, you've got a family life as well. Like I've got a girlfriend that obviously I want to progress that in a few years, but then I'm away Wednesday to Sunday, Wednesday to Saturday. So

Every week,

Every week. And it's like so many things to juggle.

So, but then I'm very fortunate cuz I've got another few years of doing this. I won't be able to do this forever. Won't be able to play for GB forever. Won't be able to play with these guys who I look up to forever. So really utilizing my time as much as I can and trying to find a fixed routine is the key.

Age, Careers & Longevity in Paddle

What's the age?

Yeah. Like or how old are some of how old are some of the players coming up to you slash do you have players at 18 19 coming in and doing type thing.

Exactly. You got youngsters 17, 18, 19 who who are coming through who are the unique players like you like you said your sinner and your alkaras but then you've also got your Joviches who you've got some people at 39 38 who are still playing the sport. They're partnering with younger people and they're the experienced ones. Experience buys you a lot of points, gets you a lot of points in paddle.

So it's it's a mix. If I had to give an age to where you can compete like obviously depends on how you look after your body, I'd say

35 36. So yeah.

So similar similar to other sports.

Exactly.

Kind of top end.

The Mental Game: Feeling Your Fingerprints

And if Okay. So if you're looking at that kind of training side of it, what are you actually doing in the training? Is it skills and drills type thing? Is it because again like I always find this fascinating when you see like people talk about

Rogers better as tennis coaches who who's looking after Novaj's time

When it gets to a point

And you've got that level of of skill and depth right to your games. How do you train? What is it that you really have to focus on?

The most important thing is the mental aspect. The most important thing. I mean, speaking on on Roger Federra, he said he won across his career 51% of his points.

54

  1. And you'd think he'd win 90% of the points, the amount of grand slams and titles he won. But anyone there's not anyone in the top 100 that can't hit a shot like Roger Fedra. There's they'll all have the technical same ability.

And it's similar in paddle, right? When I'm when I'm feeling loose, relaxed, I could hit any kind of forehand, backhand smash. But when it comes to when that point is, can you do it?

And for me, that's the hardest thing, like when it gets to that golden point or the set match point, whatever it is,

It's being able to just calm yourself. And I've had a lot of like um like consulting with uh psychologists about this. And one kind of tip that works for me is feeling the grooves on your fingers. So, you don't really think about it ever. And you don't really think about the clothes touching your body as well, do you? But when I'm in a kind of a tight position, I'll go to the net, kind of take my time, and then with with my thumb, I'll feel the kind of grooves of my fingerprints.

And that kind of like humbles me thinking this is quite unique to me, but I'm like, there's so many things happening in this world. You're playing a point of paddle. Like, there's people, there's wars going on. There's people that don't have access to water, whatever. And you're playing at a point. Like, come on. If you lose this, you lose the match. You go home to your bed, whatever. But like, just relax. The the action just grounds you basically in in a thought.

Absolutely. And then I relax and I still also miss the ball probably because I'm not very good. But yeah, that's

It's probably in a uh world where we are force-fed motivational videos.

Yeah. I mean my Tik Tok is like be a man do this screaming down the phone. I'm like okay.

It's hard isn't it to figure out what actually works. But I mean yeah that that Feder video I mean the point I think he made makes on it was if you look at the points he lost as much as he won pretty much 54%. matter.

If you look at the matches, it was 82 83%. And the point was therefore, what's the difference? Well, when those points mattered the most,

Then he

He could lock in. But in any in a sport like what you're playing, if it's a golf and the last shot, I mean, look, to a mere mortal, right, who never will hit the heights of anything like that, it's so hard to forget something that's just happened and only think about that small

Point. focus it down to that one shot, right? It sounds great,

But to be able to actually harness that is

Takes years. I mean, you hear Jovovich speaking about it. It takes meditation. It takes training as hard as building muscle like Yeah.

Closing: The Future of Paddle & the Need for a Superstar

Yeah. Okay. What excites you the most? You got this incredible sport.

Amazing participation base. I'm going to be honest, Ryan. I want your reaction to it. I think this could be a sport which holds the participation. It will get amazing engagement. lots of different people, lots of different ages, demographics, etc. I think it could struggle at the professional end to hit the heights of interest that it gets at a participation level.

I I think there's a reason why the stadiums are always sold out uh when you go to Spain or South America. It's because it is an amazing sport to watch at the top level. So, I think it will there is a point like for example at the P1, no one really wanted to go and watch it on the starting days, right? But just because the big names aren't there, it's not obviously you go to any FA Cup in football, it's going to be full because of the this such a big sport. And I think paddle will definitely get to that point where the first rounds are the best of your countries and you'll be watching it and stadiums will be full.

I think I don't think there'll be a point where people get bored of paddle cuz there's not one point that's the same

And it's not any all the pairs are always changing and just it's so intriguing to watch. Like I said about Wimbledon, in Wimbledon, it's like tennis. You're hitting from the back. Ground stroke, ground stroke, ground stroke. Occasionally you go to the net.

Like I actually prefer watching doubles in in like if if I didn't know the names of the people playing.

Skill is awesome, isn't it?

Yeah. I'd rather speed as well.

100%. A lot of people just go for the names, right? But the level difference actually isn't that much.

But in paddle, I don't see there being a point where people will plateau of watching it.

How important is it that we get a global superstar coming out of paddle to help drive that?

That is also of course pivotal because that just if people not interested in it like when Emma Radikanu won the US like a lot of people who never watched tennis they tuned in to watch a British player winning the US Open and then it went nuts from there. She was on billboards. was earning million dollar deals with Dior and everyone was supporting her and still to this day even though she hasn't still pushed on she's still a phenomenal tennis player but people still supporting her people never knew what tennis is like they've come into tennis and probably playing now because of that moment

So I think that's a really important thing to be able to get a star that everyone can get behind and and kind of like for the next generation motivate them and be a role model

And look with brands coming into as you said at the beginning that will help. Um I'd imagine broadcast deals of course helps take it to as many places as possible and just put it on people's TVs as much as you can but also you know whether it's Cristiano Ronaldo putting it on his YouTube channel that's all going to play a part.

Absolutely. No, it's it's the exposure is the biggest thing I think like these guys like just promoting it and getting it to their millions of followers as well. It helps.

Wrap-Up

Amazing. Um I'm conscious I just had a look at my watch. you know, you have you have training, right? After this,

Sorry. Yeah,

You should apologize to everyone.

Sorry.

Yeah, but I think I think for all the reasons that we generally have to stop these uh that that's that's a good one. But no, look, seriously, um it's very hard to condense all of that and all of your experience into just over an hour, especially when, as I said, we've had so much demand on it. Uh you've done an amazing job and it is it's so interesting to properly get under the skin of what it is to not just be a professional in it but actually you know operate in the broader industry and look at how you can build some some value for yourself as well as obviously everyone else that's engaged in it is is is awesome to see. Um so thank you for coming in and doing it and uh

It's been a pleasure. Thank you.

I look forward to all the coaching that I'll get as well.

100% anytime you just drop me a message

And anyone else. No, I'm joking. He's all mine. But yeah, seriously, thanks so much mate.

No, thank you.

item.description:
## 一、"英国税"悖论：稀缺套利如何战胜纯粹实力
Nikhil 无意间揭示了一个反直觉的市场规律——**一个排名远低于西班牙同行的英国球员，商业收入却可能高出对方数倍**。原因不是他打得更好，而是他"更稀缺"。当西班牙的顶级人才池像一个过饱和溶液时，任何单独的水分子都无法结晶；而在英国这片相对空旷的溶液里，他就是那颗最先析出的晶体。
这与学术界的"小池塘大鱼理论"惊人吻合——三线大学的博士常能获得比一线大学同行更多的教职机会，因为竞争密度不同；也解释了为什么很多好莱坞明星去中国拍烂片的酬劳，反而高于在美国主演大制作。**能力的市场价格，是"能力密度 ÷ 市场密度"的比值，不是能力本身**。这意味着体育经纪人未来应像基金经理选股一样，主动寻找"低估值高稀缺"的地理套利机会——去非西班牙、非阿根廷的国家扫号码位。
## 二、可及性悖论：世界上"最平民"的运动，正在变成最贵的运动之一
板网球的整个设计哲学是**降低门槛**——球拍小、球场玻璃兜底、发球必须下手、70 岁的老人也能对打。它的技术 DNA 里写满了"人人能玩"。但英国的现实：伦敦球场每小时 £100，教练课 £70–9

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib's story of digging a big hole | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"挖一个用不上的冰窖"：把无意义变成结构的父亲

表面上，这是一个关于"勤奋"的故事。但真正令人意外的观察是——哈比布父亲让孩子挖的坑，从一开始就不是为了用。所谓"以前人们用来当冰箱"只是一个借口式的合理化。父亲清楚地知道，1200 米高山营地里根本不需要第二个冷藏坑。

这就把整件事的性质彻底翻转了：这不是劳动教育，而是"反空虚工程"。父亲提供的不是任务的意义，而是任务本身的存在。意义是事后被孩子自己填进去的——多年后成为 UFC 冠军的哈比布，回望时才把它命名为"智慧"。

换句话说，父亲提前预支了一个空的容器，让未来的人生把内容倒进去。

二、跨领域连接：修道院、军队、日本"型"文化里同一个隐秘算法

哈比布父亲的做法，和三个看似毫不相干的系统惊人同构：

  • 本笃会修道院的箴言 Ora et Labora（祈祷与劳作），刻意让修士去做重复的、不"高效"的手工活——目的不是产出，而是用身体占据时间，防止心灵滑向散乱。
  • 军队的叠被子文化：叠得再整齐，敌人也不会因此少一颗子弹。真正被训练的是"在无意义中依然精确执行"的神经通路。
  • 日本剑道、茶道的"型"：一辈子重复同一个动作，练的不是动作，而是对"我为什么要做"这个问题的免疫力。

这四种系统——高加索的摔跤营、欧洲的修道院、现代军队、日本的道场——独立演化出了同一个隐秘算法：

用身体的忙碌，为尚未成型的自我，撑出一个不塌陷的框架。

哈比布的父亲不是在教他挖坑，是在给他的青春期预装一个反熵结构。

三、真正打破常规的洞见：这段话里藏着一个关于"自由时间"的反直觉命题

现代教育、心理学、育儿书几乎异口同声地告诉我们："要给孩子留白，要有非结构化的自由时间，创造力从无聊中诞生。"

哈比布却在结尾扔下一句极其危险的话："在青春期给孩子自由时间是非常危险的。"

如果只把它读成"要孩子多干活"，就错过了真正的洞察。他说的其实是一个关于人生资源分配曲线的模型：

  • 儿童期：自由时间 = 创造力，因为身份尚未启动，随便玩都在生成新连接。
  • 青春期（12–18）：自由时间 = 高风险区，因为身份系统刚上线但没有方向舵，空闲会被最强的外部信号（同侪、算法、多巴胺）优先占据。
  • 成年后：自由时间 = 复利资产，因为已有的结构可以吸收和利用留白。

也就是说，"留白"的价值不是恒定的，而是一个 U 形曲线——中间那段最低谷，恰恰就是青春期。

哈比布父亲的直觉，等于提前几十年识别出了这个 U 形谷底，用一把铁锹替孩子把那段最脆弱的时间物理性地填满。这不是压制自由，而是在自我还没有能力保护自己之前，替它挡住外部世界的抢占。

——这大概是这段五分钟的采访里，最不易被察觉、也最颠覆常识的一层。

📝 转录文本

关于父亲让他挖大坑的故事

Lex： There's a story you told about the time he made you dig a big hole just because it was difficult. There's wisdom in that.

Khabib： Mhm. That you just need to work. You need to stay busy all the time.

山中的训练营（2005–2007）

These were training camps from 2005 to 2007. In the summer, we went to the mountains. There was a children's camp there — an old Soviet style pioneer camp — where we stayed, doing our runs in the forest.

Together, we built a small training area there with a rope, a punching bag, a pull-up bar. We did sprints there. We pulled resistance bands. After running in the mountains, we would come back and work there. There were almost no mats. We built the base ourselves.

It had a dining room on the first floor and an attic space where we slept. We would come downstairs, eat, go outside, train in that little sports area, then run in the forest. It was somewhere around 1,200 m above sea level, a coniferous forest. We spent the whole summer there.

白天没事做，父亲就给我们派活

There we'd train in the morning. Then there was nothing to do all day. And in the evening, we had training sessions again. But during the day — so we wouldn't be busy with unnecessary things — my father sometimes gave us work.

And we'd ask: "Why are we digging this pit?"

He'd say: "Well, people used to use it like a refrigerator. When you dig two or 3 m down, it is cold inside. You can put milk there, cheese, things like that, so the food does not go bad."

And we were like: "Okay, but do we really need these refrigerators every day?" [laughter]

So, in that sense, this was his approach back then. He always had this kind of unique approach.

背后的哲学

Lex： Well, what's the philosophy here? That you got to be busy all the time, working hard, doing something difficult?

Khabib： Yes. It's very dangerous to give a child free time in adolescence. They should always be busy — learning new information, improving, acquiring new skills. A person should always be busy.

When you're 16 — well, what can be on your mind? You should constantly develop and improve. And by this time, you should already, I believe, have decided what you want to become. You should already be investing in what you want to turn into.

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] What Happens When the AI Boom Runs Out of Money
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的核心观察："AI 军备竞赛的胜利"本身就是最危险的失败条件

Ben Thompson 在开场抛出了一个让整个硅谷叙事崩塌的悖论——如果美国真的赢了 AI 竞赛，那么中国炸掉台积电才是博弈论上的最优解。这不是"如果美国赢，世界更好"的问题，而是"美国赢的那一刻，恰恰是台积电必须消失的那一刻"。这颠覆了几乎所有华盛顿与湾区的政策语言：他们把"赢"当作终点，但赢本身在诱发对手的极端反应。真正稳定的均衡不是垄断，而是恰到好处的相对领先（6-9 个月的距离）——这与冷战时期"相互确保摧毁"的逻辑高度同构，只不过筹码从核弹换成了权重。

跨领域连接：AI 基础设施 = 19 世纪铁路 + 集装箱航运 + 内存芯片周期的合体

Ben 无意间揭示了一个令人震撼的历史回响链：伯克希尔用喜诗糖果的高毛利现金去买 BNSF 铁路的低毛利大绝对值——而这正是 Google 现在拿搜索现金去投 AI 的镜像。更妙的是，他把伊朗封锁霍尔木兹海峡的战略失误，映射到 TSMC 与内存厂商身上："你有筹码时不出手最强，一旦出手，全世界都会绕开你。" 台积电过度保守的产能扩张，本质上是在训练客户学会不依赖它——就像伊朗每一次威胁封锁，都在加速沙特与阿联酋修管道。

一个隐藏的意外洞察：Meta 与 YouTube 在生成式 AI 时代的边际成本方向是相反的。YouTube 现在付费给创作者，AI 生成内容对它是成本下降；而 Meta 现在内容成本是零，AI 生成对它反而是成本上升。同一场技术革命，在两个看似同类的公司里，方向完全相反。这解释了为什么 Zuckerberg 疯狂投模型而 YouTube 相对淡定——他们面对的不是同一个 AI。

更深的系统性真相："风险从不消失，只会转移"是这一切的元规律

这句话是整场对话的暗线，也是穿透所有商业模式的透视仪。台积电把过剩产能风险转给了大科技公司（表现为"未赚到的钱"，而非"亏掉的钱"）；Nvidia 通过循环融资把定价风险转成了资产负债表风险（隐性降价却不体现在毛利率上）；微软通过按用量计费把预算复杂性转给了客户（打破了"人头 = 收入"的无思考模型）。

最出乎意料的连接：Ben 指出苹果的 ATT（App 追踪透明度）与 Meta 的 PR 无能之间的关系——Meta 输的不是产品战，是叙事战。他们做着一门在社会学意义上真正积极的生意（帮小商家找到不知道自己想要产品的顾客），却从 Sheryl Sandberg 离职后就再没人讲这个故事。这是硅谷少见的"技术领先 + 叙事真空"的组合，而叙事真空最终会变成监管风险和资本市场折价。

一个终极的反直觉：整场对话里最乐观的情景，不是 AI 成功，而是 "AI 泡沫破裂后留下过剩的电力"。因为人类历史上从未真正经历过能源丰裕，我们的想象力都被能源稀缺塑造。如果这轮周期像铁路留下 BNSF、像 dot-com 留下暗光纤那样，最终给我们留下的是过剩的电——那才是文明层面的解锁。Bubble 的价值不在于它是否破裂，而在于它破裂后给后代留下了什么样的沉没资产。

item.description:
## 一个反直觉的核心观察：**"AI 军备竞赛的胜利"本身就是最危险的失败条件**
Ben Thompson 在开场抛出了一个让整个硅谷叙事崩塌的悖论——**如果美国真的赢了 AI 竞赛，那么中国炸掉台积电才是博弈论上的最优解**。这不是"如果美国赢，世界更好"的问题，而是"美国赢的那一刻，恰恰是台积电必须消失的那一刻"。这颠覆了几乎所有华盛顿与湾区的政策语言：他们把"赢"当作终点，但赢本身在诱发对手的极端反应。真正稳定的均衡不是垄断，而是**恰到好处的相对领先（6-9 个月的距离）**——这与冷战时期"相互确保摧毁"的逻辑高度同构，只不过筹码从核弹换成了权重。
## 跨领域连接：**AI 基础设施 = 19 世纪铁路 + 集装箱航运 + 内存芯片周期的合体**
Ben 无意间揭示了一个令人震撼的历史回响链：伯克希尔用喜诗糖果的高毛利现金去买 BNSF 铁路的低毛利大绝对值——**而这正是 Google 现在拿搜索现金去投 AI 的镜像**。更妙的是，他把伊朗封锁霍尔木兹海峡的战略失误，映射到 TSMC 与内存厂商身上：**"你有筹码时不出手最强，一旦出手，全世界都会绕开你。"

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Rich Sutton and Khurram Javed: Why AI Models Stop Learning, and How to Start It Again
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Sutton 不是激进派，LLM 才是"人类学习史的例外"

多数人把 Sutton 视为"叛逆者"——一个坚持古老强化学习旗帜、反对主流 LLM 范式的老学者。但他自己反复强调："我不奇怪，是这个领域奇怪了。" 这不是修辞，而是一个深刻的历史校准：

在几乎所有生物、儿童、动物的学习史中，"学习"从来不需要加"continual"这个前缀——因为不存在"非持续的学习"。是 LLM 时代创造了一个古怪的怪物：一个"学完就冻结、之后只会重复"的智能体，然后我们不得不发明"continual learning"这个词去描述"正常的学习"。

这就像我们不得不发明"面对面对话"来区别 Zoom——语言的通胀，暗示着现实的畸形。Sutton 真正的洞见是：LLM 不是 AI 的顶点，而是一个"学习史上的例外物种"——一个不会更新的智能体，在自然界从未存在过。

二、隐藏的跨领域连接：Big World Hypothesis 与热力学第二定律的镜像

Kurram 的"大世界假说"（Big World Hypothesis）表面上看只是在说"世界比模型复杂"，但它其实是认知领域的热力学第二定律：

  • 热力学第二定律说：任何封闭系统的熵必然增加，你无法在有限空间里维持完美秩序。
  • 大世界假说说：任何智能体的复杂度都小于世界的复杂度，你无法在有限权重里存下完整世界。

这带来一个惊人的推论——"合成数据"本质上是在造一个"熵较低的假世界"，让模型在其中训练，然后期望它能应对"真实的高熵世界"。这在物理上是 Maxwell 妖式的幻觉：你不可能通过一个更小的模拟系统来完全覆盖一个更大的真实系统。

再深一层：Sutton 说"世界包含许多其他心智，所以世界必然比你复杂"——这几乎是哥德尔不完备定理的智能体版本：一个系统无法完整建模包含自己的更大系统。合成数据的根本悖论，与"一个形式系统无法证明自己的一致性"，是同一种数学结构的两面。

三、被所有人忽略的战略暗流：现有大厂"回不去"了

访谈中最容易被略过、但商业含金量最高的一段是 Kurram 那句：

"大厂锁死在产品里，所以他们不可能走一条会先变差再变好的路。"

这不是技术判断，是组织进化论。它揭示了一个反直觉的市场结构：

  • OpenAI、Anthropic 越成功，就越不可能做 continual learning。
  • 因为 continual learning 要求"先允许模型退化，再迎接指数级增长"——这在有 KPI、有客户 SLA、有股价的组织里是政治自杀。
  • 于是最有资源的团队，反而最没有资格探索最重要的算法。

这与克里斯坦森的"创新者窘境"完美同构：磁盘行业的 IBM 无法做 5.25 英寸盘，柯达无法做数码相机，不是不知道，而是不能承受"暂时变差"。Sutton 和 Kurram 的赌注，本质上是在赌一个组织性套利：科学层面的洞见早已存在（"我们认识的人已经想了很多年"），但唯一能实施它的组织，必须是一个新的、小的、"能承受暂时难看"的团队。

一个惊人的推论：下一代 AI 突破的瓶颈，可能根本不是算法，也不是算力，而是"组织形态"——一个小到还有权失败的团队 + 一群还没被"scale 至上"世界观改造的头脑。这或许就是 Oak Lab "刻意保持极小规模"的深层原因——不是保守，而是一种认知隔离，避免被主流范式同化。

So, one of the things I like about what you're doing here is you're not just sitting around pontificating or lamenting the state of the world as it is. You're very actionoriented. It's why you've started a company. So, let's let's start talking about that a bit. Uh, in 2022, Rich, you laid out a very specific 12-point plan, the Alberta plan for AI research. Maybe tell us about that.

So the Alberta plan came about because we did have general ideas but we also needed to convert them into smaller chunks. So the 12 steps are an attempt to crystallize particular chunks. There's a very important early step two uh which is continual deep learning and we think that one is like almost the most important because it unlocks everything else. If you could do continual deep learning, you could then continually update your model of the world. And then if you knew how to do the abstraction rights and like the second half of of the the steps are all about how to get the abstractions right.

So, and not only by abstractions right, what do I mean by I don't mean get the right abstractions because no one can say what the right abstractions are. That depends on the world that you're in. Your agent would have to learn the correct abstractions for whatever world it's in. And so you know if you maybe those are the two key things you have to find the right abstractions and then you have to do able to do continual deep learning.

I think that a lot of the people in the field realize that we need models we need to plan with them but the abstractions tell us what the model should be conditioned on. So what should you what should the model predict? What are you going to do and then something is going to happen and more importantly where would that come from? So I really like the example of um elite athletes. If you ask elite athletes about how they do certain things, they would have weird niche terminologies for doing very specific things. They were like, you know, I do this thing and they would have a name for it. If they communicate, sometimes they don't even have a name for it if they're just doing it alone. So, how did they come up with those abstractions? That's in some sense a crucial thing that's missing that the later half of Alberta plan answers.

十三、Continual Deep Learning 的算法鸿沟

Can we talk about the continual deep learning part? Is it an algorithmic gap that exists today or is it a just a practical deployment infrastructure data privacy gap because if I wanted to do call it naive updating of weights based on user interaction I can do that today right and so what what in your opinion is the biggest thing that we're missing to kind of get to continual deep learning

yeah so it's absolutely an algorithmic gap you you can do the naive thing but then you'll see all sorts of problems so for example if you say um I'm going to take u one sample and then I'm going to update my whole model with that one sample. You will run into this problem that now all of the previous knowledge in the model it's impacted negatively.

And the way currently we we get around this is exactly what cursor does. They don't use one example. They use a large batch coming from a lot of users. So in use cases where you can have that you can do continual learning. Well most use cases you don't have that. Most use cases you have a single stream of data and then if you apply it do the naive thing it just completely destroys your prior knowledge in a very um destructive way

catastrophic forgetting. Yeah

that is the yeah

but it's totally curable [laughter] to have the right algorith yeah exactly what is it

well you know first you need to do what we call step size optimization and means every wade in your network has to have a separate step size. So somes will move fast, some will move slow and you will we you will have to metalarn the step sizes for each weight. Most of your network will be have have weights that have tiny step sizes. So then when you train on a new example, they don't get destroyed.

Happens just to the right places.

And then secondly, you have to use some form of generate and test um which is uh in feature space. So you come up with new features or new units and and without following gradients because gradients is a very slow process. You only move in a direction if you know it's the helpful one and uh that's always going to be very slow and doesn't give you a path to grow more and more complex and and to have sustained learning. You need to have something that just proposes a bunch of new units and uh and and and then goes from there I guess.

So there is a specific thing I can say to make it at least concrete which is to say we have this algorithm called continual backrop we used published in in nature a couple years ago and it is exactly like backrop but every but you also plant new seeds of units that are re newly initialized with random weights. Back prop only has random weights at the beginning of time and then as you go on all that randomness all that variety from the randomness gets used up and with continual backdrop you keep injecting a bit of randomness a bit of generate and test a bit of generate and then the the operation of backrop is the tester so you need you need that and and if you put those together really well I think you'll have a new generation of massively superior uh continual deep learning And that's what we hope to do in the next couple years.

Wonderful. Do you think that these algorithms can be applied to the current state of affairs with people scaling LLMs and trying to get them to do continual learning without catastrophic forgetting?

Yeah, absolutely. I think it's uh so I don't think that you could take an existing model and say I'm going to just start updating it with these algorithms because these algorithms metal learn how to learn. So really you have to say I'm going to learn from scratch. So let's say learn a new foundation model but I'm going to learn with this these new algorithms. These new algorithms in addition to learning the knowledge they're also going to learn how to learn future things. So they're learning two things at the same time and then u then I think you would be able to learn new things without catastrophic.

十四、Oak Lab 的野心：一个自洽的心智

Is that the most radical thing in that you're trying to do in your company in terms of from the current state of affairs to try to do these two things at the same time?

Most radical thing is I think that's

this goes back to I'm not crazy, everyone else is crazy. [laughter]

Yeah, that's perhaps not totally radical. There was a point in like 2016 to 2018 where a lot of people were exploring these ideas uh quite a bit. They were doing it in a much more limited setting. So they would say we have a distribution of problems and then in this specific case we'll do it whereas we want to do it from a single stream of experience. So our method should be more generally applicable. So I think many people have explored this but no one has explored this in the general setting where the resulting algorithm would be applicable everywhere.

So what would be the most radical thing that your company your new company is trying to do that other people are not doing?

What's the most ambitious thing? Remember I don't think I'm weird so I don't want to say what's the most ambitious most ambitious thing I think is to try to have the full spectrum of knowledge both about the tiny things and about the big things you know like thinking about how you take an airplane from one city to another that's a a very big you know it's it's more it's like your your uh space flight example but it's just kind of more common sensal to think about because we all Many of us take airplanes and all of us use abstractions in all kinds of our life and even even the squirrels use abstractions.

So to have that spectrum of of knowledge u from the small to the big and to treat it in a uniform way and to be able to have have it self uh maintaining. You know the big question is always you have your knowledgebased system and what keeps the knowledge in it correct? Well, what keeps the knowledge correct in a large language model is well, people did a lot of post-training and and they they they made it sure it was correct and then they freeze it after that. So that's what keeps it correct.

But really our minds we are we're always changing things and yet something keeps it organized and coherent and and and settling back into a good place rather than drifting off into crazy land. That is an I think our our biggest ambition to have a mind that is self-consistent and and can keep training itself and making it

coherent.

I love that.

十五、算力、Moore's Law 与"局部最优"陷阱

Can I ask it almost seems that it's it's such a ambitious vision and the idea that all these things can be unified into a single mind is so ambitious.

It's within reach. I think it's within reach. It's here it's 2026. Yeah. And our computers are so fast,

you know. Is it is it so ambitious it's out of reach uh or or do we have already inklings of how all the steps can be done and we I I think we have a vision and inklings um I don't think it's I don't think it's inappropriate

your vision involves a trillion parameter model with 20 watts that seems pretty ambitious

that is ambitious uh in some sense with current technology I would say it's also impossible Like just storing a trillion parameters in memory would probably use more than 20 watts of energy with memory technologies but we are really thinking of okay things are getting better computation is getting cheaper it is getting more energy efficient so where would be would be in 5 to 10 years and I think 5 to 10 years with the right algorithms and we can totally be in a world where this would be possible.

So 5 to 10 years is two orders of magnitude of Moore's law. It's a standard improvement. If we double every 18 months, 10 years would give you two orders of magnitude. And so for Kerm's statement to be plausible, then today you should be able to do it for for what? 20 watts, 200 magnitude,

2,000 watts. If you can do it with 2,000 watts today,

y

then in 10 years you'll be able to do it for 20 watts.

You think you can do it for 2,000 watts? You have

lots of people at research labs that have access to way more than that.

Yeah, I think we can can be more efficient than that even now with the right algorithm.

If we can be more efficient than that, then why aren't we? It's not like people just want to spend all their money, spend all our money.

Sometimes it seems like

all money. Sometimes [laughter] it seems like they want to.

Yeah, I I

doesn't it?

I think that's how they show they're they're real men by using lots of energy.

At least when I look at different research groups, I don't even see anyone believing in it's possible. And I think if you don't believe in it, you're just not going to work on the technical problems and work through them.

Is it that it's not possible or it's that there's so much waste in the system? Like one, which one is it? Like is is there someone who knows how to do it efficiently?

Yeah. And then there's 10 times the number of people in the same lab doing all these other things. And so nine out of 10 people are wasting in some sense. I the way I think about it is that we are stuck in a local menu. So if we want to move towards this new kind of algorithms, it is almost impossible that things will not get worse before they get better. So when we start exploring this new directions, you're not going to get state-of-the-art performance from day one. But it is because it is a different paradigm. Um but that path leads to similar performance at a higher energy and these big labs they are so locked into a product that they like it it is not possible for them to pursue a path where things get worse worse

because their current paradigm allows them to keep scaling and this new paradigm they have to take a bet and they

and they have to figure out some some technical things that are difficult that we have thought about it for many years. We know people who have thought about these things for many years and when I talk to them it makes sense that it's doable but you need to think about those challenges for a long period of time.

十六、如果一切成真：多个心智，多种未来

So if everything goes right with Oaks with the company what do you what kind of company are you building?

uh if everything goes right, we uh implement the architecture. We can have genuine uh continual learning and we can form abstractions so that we can do planning and reasoning and and we so sort of like true intelligence and then you know it's hard to imagine just exactly what will happen by then but I think

humans will become irrelevant. I

I don't think that's true at all. I I

we don't either. I think the world becomes exciting and and even more exciting and interesting and for humans but in particular I think there are the you have to wonder about the large language models they might be at risk uh when this eventually happens you know I'm sure they'll get a good run they've already had a good run you know they've been very successful and let me say just for for clarity that uh large language models are an amazing scientific breakthrough a breakthrough in the skill skillful use of language by neural networks.

It's totally unanticipated. You know, it was a it was always a hold out for uh symbolic methods in language and they they have totally changed how that's thought about now. Yeah, it's it's a big breakthrough. So, it's frustrating to me that we have to you don't just celebrate that we've made this great progress in this sub subset of the problem of AI and enjoy that. Instead, it has to pretend to be all of AI. All of intelligence is not fluid, capable use of language. There's so much more. It's an important part. You know, it's like 20% or a quarter of intelligence. There's there's more.

Yeah.

We're not done.

Yeah. If everything goes right, are you imagining that there's a single mind that can do everything from learn how to swing from tree branches to make a spaceship uh to you know all these various things we've talked about today. Is it a single mind and is it a single set of weights that can that can do all these things or is it

it's a single design?

Okay.

Many different there'll be many minds.

Okay. Okay, so it's a single design that reacts to different environments

and it it and different versions of that mind would learn different things because they have different experience. This sort of goes back to the big world hypothesis that there are infinitely many things to learn. So one system cannot learn infinitely many things and like I think rich already mentioned this but if you have two of these systems if you have two of the largest systems in the world then it is trivial that they cannot model each other because they are equally complex. So a single system would never be able to get to a point where it can learn everything. It would always be multiple systems that are learning from their own experience.

十七、招人策略：小而对齐

You guys are hiring. What kind of people are you looking for?

We are hiring uh the initial team most of it we already have in our mind. So these are people who have thought about these ideas in the p in many uh for a long time and we are going to take a slightly different approach because this is a different paradigm. It doesn't make sense to become large very quickly because uh in some sense everyone we hire has to uh come to see what we see and not everyone sees that. So we're going to start small slowly grow to maybe a handful or two or three uh and then go from there. We want to be super aligned.

Want to be super aligned

so that we can be u very productive working together and and scaling the progress.

Absolutely.

Very very cool. Wonderful. I loved this conversation. Thank you for taking the time to share what you're up to. You are, you know, an unusually deep thinker about where reinforcement learning and algorithmic design will go

and it was a true pleasure to get to explore it together with you today. So, thank you.

Thank you very much.

Our pleasure.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Sutton 不是激进派，LLM 才是"人类学习史的例外"
多数人把 Sutton 视为"叛逆者"——一个坚持古老强化学习旗帜、反对主流 LLM 范式的老学者。但他自己反复强调："**我不奇怪，是这个领域奇怪了**。" 这不是修辞，而是一个深刻的历史校准：
在几乎所有生物、儿童、动物的学习史中，"学习"从来不需要加"continual"这个前缀——因为**不存在"非持续的学习"**。是 LLM 时代创造了一个古怪的怪物：一个"学完就冻结、之后只会重复"的智能体，然后我们不得不发明"continual learning"这个词去描述"正常的学习"。
这就像我们不得不发明"面对面对话"来区别 Zoom——**语言的通胀，暗示着现实的畸形**。Sutton 真正的洞见是：LLM 不是 AI 的顶点，而是一个"**学习史上的例外物种**"——一个不会更新的智能体，在自然界从未存在过。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三段关于"隐形训练"的反常观察

一、真正的分界线不在训练里，而在"没人看见"的那一小时

大多数人以为冠军的秘密是"训练量大"——每天四五个小时、晨昏两练。但Khabib讲的最惊人的细节，其实是那第三次训练：深夜，父亲已经睡了，他偷偷打电话叫朋友开车带他去海边，跑一个半小时再溜回家。

注意这里的反常识：他不是在父亲的高压下多练，而是瞒着父亲多练。父亲代表"合理的、科学的训练计划"，而那第三次训练是逃离计划、逃离监督的产物。冠军的分水岭，不在教练能看见的地方，而在没有任何观众、没有任何记录、甚至违反教练意愿的那段时间。这也解释了一个吊诡：为什么许多训练系统完备、资源顶级的运动员反而拿不到金牌——因为可被观测的努力，天花板是一样的。

二、"想赢"和"想统治"是两个完全不同的物种——这个区分可以直接迁移到创业与写作

Khabib说了一句被中文解说常常忽略的关键话："There are athletes who simply want to win, and then there are some for whom victory isn't enough. They want domination."

这不是程度差异，是目标函数的差异。想赢的人，赢了就停；想统治的人，赢了反而更饥饿，因为"赢一次"证明的是可能性，而"统治"要求把可能性变成必然性。

跨领域连接一下： - 创业圈：PMF（product-market fit）之后就松懈的团队，是"想赢"型；PMF之后反而更疯狂扩张的团队（贝索斯的"Day 1"哲学），是"想统治"型。 - 写作与研究：写出一篇爆款就满足的作者，vs. 写出爆款后立刻觉得"这个还不够"的作者（村上春树每天准时四点起床跑步二十年）。 - 投资：巴菲特在已经"赢"了几十年之后，93岁还每天读年报——他要的不是赢，是让"赢"这件事变成一种物理规律。

一句话总结："想赢"是事件驱动，"想统治"是状态驱动。 前者有终点，后者没有。Khabib从不为某场比赛而训练——他为"永远不可被击败"这个状态而训练。

三、最反直觉的发现：Khabib的"疯"，本质上是一种成瘾模型，而不是意志力模型

我们通常把这种训练强度解读为"钢铁意志"，但仔细听他的原话："you have to be addicted to it" — 你得对它上瘾。

这里藏着一个被严重低估的真相：顶级表现者靠的不是意志力，而是把自己改造成一个"不训练就难受"的系统。 意志力是有限资源（Baumeister的自我损耗理论），每天消耗；而成瘾是自我强化的正反馈回路，越用越强。

这解释了为什么"自律"作为一种流行叙事在普通人身上几乎从不奏效——他们试图用有限的意志力对抗生理惰性。而Khabib的路径其实是结构性替代： - 父亲的晨祷把"清晨睡懒觉"这个选项从物理上删除了； - 童年的重复把训练变成像刷牙一样的无意识动作； - "hate to lose"不是情绪，是被反复烙进神经系统的厌恶反射。

于是他真正的秘密是：他从来不需要"决定"去训练。决定是消耗能量的，而习惯不是。

啊哈时刻：当他描述"我总觉得少了点什么"（something was missing），然后半夜爬起来去海边跑步——这不是纪律，这是戒断反应。他和那些晚上不喝酒就睡不着的人，在神经机制上是同一种人，只是成瘾对象不同。

这也是为什么"励志故事"从来不能复制冠军——你复制的是行为，而没有复制那套"不做就痛苦"的底层化学结构。要真正达到那个层次，需要的不是模仿他的日程表，而是问自己：什么东西，我不做就会难受？ 找到那个东西，才是起点。

📝 转录文本

训练的燃料：对失败的恐惧

So in all those hard training sessions, you were thinking about not losing. That's the fuel. The fuel. Four to five hours every single day. Every day.

与传奇摔跤手的偶遇

There is a story that I heard. Sadulaev, the legendary wrestler, told a story that he went to a hotel — I think it was in Moscow — to train in the gym, and he was the only one... it was during the night. I don't know. He was the only one who was there. And you came down and you actually trained together.

And he said a lot of great things about you. He said that you gave him some really deep wisdom which helped him to win the gold medal at the Olympic Games. I'm curious, could you tell us now what you told him? What kind of wisdom did you give him?

I can't remember exactly, but we had really great conversations.

It's a great story that the two of you — like two legends like that — just met completely by chance.

想赢 vs. 想统治

Well, look, he's a two-time Olympic champion. Right. Right. I think he doesn't skip his training either. He never missed one back then. I believe that we both ended up there because we both, you know, hate to lose, and we both really want to win.

And you know, recently I came across this idea. There are athletes who simply want to win, and then there are some for whom victory isn't enough. They want domination. I believe that he is one of those as well.

They want domination. And for that, what does a person have to do? They have to train. They have to grind morning and night.

父亲的"热身"：清晨的两小时

And there was this thing with us: after the morning... My father never let us sleep. When I say the morning, I mean after fajr, the dawn prayer. He just wouldn't sleep himself, so we couldn't either.

So every morning, 6, 7, we'd be out doing our warm-up. Some people might call it a warm-up, but when you show up at the stadium in the morning, you run 5 kilometers, you do sprints, you work with resistance bands, you work on the pull-up bar, you do push-ups, dips, jumps, you know, the bands, then work with the partner, drilling, and so on. That's about 2 hours of work. You drop two, two and a half kilos there.

Not really a warm-up, but father always called it that, right? That was a full morning training at 7:00 a.m.

一天三练：秘密的第三次训练

Then I came home to rest, and at 4:00 we'd head to the gym. The training would start at 5:00 and end at 7. By 8 I'd be home, and by 11 I'd rest up — and yet I kept thinking that something was missing.

Like, I know that I have a start, a competition coming up in like 40 or 30 days, and I would wake up and I'd be like, "Let me go to the sea. I'm going to go down to the sea, do some running, some sprints on the sand, work out," and so on. And so many times I ended up going out for a third training session as well.

Sometimes father would say rest — in the morning we're going to have a heavy workload. But sometimes I wouldn't tell father. I just go out at night, head out, and train. At night, when everyone's asleep, when nobody's around, I'd grab one of my close friends, give them a call, have them pick me up, then hop in the car, and head to the sea. I train for an hour or an hour and a half, come back, and crash. Next morning, I'd get up and start all over again. And just this routine, non-stop.

对普通训练态度的反驳

And when I see guys, you know, when they do just one training session, or like they say, "On Wednesday we have a morning training then an evening sauna session" — what do you mean? You have to fight in 50 days. You have a huge fight ahead and you want to take a rest in the middle of the week?

Well, rest on Sunday. On Saturday, do a morning training, hit the sauna in the evening, take a complete rest on Sunday, and start all over again on Monday. That was just my approach. Everyone does it differently. I don't know. I just think it has to be in your head. You've got to want it incredibly badly.

冠军的核心：狂热式的专注

So, you believe that to be a champion, you have to train like that. You have to be that serious.

For the majority of people, let's say, I believe that to be at the top — the top tier, right, one of the best in the world — a person has to always be, you know, a little bit — let's say just a little bit — crazy, but in a good sense of the word. You have to be addicted to it and to want this incredibly bad. You have to take a fanatical approach to the training process.

Just showing up and working out — that's what hundreds of thousands of guys are doing around the world. To stand out from that, from this crowd, let's say, who have the exact same goals as you do — to stand out from that, you have to take a fanatical approach to it.
